BALI_PRATIPADA.about: Bali Pratipada, the first day of Kartik's bright half and the day after the Diwali new moon, honours the demon king Bali. It recalls Vishnu, as the dwarf Vamana, sending Bali down to the underworld and granting him a day each year among his people. In Karnataka and Maharashtra his image is drawn or shaped and worshipped, and in Maharashtra, as Padva, husbands give their wives gifts.

HOLIKA.about: Holika Dahan is the bonfire lit on the night of Falgun's full moon, on the eve of the day of colours. It recalls the demoness Holika, who burned in the fire while the young devotee Prahlad, whom she held in her lap, came out unharmed. In the Terai and northern India wood and dung cakes are piled at the crossroads and burned after dusk, and the next day people play with colours.

UPAKARMA_MADHYANDINA.about: The Madhyandina Upakarma is the yearly renewal of Vedic study kept by Brahmins of the Shukla Yajurveda's Madhyandina and Kanva schools, the branch most of Nepal's Brahmins follow. It falls on the full moon of Shrawan, so in Nepal it is Janai Purnima itself. After a bath and the upakarma rite, with water offered to the sages, men put on a new sacred thread.

UPAKARMA_TAITTIRIYA.about: Taittiriya Upakarma is the yearly renewal of Vedic study kept by Brahmins of the Taittiriya branch of the Krishna Yajurveda, on the full moon of Shravan. After a purifying bath they offer water to the seers of the Veda, put on a new sacred thread, and begin the Veda's recitation afresh. In the south it is known by its Tamil name, Avani Avittam.

UPAKARMA_SAMAVEDI.about: The Samavedi Upakarma is the yearly renewal of Vedic study kept by Brahmins of the Samaveda. Unlike the Yajurvedis, who keep it on Shrawan's full moon, Samavedis keep it on the day the Moon is in the asterism Hasta during the bright half of Bhadra, judged by the afternoon. They bathe, perform the upakarma rite with offerings to the sages, and put on a new sacred thread.

PURNIMA_VRATA.about: The Purnima Vrata is the fast kept on the full moon of every lunar month, the intercalary month included. Nepal's national panchanga sets it on the day whose sunset the full moon holds, which can be the day before the full moon's own sunrise date. Those who keep it fast through the day, and many households hold the Satyanarayan puja and hear its story.

EKADASHI_SMARTA.about: The Smarta Ekadashi is the fast on the eleventh tithi of each fortnight as the Dharmasindhu sets it for the householder. The eleventh counts as pierced by the tenth only if the tenth holds sunrise, and the day is then chosen by which of the eleventh and twelfth outlasts the next sunrise. Vishnu is worshipped, and the fast is broken on the twelfth, at the parana.

EKADASHI_SMARTA_RENUNCIANT.about: The Renunciants' Ekadashi is the Smarta Ekadashi as the Dharmasindhu sets it for ascetics, forest-dwellers, widows, householders without worldly aims and those seeking release. It follows the householder's rule except where the eleventh runs past the next sunrise, or is pierced with neither tithi in excess; then these keepers fast on the later day. The fast is broken on the twelfth.

EKADASHI_VAISHNAVA.about: The Vaishnava Ekadashi is the eleventh-day fast as the Dharmasindhu sets it for Vaishnavas. Its test is stricter than the Smarta's: if the tenth tithi touches the eleventh's day even at arunodaya, about an hour and a half before sunrise, the eleventh is left and the fast moves to the next day. Vaishnavas worship Vishnu, often keep vigil, and break the fast on the twelfth.

EKADASHI_GAUDIYA.about: The Gaudiya Ekadashi is the eleventh-day fast as the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, followers of Chaitanya, keep it after the Hari Bhakti Vilasa. Like other Vaishnavas they leave an eleventh pierced by the tenth at arunodaya, and they also keep the eight great twelfths, the mahadvadashis, which can move the fast. They chant and sing kirtan, and break the fast on the twelfth.

JANMASHTAMI_VAISHNAVA.about: Vaishnava Janmashtami keeps Krishna's birth on the eighth of Bhadra's dark half by the Vaishnava rule, which sets aside an eighth that the seventh still touches at dawn, so it can fall a day after the Smarta date. Devotees fast until midnight, the hour of the birth, bathe and dress the image, and sing kirtan through the night. Vaishnava temples and the Gaudiya communities keep this date.

RAMA_NAVAMI_VAISHNAVA.about: Vaishnava Rama Navami keeps the birth of Rama on the ninth of Chaitra's bright half by the Vaishnava rule, which sets aside a ninth that the eighth still touches at dawn, so it can fall a day after the Smarta date. Vaishnavas fast through the day, worship Rama with Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman at midday, and read and sing the Ramayana.

NRISIMHA_CHATURDASHI.about: Nrisimha Chaturdashi, the fourteenth of Baishakh's bright half, marks the appearance of Vishnu as Nrisimha, the man-lion. It recalls how he burst from a pillar at dusk to kill the demon king Hiranyakashipu and protect the boy Prahlada. Vaishnavas fast until dusk, the hour of his appearance, then bathe his image and worship him.

RADHASHTAMI_VAISHNAVA.about: Vaishnava Radhashtami, the eighth of Bhadra's bright half, a fortnight after Janmashtami, keeps the birth of Radha, Krishna's beloved, by the Vaishnava rule for the tithi. Gaudiya Vaishnavas fast until midday, bathe and dress her image, and sing her praises; at Barsana in Braj, held to be her childhood home, pilgrims climb to her hilltop temple.

GAURA_PURNIMA.about: Gaura Purnima, the full moon of Falgun, marks the birth of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu at Navadvip in Bengal in 1486, during an eclipse of the moon, as his biographers tell it. Gaudiya Vaishnavas, who hold him to be Krishna himself, fast until moonrise, then feast, and spend the day in kirtan. In the days before, pilgrims at Mayapur walk the circuit of Navadvip's nine islands.

CHAITE_DASHAIN.about: Chaite Dashain, the eighth day of Chaitra's bright half, is the spring Dashain, half a year from the great Dashain of Ashwin. It falls in the Chaitra Navaratri and is given to Durga, whose Chandi is recited at the Dashain Ghar of Hanuman Dhoka from the first of the fortnight. Families worship the goddess at home and crowd her temples and shakti peeths, and some temples offer animal sacrifice.

SETO_MACHHINDRANATH_JATRA.about: Seto Machhindranath's chariot festival begins on Chaite Dashain, the eighth day of Chaitra's bright half. The white image of Karunamaya, Jana Baha Dyah, is brought from his temple at Jana Baha in Kathmandu and set on a tall chariot at Jamal. Over three days the chariot is pulled through Asan and Hanuman Dhoka to Lagan, with music and crowds along the way, and the god is then carried back to his temple.

PARASHURAMA_JAYANTI.about: Parashurama Jayanti, the third day of Baishakh's bright half, is the birthday of Parashurama, Rama with the axe, the sixth of Vishnu's ten avatars, a Brahmin sage who took up arms. It falls with Akshaya Tritiya, and the jayanti is kept on the day whose early evening, held to be the hour of his birth, has the tithi. Devotees fast, worship him at dusk and hear his story.

SHANKARACHARYA_JAYANTI.about: Shankaracharya Jayanti, the fifth day of Baishakh's bright half, honours Adi Shankara, the early medieval teacher of Advaita Vedanta, the doctrine that the self and Brahman are one, who is held to have founded four great monasteries in India. Monasteries of his order, Sanskrit schools and temples worship his image, recite his hymns and commentaries, and hold talks on his teaching.

GANGA_SAPTAMI.about: Ganga Saptami, the seventh day of Baishakh's bright half, recalls the rebirth of the river Ganga. It is told that the sage Jahnu, whose sacrifice her waters swept away, drank her up, and let her flow again from his ear, so that she is also called Jahnavi, Jahnu's daughter. Devotees bathe in the Ganga or another sacred river and worship the river goddess at midday.

SITA_NAVAMI.about: Sita Navami, the ninth day of Baishakh's bright half, is kept as the birthday of Sita, Rama's queen. The Ramayana tells that King Janaka of Mithila found her in the furrow as he ploughed the ground for a sacrifice, and so she is called a daughter of the earth. Devotees fast and worship Sita with Rama at midday, and the Janaki Mandir in Janakpur, Janaka's city, holds special worship.

KURMA_JAYANTI.about: Kurma Jayanti, the full moon of Baishakh, honours Kurma, the tortoise, the second of Vishnu's ten avatars. The Puranas tell that when the gods and the demons churned the ocean of milk for the nectar of immortality, Vishnu as a great tortoise bore the churning mountain, Mandara, on his back. Devotees fast and worship Vishnu; the day is also Buddha Jayanti.

DASHAHARA_SNANA_ARAMBHA.about: The Dashahara bathing begins on the first day of Jestha's bright half and runs for ten days, to Ganga Dashahara on the tenth. A bath on each of the ten days, in the Ganga or another sacred river, is held to wash away one of ten sins of body, speech and mind, which gives the observance its name. Pilgrims gather at rivers and confluences, and the bathing season at Gosainkunda opens on the same day.

GOSAIKUNDA_SNANA_ARAMBHA.about: On the first day of Jestha's bright half, with the Dashahara bathing, the bathing season opens at Gosainkunda, the high lake in Rasuwa held sacred to Shiva. It is told that Shiva struck the mountainside with his trident to make the lake and cool the poison he had swallowed. Through the ten days to Ganga Dashahara pilgrims climb to the lake to bathe; its larger fair comes at Janai Purnima.

KUMARA_JATRA.about: Kumar Jatra, the seventh day of Jestha's bright half, follows Sithi Nakha, kept as the birthday of Kumar, the warrior god Kartikeya, son of Shiva and Parvati. In Kathmandu his image is brought out of his shrine near Jaisidewal and carried on a peacock-shaped palanquin, his mount, through the old city's lanes to drums and cymbals, and then returned to the shrine.

GANGA_DASHAHARA.about: Ganga Dashahara, the tenth day of Jestha's bright half, recalls the descent of the Ganga from heaven to earth, brought down by the penance of King Bhagiratha. It closes ten days of bathing, and a bath on the day, in the Ganga or any sacred river, is held to remove ten kinds of sin. People bathe at rivers and confluences, worship the river with lamps and flowers, and give alms.

GOSAIKUNDA_SNANA_SAMAPTI.about: Ganga Dashahara, the tenth day of Jestha's bright half, closes the ten days of bathing at Gosainkunda, the sacred lake high in Rasuwa that opened with the Dashahara bathing. Pilgrims who have made the climb take their last bath in its cold water, worship Shiva at the lakeside shrine and begin the walk down; the lake's next great gathering comes at Janai Purnima.

NIRJALA_EKADASHI.about: Nirjala Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Jestha's bright half, is the strictest of the year's ekadashis: those who keep it go without food and even water from sunrise to the next sunrise. It is told that Bhima, who could not bear to fast on every ekadashi, was taught that this one fast would earn the merit of all of them. In Nepal tulsi sprigs are set in the household shrine on this day.

ANALA_PUNHI.about: Anala Punhi is the Newar name for the full moon of the intercalary month, anala, the month the lunar calendar inserts about once in three years to keep step with the Sun; in years without one there is no Anala Punhi. The extra month, also called Purushottam, is given over to the worship of Vishnu, to bathing and to charity, and its full moon is kept in that spirit.

DILA_CHARHE.about: Dila Charhe is the Newar name for the fourteenth day of Ashadh's dark half. The Newar year has twelve charhes, the dark fourteenths of its months, and each has a name of its own; this one comes a month before Gathamuga Charhe. Newar households mark the day with a puja at home, and the calendar prints it in parentheses as a Newar observance.

DURVA_ASHTAMI.about: Durva Ashtami, the eighth day of Bhadra's bright half, honours durva, the sacred grass offered in every puja. Women fast and worship durva with Shiva and Parvati for their families' long life. The Dharmasindhu keeps the fast only before the star Agastya rises, so in some years it moves to the eighth of Bhadra's dark half. In the far west it is the main day of Gaura, when women put on the durva thread.

AJA_EKADASHI.about: Aja Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Bhadra's dark half, is the ekadashi fast that comes three days after Krishna Janmashtami. Its story is told of King Harishchandra, who lost his kingdom, his wife and son and his freedom, and had them all restored after keeping this fast on a sage's advice. Devotees fast, worship Vishnu and hear the story, and break the fast the next morning.

CHATHA.about: Chatha is the Newar name for the night of the fourth of Bhadra's bright half, the night of Ganesh Chaturthi. It is told that Ganesh, mocked by the Moon, cursed it so that anyone who saw it that night would be falsely accused of theft. Newar families worship Ganesh with an evening puja at home and at his shrines, and many take care not to look at the moon.

GANESHA_CHATURTHI.about: Ganesh Chaturthi, the fourth day of Bhadra's bright half, is kept as the birthday of Ganesh, the elephant-headed god of beginnings and remover of obstacles. Devotees fast and worship him at midday with durva grass, red flowers and modak, and crowds visit his temples. In Maharashtra and much of southern India clay images are worshipped in homes and public halls for days and then immersed in water.

GAURA_SAPTAMI.about: Gaura Saptami, the seventh day of Bhadra's bright half, is the day Gaura is brought home in the Gaura festival of Nepal's far west. Women shape the goddess Gaura, Parvati, from grasses and grain stalks, carry her home to music and seat her beside Maheshwar, Shiva. They fast, worship the pair and the durva thread they will wear the next day, and the night is spent in Gaura songs and dances.

AMUKTABHARANA_SAPTAMI.about: Amuktabharana Saptami, the seventh day of Bhadra's bright half, is a vrata to Shiva and Parvati, Uma and Maheshwar, kept mainly by women for the welfare of their children. A thread offered to the divine pair is tied on the arm and worn as an ornament not to be taken off, which is what the name means. It falls on the day of Gaura Saptami.

VAMANA_DWADASHI.about: Vamana Dwadashi, the twelfth day of Bhadra's bright half, is kept as the birthday of Vamana, the dwarf, the fifth of Vishnu's ten avatars. The Bhagavata tells how he asked the demon king Bali for as much land as he could cover in three steps, then grew to span earth and heaven in two strides and set the third on Bali's head. Devotees fast, worship Vamana at midday and give alms.

PRATIPADA_SHRADDHA.about: Pratipada Shraddha, the first day of Ashwin's dark half, opens the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight given to the ancestors. Families whose father, mother or other forebear died on a first day give them shraddha now, whatever the month of the death. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

DWITIYA_SHRADDHA.about: Dwitiya Shraddha is the second day of the Sorha Shraddha, the ancestors' fortnight in Ashwin's dark half. On it families honour forebears who died on a second day, in any month of the year, for a shraddha follows the tithi of death, not its date. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

TRITIYA_SHRADDHA.about: Tritiya Shraddha, the third day of Ashwin's dark half, is the day of the ancestors' fortnight for forebears who died on a third day. The Newars of the valley also keep the day as Gatila. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

CHATURTHI_SHRADDHA.about: Chaturthi Shraddha, the fourth day of Ashwin's dark half, falls in the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight of the ancestors. It is the shraddha day for those whose father, mother or grandparents died on a fourth day of either half of any month. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

PANCHAMI_SHRADDHA.about: Panchami Shraddha, the fifth day of Ashwin's dark half, is a day of the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight of the ancestors. On it shraddha is given to forebears who died on a fifth day, the fortnight's day for each ancestor being the tithi of the death. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

SHASHTHI_SHRADDHA.about: Shashthi Shraddha, the sixth day of Ashwin's dark half, falls in the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight given to the ancestors before Dashain. Families whose forebears died on a sixth day of any month honour them on this day. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

SAPTAMI_SHRADDHA.about: Saptami Shraddha, the seventh day of Ashwin's dark half, is a day of the Sorha Shraddha, the ancestors' fortnight. It belongs to the forebears who died on a seventh day, in whichever month and half the death fell. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

ASHTAMI_SHRADDHA.about: Ashtami Shraddha, the eighth day of Ashwin's dark half, falls in the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight of the ancestors. On it families give shraddha to forebears who died on an eighth day of any month. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

NAVAMI_SHRADDHA.about: Navami Shraddha, the ninth day of Ashwin's dark half, is the Matri Navami of the ancestors' fortnight. Besides forebears who died on a ninth day, it is given to mothers and to women of the family who died while their husbands lived. Families offer pinda and tarpan in the afternoon with a priest's help, and feed Brahmins, among them married women.

DASHAMI_SHRADDHA.about: Dashami Shraddha, the tenth day of Ashwin's dark half, is a day of the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight given to the ancestors. Forebears who died on a tenth day, in any month, receive their shraddha on it. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

EKADASHI_SHRADDHA.about: Ekadashi Shraddha, the eleventh day of Ashwin's dark half, falls in the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight of the ancestors; it is also Indira Ekadashi. Families whose forebears died on an eleventh day give them shraddha on it. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

DWADASHI_SHRADDHA.about: Dwadashi Shraddha, the twelfth day of Ashwin's dark half, falls in the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight of the ancestors. Besides forebears who died on a twelfth day, it is the day the texts set for the shraddha of renunciants, sannyasis, whatever the day of their death. Families give pinda and tarpan in the afternoon and feed Brahmins and relatives.

TRAYODASHI_SHRADDHA.about: Trayodashi Shraddha, the thirteenth day of Ashwin's dark half, falls in the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight of the ancestors. It is the day for forebears who died on a thirteenth, and the same day is Kaliyugadi, held to begin the present age. Shraddha is given in the afternoon, the hour the texts set for it: rice balls, the pinda, and water with sesame, the tarpan, offered with a priest's help, after which Brahmins and relatives are fed.

CHATURDASHI_SHRADDHA.about: Chaturdashi Shraddha, the fourteenth day of Ashwin's dark half, is kept in the ancestors' fortnight only for those who died by weapons, by accident or by violence. Forebears who died naturally on a fourteenth are honoured on the new moon instead. The rite is an ekoddishta, a shraddha for one person, and it is given at midday rather than in the afternoon.

AMAVASYA_SHRADDHA.about: Amavasya Shraddha, the new moon of Ashwin's dark half, closes the ancestors' fortnight and is given to all the forebears, above all those whose day of death is not known; it is also called Pitri Visarjan, the ancestors' farewell. Families bathe at rivers and ghats and offer pinda and tarpan. In Bengal the day is Mahalaya, which opens the Durga Puja season.

SORHA_SHRADDHA_ARAMBHA.about: The Sorha Shraddha, the sixteen shraddhas, is the ancestors' fortnight, the pitri paksha, which begins on the first day of Ashwin's dark half and closes on its new moon, the eve of Dashain. Each family gives shraddha to every forebear on the tithi of the death; those who died by violence are honoured on the fourteenth, and the new moon serves for all whose day is not known.

KALI_YUGADI.about: Kaliyugadi, the thirteenth day of Ashwin's dark half, is one of the four yugadis, the days held to begin the four ages of the world, and is told as the first day of the Kali age, the present one. The Vishnu Purana commends shraddha on the yugadis, and families give this one in the afternoon together with the thirteenth's shraddha of the ancestors' fortnight.

UPANGA_LALITA_VRATA.about: Upanga Lalita Vrata, the fifth day of Ashwin's bright half, falls in the Navaratri of Dashain and is a fast to the goddess Lalita, Tripura Sundari. Devotees fast through the day and worship her in the afternoon, the time the Dharmasindhu sets for the rite, often with recitation of her thousand names. The day is also known as Lalita Panchami.

KUCHHI_BHOYE.about: Kuchhi Bhoye is the Newar feast of Maha Ashtami, the eighth day of Ashwin's bright half in Dashain, which the Newars call Mohani. The family sits down together on the floor in strict order of age, the eldest at the head, and eats from leaf plates beaten rice with lentils, meats, gundruk and other dishes. Rice is not cooked on the day, and the meal follows the household's worship of the goddess.

YAMAPANCHAKA_ARAMBHA.about: Yamapanchak, the five days of Yama, begins on the thirteenth of Kartik's dark half and runs to Bhai Tika: the festival of Tihar. Its first day, Kag Tihar, honours the crow, held to be the messenger of Yama, god of death, and food is set out for crows in the morning. The days that follow honour the dog, the cow and Lakshmi, the ox and Govardhan, and brothers.

DHANVANTARI_JAYANTI.about: Dhanvantari Jayanti, the thirteenth day of Kartik's dark half, honours Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, who the Bhagavata tells rose from the churned ocean of milk carrying the pot of nectar. He is held to be the source of Ayurveda, and on his day Ayurvedic physicians and colleges worship him in the morning and hold talks on the science. The day is also Dhanteras, the first of Tihar.

LAXMI_PRASAD_DEVKOTA_JAYANTI.about: Laxmi Prasad Devkota Jayanti is kept on Lakshmi Puja, the new moon of Kartik, for the poet was born on that night in 1909 and named for the goddess. Devkota, called the Mahakavi, the great poet, wrote Muna Madan and Shakuntal and did much to shape modern Nepali poetry. Writers, schools and literary bodies hold readings and talks and lay garlands at his statues.

HARIBODHINI_EKADASHI.about: Haribodhini Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Kartik's bright half, is the day Vishnu is held to wake from the four months' sleep he began on Harishayani Ekadashi, which ends the Chaturmas. Devotees fast and crowd his temples, Budhanilkantha and the four Narayans of the valley above all, and households marry the tulsi plant to Vishnu as Damodar.

BHISHMA_PANCHAKA_ARAMBHA.about: Bhishma Panchak, the last five days of Kartik, begins on Haribodhini Ekadashi and ends on the full moon. It is named for Bhishma, the Mahabharata's grandsire, told to have taught the Pandavas on these days as he lay on his bed of arrows. Devotees keep a five-day fast, some on fruit or milk alone, worship Vishnu and offer water to Bhishma.

TULASI_VIVAHA.about: Tulsi Vivah, the wedding of the tulsi plant, is kept in Nepal on Haribodhini Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Kartik's bright half, the day Vishnu wakes. The tulsi planted at Harishayani is married to Vishnu as Damodar, or as a shaligram stone, with the rites of a human wedding. In India the wedding is held on any day from the eleventh to the full moon.

PASHUPATI_HALESI_MELA.about: On the thirteenth of Mangsir's dark half, the eve of Bala Chaturdashi, fairs gather at Pashupatinath and at Halesi Mahadev, the cave shrine of Shiva in Khotang. Families who have lost someone in the year keep a vigil through the night at Pashupati with oil lamps, and the next morning scatter grain for the dead. In Jhapa the fairs of Satakshi Dham and Arjundhara fall on the same day.

BALA_CHATURDASHI.about: Bala Chaturdashi, the fourteenth of Mangsir's dark half, is the Newars' Bala Charhe, a day for the dead. After a night's vigil with lamps, families bathe in the Bagmati at Pashupatinath and walk through the forest of Mrigasthali and the temple grounds scattering satbij, seven kinds of grain, in memory of relatives who have died. The day is told in memory of a man named Bala.

DATTATREYA_JAYANTI.about: Dattatreya Jayanti, the full moon of Mangsir, is the birthday of Dattatreya, son of the sage Atri and Anasuya, a teacher-sage revered as one with Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva. It is kept on the day whose early evening holds the full moon. Devotees fast and worship him, and the old Dattatreya temple at Tachapal in Bhaktapur draws great crowds.

NUWAKOT_DUPCHESHWAR_MELA.about: The Dupcheshwar Mela is the great fair of Dupcheshwar Mahadev, a Shiva temple in the hills of Nuwakot, about sixty kilometres north of Kathmandu, which its devotees call a second Pashupati. The fair runs from the eleventh of Mangsir's bright half to the full moon, Dhanya Purnima, and its main day draws thousands of pilgrims, Hindu and Buddhist, to worship Shiva there.

PISHACHAMOCHANA_SHRADDHA.about: Pishachmochan Shraddha, the fourteenth day of Mangsir's bright half, is a shraddha at the Pishachmochan pond in Varanasi for relatives who died untimely deaths, by accident or violence. The Kashi Khanda tells that a restless spirit was freed there by bathing, which gave the pond its name. Pilgrims bathe and offer pinda and tarpan in the afternoon, so that such dead may find release.

GAIDU_PUJA.about: Gaidu Puja falls on the full moon of Mangsir, Dhanya Purnima, when the rice harvest is in. Families of the hills worship Gaidu, the guardian of the cattle, at the cowshed, together with their ancestors and household gods, and offer and eat dishes made from the new rice. The same full moon is Yomari Punhi for the Newars and Udhauli for the Kirat peoples.

PAUSHA_PUTRADA_EKADASHI.about: Pausha Putrada Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Poush's bright half, is the first of the year's two Putrada ekadashis, the givers of sons; the other falls in Shrawan. Its story is told of King Suketuman of Bhadravati, who had no heir until he kept this fast on the counsel of sages and was granted a son. Couples who wish for children keep the fast and worship Vishnu.

LAI_CHARHE.about: Lai Charhe is the Newar name for the fourteenth day of Magh's dark half, the charhe of the Newar month Pohela. Each of the twelve charhes, the dark fourteenths of the Nepal Sambat year, has a name of its own, and Lai Charhe falls between Dishi Charhe and Sila Charhe, the night of Shivaratri. Newar households mark it with a puja at home.

TILAKUNDA_CHATURTHI.about: Tilkunda Chaturthi, the fourth day of Magh's bright half, is a fast to Ganesh, also kept as his birthday, Ganesh Jayanti. Devotees fast through the day and worship Ganesh at dusk with sesame, til, and kunda, white jasmine, which give the day its name. They break the fast after the evening worship with sweets of sesame, and gifts of sesame are made to the poor.

BHIMA_EKADASHI.about: Bhima Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Magh's bright half, is named for Bhima, the second of the five Pandava brothers, who is told to have kept this fast and been freed by it of his debt to the ancestors. It is kept with fasting and the worship of Vishnu, and is held to bring both worldly good and release. In India the same day is called Jaya Ekadashi.

VIJAYA_EKADASHI.about: Vijaya Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Falgun's dark half, takes its name from victory. Its story is told of Rama, who, halted at the ocean's shore on his way to Lanka, kept this fast on the advice of the sage Bakadalbhya and went on to defeat Ravana. Devotees fast, worship Vishnu at a pot set up with grains for the rite, and break the fast the next morning.

SHILA_CHARHE.about: Shila Charhe is the Newar name for Maha Shivaratri, the fourteenth of Falgun's dark half, the charhe of the Newar month Sila. Newar families keep it as the rest of Nepal does, worshipping Shiva at home and at Pashupatinath. In the valley's courtyards fires are lit through the night, and children stretch ropes across the lanes to collect money for firewood.

DVAPARA_YUGADI.about: Dwaparyugadi, the new moon of Falgun's dark half, is one of the four yugadis, the days held to begin the four ages of the world, and is told as the first day of the Dvapara age. The Vishnu Purana names the new moon that closes Magh, as the texts count the months, among these days and commends shraddha and gifts on them, and families offer shraddha to the ancestors and give alms.

PAHAN_CHARHE.about: Pahan Charhe, the fourteenth of Chaitra's dark half, opens a three-day Newar festival of Kathmandu; the night is also called Pishach Chaturdashi, the night of the spirits. The city's mother goddesses, the Ajimas, are carried in palanquins to Asan and other squares, where they meet, and families invite married daughters and relatives to feasts. Ghode Jatra follows the next day.

MATSYANARAYANA_MELA.about: The Machhenarayan Mela, on the third day of Chaitra's bright half, Matsya Jayanti, is the fair of the Machhenarayan temple at Machhegaun, about eight kilometres southwest of Kathmandu, a shrine of Vishnu as the fish set in a pond. Devotees fast, bathe and worship there for the day. In a year with an intercalary month, a month-long fair is held at the temple through that month.

MATSYA_JAYANTI.about: Matsya Jayanti, the third day of Chaitra's bright half, honours Matsya, the fish, the first of Vishnu's ten avatars. The Bhagavata tells how a tiny fish asked King Satyavrata, the Manu, for shelter, grew to a vast size, and towed his boat, carrying the sages and the seeds of all life, through the great flood. Devotees fast and worship Vishnu in the afternoon.

VAISHAKHA_SNANA_ARAMBHA.about: The Baisakh bathing begins on the full moon of Chaitra and runs a lunar month, to the full moon of Baishakh. Through the month devotees bathe at dawn in a river or under a stone spout, worship Vishnu, and give water, fans and sandals against the summer heat, as the Vaishakha Mahatmya of the Skanda Purana commends. The same full moon draws bathers to Balaju's twenty-two spouts.

PRADOSHA_VRATA.about: Pradosha Vrata is a fast to Shiva kept on the thirteenth day of each half of the lunar month, on the day whose dusk, the pradosha, holds the tithi. Devotees fast through the day and worship Shiva in the period after sunset, when he is told to dance on Kailash. A pradosha that falls on a Monday or a Saturday is held especially fruitful and is named for the day.

MANGALA_CHATURTHI.about: Mangala Chaturthi is the fourth day of either half of the lunar month when it falls on a Tuesday, Mangalbar, the day of Mars. It is a fast to Ganesh, held especially fruitful for the coincidence of day and tithi. Devotees fast, worship Ganesh with red flowers, durva and sweets, and crowd his temples, among them the Ganesh shrines of the Kathmandu Valley.

RAVI_SAPTAMI.about: Ravi Saptami is the seventh day of either half of the lunar month when it falls on a Sunday, Aitabar, the Sun's own day. The seventh is the Sun's tithi, and the coincidence makes it a vrata to the Sun. Devotees bathe early, offer water, the arghya, to the rising Sun with red flowers and rice, and keep a fast or eat a single meal without salt.

BHAUMASHTAMI.about: Bhaumashtami is the eighth day of either half of the lunar month when it falls on a Tuesday, the day of Mars, Bhauma. The eighth is a tithi of the goddess, and the coincidence is kept as a fast to Durga in her forms, with prayers to Mars for planetary peace. In Gorkha it draws devotees to the temple of the goddess Gorakhkali.

BUDHASHTAMI.about: Budhashtami is the eighth day of either half of the lunar month when it falls on a Wednesday, the day of Mercury, Budha. It is kept as a fast, mainly by women, to the goddess Parvati and to Budha for the family's well-being, and its story is told in the Bhavishya Purana. Devotees fast, worship and hear the vrata's story, and the fast is held to ease Mercury's ill influence.

SOMAVATI_AMAVASYA.about: Somavati Amavasya is a new moon that falls on a Monday, Sombar, the Moon's day, a coincidence that comes only a few times a year. A bath in a river on it is held to be of great merit. Married women worship the pipal tree and walk around it, winding a thread, for their husbands' long life; others worship Shiva and offer tarpan and shraddha to the ancestors.

CHANDRODAYA.about: Chandrodaya, the moonrise of the second day of the bright half, marks the first evening of each lunar month on which the young crescent can usually be seen, low in the west just after sunset. The Dharmasindhu commends seeing the moon on this evening, and many Hindus look for the thin crescent and greet it with folded hands, as a sign of the month's growing light.

SANKASHTA_CHATURTHI.about: Sankashta Chaturthi is the monthly fast to Ganesha, remover of obstacles, on the fourth tithi of every dark fortnight. The day is the one whose moonrise the fourth holds, since the fast ends when the Moon comes up. Devotees fast through the day, worship Ganesha in the evening, offer arghya to the rising Moon, and then eat.

KARAKA_CHATURTHI.about: Karaka Chaturthi, known in northern India as Karva Chauth, is the fourth tithi of Ashwin's dark half by the month that ends at the new moon, Kartik's by the month that ends at the full moon. Married women fast from dawn without food or water for their husbands' long life, worship Shiva, Parvati and Ganesha with a spouted pot, the karaka, and break the fast after offering arghya to the risen Moon.

VRISHABHA_SANKRANTI.about: Vrishabha Sankranti is the Sun's entry into Taurus, which opens the month of Jestha, usually in mid-May. It is one of the four Vishnupadi sankrantis, with Simha, Vrishchika and Kumbha, whose holy period falls in the hours before the Sun crosses over. As at every sankranti, the devout bathe in a river and give gifts and alms.

MITHUNA_SANKRANTI.about: Mithuna Sankranti, around 15 June, is the day the Sun enters Gemini and the solar month of Mithuna begins, as the rains set in. In Odisha it is Raja Sankranti, the middle of the three days of Raja, when the earth is held to be menstruating and at rest: ploughing stops, and girls in new clothes play on swings and eat pitha.

KARKATA_SANKRANTI.about: Karkata Sankranti is the Sun's entry into Cancer, which opens the month of Shrawan, usually in mid-July. The calendar marks it as the start of Dakshinayana, the Sun's southward half of the year. People bathe and give alms, and in many hill homes burning torches are thrown out at dusk to drive away luto, the itch of the planting season.

SIMHA_SANKRANTI.about: Simha Sankranti is the Sun's entry into Leo, which opens the month of Bhadra, usually in mid-August. It is one of the four Vishnupadi sankrantis, whose holy period falls in the hours before the crossing. The devout bathe and give alms, and the same day the national panchanga lists local observances such as Kirtipur's Bagh Bhairav jatra.

KANYA_SANKRANTI.about: Kanya Sankranti is the Sun's entry into Virgo, which opens the month of Ashwin, usually in mid-September. In Nepal it is the day of the Vishwakarma Puja, when the divine craftsman is honoured in workshops, factories and offices, and tools, machines and vehicles are worshipped. The same day is kept as Vastu Diwas.

TULA_SANKRANTI.about: Tula Sankranti, around 17 October, is the day the Sun enters Libra. In Karnataka it is Kaveri Sankramana, the birth of the Kaveri: at Talakaveri in Kodagu, where the river rises, pilgrims wait at the sacred pool for the moment the spring wells up, the tirthodbhava, and carry its water home, and many bathe at Bhagamandala below.

VRISHCHIKA_SANKRANTI.about: Vrishchika Sankranti is the Sun's entry into Scorpio, which opens the month of Mangsir, usually in mid-November. It is one of the four Vishnupadi sankrantis, with Vrishabha, Simha and Kumbha, whose holy period falls in the hours before the Sun crosses over. The devout mark it with a bath and gifts to Brahmins and the poor.

DHANU_SANKRANTI.about: Dhanu Sankranti is the Sun's entry into Sagittarius, which opens the month of Poush, usually in mid-December. Poush is held unsuited to weddings and other auspicious rites, which wait until Maghe Sankranti a month later. The day itself is kept with a bath and alms, like every sankranti.

KUMBHA_SANKRANTI.about: Kumbha Sankranti is the Sun's entry into Aquarius, which opens the month of Falgun, usually in mid-February. It is the last of the four Vishnupadi sankrantis of the year, whose holy period falls in the hours before the crossing. A river bath and gifts to the needy mark the day.

MINA_SANKRANTI.about: Mina Sankranti is the Sun's entry into Pisces, which opens Chaitra, the last month of the Bikram Sambat year, usually in mid-March. Like Mithuna, Kanya and Dhanu it is a Shadashiti sankranti, whose holy period falls in the hours after the crossing. The devout bathe and give alms.

BAISAKH_SANKRANTI.about: Baisakh Sankranti is Mesha Sankranti named by its month: the Sun's entry into Aries on the first of Baisakh, in mid-April, which begins the Bikram Sambat year. It is a public holiday. People bathe, greet the new year and visit temples, and in Bhaktapur the Bisket Jatra fells the yosin pole and pulls Bhairav's chariot.

JESTHA_SANKRANTI.about: Jestha Sankranti is Vrishabha Sankranti named by the month it opens: the Sun's entry into Taurus on the first of Jestha, usually in mid-May. It is a Vishnupadi sankranti, its holy period in the hours before the crossing. The devout keep it with a bath and alms.

ASAR_SANKRANTI.about: Asar Sankranti is Mithuna Sankranti named by the month it opens: the Sun's entry into Gemini on the first of Asar, usually in mid-June, as the monsoon and the rice planting begin. It is a Shadashiti sankranti, its holy period in the hours after the crossing, and is kept with a bath and alms.

SAUNE_SANKRANTI.about: Saune Sankranti is the Nepali name for Karkata Sankranti, the first of Shrawan, when the Sun enters Cancer in mid-July and its southward half-year begins. In the hills, and above all in Karnali, families burn torches of straw or pine at dusk and throw them out of the house to cast off luto, the itch and sickness of the muddy planting season. The demon Kandakarna is worshipped the same evening.

SHRAWAN_SANKRANTI.about: Shrawan Sankranti is Karkata Sankranti named by its month: the first of Shrawan, in mid-July, when the Sun enters Cancer. The national panchanga marks it as the start of Dakshinayana and lists the Kandakarak puja the same day. It opens Shrawan, the month many devote to Shiva, and in the hills torches are thrown out at dusk to cast off luto.

BHADRA_SANKRANTI.about: Bhadra Sankranti is Simha Sankranti named by its month: the first of Bhadra, in mid-August, when the Sun enters Leo. It is a Vishnupadi sankranti, kept with a bath and alms. The national panchanga sets several local observances on it, among them Walke Parva and Kirtipur's Bagh Bhairav jatra.

ASHWIN_SANKRANTI.about: Ashwin Sankranti is Kanya Sankranti named by its month: the first of Ashwin, in mid-September, when the Sun enters Virgo. Across Nepal it is the day of the Vishwakarma Puja, when workshops, factories and drivers worship their tools, machines and vehicles. It is also kept as Vastu Diwas, the day of architecture and building.

KARTIK_SANKRANTI.about: Kartik Sankranti is Tula Sankranti named by its month: the first of Kartik, in mid-October, when the Sun enters Libra. With Mesha it is one of the two equinoctial sankrantis, the vishuva, held especially holy for bathing and giving. It usually falls in the season of Dashain and Tihar.

MANGSIR_SANKRANTI.about: Mangsir Sankranti is Vrishchika Sankranti named by its month: the first of Mangsir, in mid-November, when the Sun enters Scorpio. It is a Vishnupadi sankranti, its holy period in the hours before the crossing, and the devout mark it with a bath and alms as the rice harvest is brought in.

POUSH_SANKRANTI.about: Poush Sankranti is Dhanu Sankranti named by its month: the first of Poush, in mid-December, when the Sun enters Sagittarius. It opens a month held unsuited to weddings and other auspicious rites, which resume at Maghe Sankranti. The day is kept with a bath and alms, and the same date is National Flag Day.

MAGHE_SANKRANTI.about: Maghe Sankranti, Makara Sankranti, falls on the first of Magh in mid-January, when the Sun enters Capricorn and its northward half-year, Uttarayana, is reckoned to begin. It marks the turn from the cold months. People bathe at confluences such as Devghat, and families gather to eat sesame laddus, chaku, ghee, sweet potato and yam; it is also Maghi, the Tharu new year.

FALGUN_SANKRANTI.about: Falgun Sankranti is Kumbha Sankranti named by its month: the first of Falgun, in mid-February, when the Sun enters Aquarius. It is a Vishnupadi sankranti, its holy period in the hours before the crossing. A bath and gifts to the needy mark the day as the winter eases.

CHAITRA_SANKRANTI.about: Chaitra Sankranti is Mina Sankranti named by its month: the first of Chaitra, in mid-March, when the Sun enters Pisces and the last month of the Bikram Sambat year begins. It is a Shadashiti sankranti, its holy period in the hours after the crossing, and is kept with a bath and alms.

JANAI_PURNIMA.about: Janai Purnima, the full moon of Shrawan, is the day Hindu men who wear the sacred thread change it after a bath and the upakarma rite. Priests tie a protective doro on the wrists of all who come, and sisters tie rakhi on their brothers. Pilgrims climb to Gosainkunda and bathe at Kumbheshwar in Patan, and Newars eat kwati, a soup of sprouted beans.

RISHI_TARPANI.about: Rishi Tarpani is a name for Janai Purnima, the full moon of Shrawan, taken from the rite at its heart. In the upakarma that begins the year's Vedic study, Brahmins offer water to the sages who first heard the Vedas, the rishi tarpan, after a bath in a river or at home. They then put on a new sacred thread.

SARASWATI_PUJA.about: Saraswati Puja is Basanta Panchami named by its worship: the fifth day of Magh's bright half, given to Saraswati, goddess of learning, speech and the arts. Schools and colleges hold her puja, students set their books and pens before her, and small children are taught their first letters. Crowds visit her shrine at Swayambhu and other temples.

SHREE_PANCHAMI.about: Shree Panchami is another name for Basanta Panchami, the fifth day of Magh's bright half, which welcomes spring. The day honours Saraswati, goddess of learning, and is held auspicious for beginnings, so children start their letters and many choose it for weddings and the sacred-thread rite. Students worship the goddess at schools and temples.

DAHI_CHIURA_KHANE_DIN.about: Dahi Chiura Khane Din, the fifteenth of Asar in late June, is the day of curd and beaten rice in the middle of the rice-planting season. Farmers and townspeople alike eat dahi-chiura, and the planting is done with songs and play in the mud. Since VS 2062 the state has kept the same day as National Paddy Day.

GHYU_CHAKU_KHANE_DIN.about: Ghyu Chaku Khane Din, the day of eating ghee and chaku, is a name for Maghe Sankranti, the first of Magh in mid-January. Families gather to eat ghee, chaku made from boiled-down cane juice, sesame laddus, sweet potato and yam, foods held to warm the body in the cold. Married daughters often come home, and many bathe at the rivers.

UTTARAYANA_ARAMBHA.about: Uttarayana Arambha, the start of the Sun's northward half-year, is how the calendar names Makara Sankranti, the first of Magh in mid-January. The Sun's six months in the north are held auspicious, and the hours after the crossing are a holy period for bathing and giving. The day is kept as Maghe Sankranti, with river baths and winter foods.

DAKSHINAYANA_ARAMBHA.about: Dakshinayana Arambha, the start of the Sun's southward half-year, is how the national panchanga names Karkata Sankranti, the first of Shrawan in mid-July, when the Sun enters Cancer. The six months that follow are the gods' night in the old reckoning. The hours before the crossing are a holy period for bathing and giving alms.

LUTO_FALNE_DIN.about: Luto Falne Din, the day of throwing out the itch, is a name for Saune Sankranti, the first of Shrawan in mid-July. After weeks of planting rice in mud, families light torches of straw or pine at dusk and fling them out of the house or from the rooftops, calling on luto, scabies and sickness, to leave. The custom is strongest in Karnali and the western hills.

RASHTRIYA_EKATA_DIWAS.about: Rashtriya Ekata Diwas, National Unity Day, falls on the twenty-seventh of Poush, in January, the birth anniversary of Prithvi Narayan Shah, the king of Gorkha who unified the Nepali state in the eighteenth century. The day is kept with garlands at his statues and programmes on national unity. It has been listed as Prithvi Jayanti and made a public holiday again since VS 2080.

BUBAKO_MUKH_HERNE_DIN.about: Bubako Mukh Herne Din, the day of looking upon one's father's face, is Kushe Aunsi, the new moon of Bhadra, Nepal's Father's Day. Sons and daughters visit their fathers with sweets and gifts and receive their blessing. Those whose fathers have died perform shraddha, many at Gokarneshwar on the Bagmati, known as Uttar Gaya. Priests also gather kush grass that day for the year's rites.

UDHAULI_PARVA.about: Udhauli Parva, on the full moon of Mangsir, is the Kirat festival of the harvest and of the move down to warmer valleys before winter. Rai, Limbu, Yakkha and Sunuwar communities thank nature and their ancestors for the crops and dance the sakela, or sakewa, in great circles. The Ministry of Home Affairs gives Kirat communities a holiday for it.

GHYA_CHAKU_SALHU.about: Ghya Chaku Salhu is the Newar name for Maghe Sankranti, the first of Magh in mid-January: salhu is the first day of a solar month, and ghya and chaku are ghee and boiled-down cane sugar. Newar families eat ghee, chaku, sesame sweets and yam together and share them with married daughters and relatives.

BISKA_JATRA.about: Biska Jatra, Bisket Jatra, is Bhaktapur's new-year festival, nine days and eight nights around the first of Baisakh in mid-April. The chariots of Bhairav and Bhadrakali are pulled through the city in a tug of war between its upper and lower halves. On the year's last day a tall pole, the yosin, is raised, and its felling on the first of Baisakh marks the new year.

KWATI_KHANE_DIN.about: Kwati Khane Din, the day of eating kwati, is Janai Purnima, the full moon of Shrawan, which the Newars call Kwati Punhi. Families soak and sprout nine kinds of beans and cook them into kwati, a thick soup held to restore strength after the planting season. It is eaten the same day the sacred thread is changed.

SHATABIJ_ROPAN.about: Shatabij Ropan, the sowing of the hundred seeds, is the central rite of Bala Chaturdashi, the fourteenth of Mangsir's dark half. Families who lost someone in the year keep vigil with lamps at Pashupati through the night, then walk through the Mrigasthali forest scattering seven kinds of grain, the satbij, for the dead.

JANA_BAHA_DYAH_NHAVAN.about: Jana Baha Dyah Nhavan is the yearly public bath of Jana Baha Dyah, Seto Machhindranath, the white Karunamaya of Kathmandu, on the eighth day of Poush's bright half, in December or January. The image is brought out of its temple at Jana Baha in Kel Tole, bathed before crowds of Buddhists and Hindus, and freshly painted before it returns to its shrine.

PISHACHA_CHATURDASHI.about: Pishacha Chaturdashi, the fourteenth of Chaitra's dark half, is the night when spirits are held to roam, and the Newars keep it within Pahan Charhe. Food is set out for the spirits, and in Kathmandu Luku Mahadyo, a Shiva kept in a pit, is brought into the open and worshipped. The mother goddesses are carried in palanquins through the old city, and families invite married daughters to a feast.

NIMKO_PAAT_KHANE_DIN.about: Nimko Paat Khane Din, the day of eating neem leaves, is the first day of Chaitra's bright half, when the lunar year, the samvatsara, begins. The Dharmasindhu prescribes eating neem leaves that morning, after rubbing the body with oil and bathing, for health in the year ahead, and the calendar's yearly reading of the new year's planetary rulers is heard the same day.

JYOTISH_DIWAS.about: Jyotish Diwas, Astrology Day, is kept on the first day of Chaitra's bright half, the start of the lunar year, the samvatsara, which tradition holds to be the day creation and the reckoning of time began. Astrologers and the panchanga's makers mark it with gatherings and talks on Nepal's tradition of jyotisha, the astronomy and astrology behind the calendar.

MOHARATRI.about: Moharatri, the night of enchantment, is a name for the night of Krishna Janmashtami, the eighth of Bhadra's dark half, when Krishna's birth at midnight is recalled. Devotees fast through the day and keep vigil, singing bhajans until midnight, when Krishna is worshipped. In Patan the crowds gather at the Krishna Mandir in Mangal Bazaar.

SAPTARSHI_PUJA.about: Saptarshi Puja, the worship of the seven sages, is the heart of Rishi Panchami, the fifth of Bhadra's bright half and the last day of Teej. Women bathe in a river, brushing their teeth many times with stalks of the datiwan plant, then worship the seven sages and Arundhati. They keep a fast for purification from faults of the past year.

PAUSHE_AUNSI.about: Paushe Aunsi is the new moon that falls in the solar month of Poush, in December or January, the new moon of Margashirsha by the lunar month. The national panchanga names it Gaya Mauni Aunsi. Like every new moon it is a day for offerings to the ancestors, the darsha shraddha, and a river bath.

NAYA_BARSHA.about: Naya Barsha, New Year, is the first of Baisakh, in mid-April, when the Bikram Sambat year begins with the Sun's entry into Aries. It is a public holiday across Nepal. People exchange greetings, visit temples and relatives and go on outings, and in Bhaktapur the Bisket Jatra fells the yosin pole that evening.

NEPAL_SAMBAT_ARAMBHA.about: Nepal Sambat Arambha, the start of the Nepal Sambat year, falls on the first day of Kartik's bright half, during Tihar. The era is counted from 879 CE, and the state recognises it as a national era. Newar communities greet the year with processions and cultural programmes, and families perform Mha Puja, the worship of the self, the same evening.

YOSIN_THANEGU.about: Yosin Thanegu, the raising of the yosin, takes place in Bhaktapur on the last day of Chaitra, during Bisket Jatra. A tall wooden pole hung with two long banners is hauled upright with ropes at Yosinkhel by crowds of men. It stands through the night and is pulled down the next evening, on the first of Baisakh, to mark the new year.

LOKTANTRA_DIWAS.about: Loktantra Diwas, Democracy Day, falls on the eleventh of Baisakh, in late April. It recalls the night of Baisakh 11, VS 2063 (24 April 2006), when King Gyanendra restored the dissolved House of Representatives after nineteen days of mass protest, the second People's Movement. The day is kept with programmes honouring the movement and those who died in it.

CONSTITUTION_DAY.about: Constitution Day, Nepal's National Day, falls on the third of Asoj, in September. It recalls the promulgation of the Constitution of Nepal on Asoj 3, VS 2072 (20 September 2015), the first written by an elected Constituent Assembly, which made Nepal a federal democratic republic. It is a public holiday, marked by an official ceremony at Tundikhel and lights on buildings in the evening.

PRITHVI_JAYANTI.about: Prithvi Jayanti, kept also as National Unity Day, falls on the twenty-seventh of Poush, in January. It marks the birth anniversary of Prithvi Narayan Shah, the eighteenth-century king of Gorkha who unified the many principalities of the hills and the valley into the Nepali state. Garlands are laid at his statues, notably at Singha Durbar, and programmes are held on national unity; it is a public holiday.

EARTHQUAKE_SAFETY_DAY.about: National Earthquake Safety Day falls on the second of Magh, in mid-January. It recalls the great Nepal–Bihar earthquake of Magh 2, VS 1990 (15 January 1934), which destroyed much of the Kathmandu Valley and killed thousands. Government bodies, schools and civil groups hold drills, rallies and awareness programmes on building safely and preparing for earthquakes.

MARTYRS_DAY.about: Martyrs' Day falls on the sixteenth of Magh, in late January, closing the Martyrs' Week that begins on Magh 10. It honours those who gave their lives for democracy, above all Shukraraj Shastri, Dharmabhakta Mathema, Dashrath Chand and Gangalal Shrestha, executed by the Rana regime in VS 1997 (1941). Garlands are laid at the Martyrs' Memorial Gate in Kathmandu, and it is a public holiday.

DEMOCRACY_DAY.about: National Democracy Day falls on the seventh of Falgun, in February. It recalls Falgun 7, VS 2007 (18 February 1951), when King Tribhuvan proclaimed the end of the hundred-and-four-year rule of the Rana family and the start of democratic government in Nepal. It is a public holiday, marked by an official ceremony at Tundikhel.

SAMVATSARA_ARAMBHA.about: Samvatsara Arambha, the first day of Chaitra's bright half, begins the lunar year, which takes its name from the sixty-year cycle of Jupiter. In Nepal it opens the Chaitra Navaratri, and the reading of the new year's almanac is heard. Maharashtra keeps the day as Gudi Padwa, raising a pole dressed in silk at the door, and Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka as Ugadi.

GAURI_VRAT.about: Gauri Vrat, the third day of Chaitra's bright half, is a fast to Gauri, Parvati, kept by married women for a happy married life and by girls for a good husband. They worship Gauri with Shiva, offering vermilion, bangles and the other marks of a married woman. In Rajasthan, and among Marwari families in Nepal, the day is Gangaur, when images of the pair are carried in procession.

MAHAVIR_JAYANTI.about: Mahavir Jayanti, the thirteenth day of Chaitra's bright half, is the birthday of Vardhamana Mahavira, the twenty-fourth and last tirthankara of the Jains, born at Kundagrama near Vaishali. Jains visit their temples, bathe the image of the tirthankara, hear the Kalpasutra's account of his life, take out processions with his image and give to the poor.

BALAJU_BAISDHARA_MELA.about: The Balaju Baisdhara Mela, on the full moon of Chaitra, is the bathing fair at the twenty-two stone spouts, the Baisdhara, of Balaju on Kathmandu's northern edge; the Newars call the day Lhuti Punhi. Crowds bathe under the spouts from before dawn, a bath held to bring the merit of a pilgrimage to Gosainkunda, and worship the reclining image of Vishnu in the garden.

HANUMAN_JAYANTI.about: Hanuman Jayanti, the full moon of Chaitra, is kept as the birthday of Hanuman, the monkey god, son of the wind god and Rama's devoted servant in the Ramayana; some regions keep the birthday on other days. Devotees fast, visit his temples, offer him vermilion and oil and recite the Hanuman Chalisa and the Sundara Kanda of the Ramayana.

CHANGUNARAYAN_CHHINNAMASTA_KILESHWOR_MUL.about: This jatra, on the new moon of Baishakh's dark half, is the main day of the Khat Jatra of Changu in Bhaktapur district, which runs over several days to Akshaya Tritiya. The palanquins of Changunarayan, the old Vishnu temple on its hill, of Kileshwor Mahadev and of the deities of the Chhinnamasta shrine are carried on shoulders through the village to music, with lamps lit at night.

MATA_TIRTHA_AUNSI.about: Mata Tirtha Aunsi, the new moon of Baishakh's dark half, is Nepal's Mother's Day, called looking upon the mother's face. Sons and daughters visit their mothers with sweets, fruit and gifts and touch their feet. Those whose mothers have died bathe at the ponds of Matatirtha, west of Kathmandu, and offer shraddha there, and a fair gathers at the spot.

RATO_MACHHINDRANATH_RATHAROHAN.about: Rato Machhindranath Ratharohan, the first day of Baishakh's bright half, is the day the red Karunamaya, the rain god of Patan and Bungamati, is set on his towering chariot at Pulchowk, after his ritual bath and renewal. The ascent opens Patan's longest festival: over the weeks that follow the chariot is pulled through the city to Jawalakhel, where the Bhoto Jatra ends it.

AKSHAYA_TRITIYA.about: Akshaya Tritiya, the third day of Baishakh's bright half, is held to make whatever is begun or given on it akshaya, undecaying. It is also counted the first day of the Treta age and Parashurama's birthday. People give water, sattu and fans against the heat, worship Vishnu and begin new ventures, and in India buying gold on the day is widespread.

TRETAYUGADI.about: Tretayugadi, the third day of Baishakh's bright half, is one of the four yugadis, the days held to begin the four ages of the world, and is told as the first day of the Treta age. It falls on Akshaya Tritiya. The Vishnu Purana commends shraddha and gifts on the yugadis, and families offer shraddha to their ancestors and give alms.

PASHUPATINATH_DAMAN_PUSHPARPAN.about: On the eighth day of Baishakh's bright half sprigs of damanaka, a fragrant southernwood, are offered to Pashupatinath. The texts prescribe offering damanaka to the gods in the spring months, each god on a tithi of his own, and treat the offering as completing the year's worship. At Pashupati the herb is offered to the god in a special puja and devotees come for his darshan.

MOHINI_EKADASHI.about: Mohini Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Baishakh's bright half, is named for Mohini, the enchantress Vishnu became when the ocean of milk was churned, to take the nectar of immortality from the demons and give it to the gods. The fast is told to have been kept by Rama on Vasishtha's advice. Devotees fast, worship Vishnu and break the fast the next morning.

BAISAKH_SNAN_ENDS.about: The full moon of Baishakh closes the month of Baisakh bathing that began at the full moon of Chaitra. Those who have kept the month take a last bath at dawn, worship Vishnu, and finish with gifts of water pots, fans, sandals and food, the gifts the Vaishakha Mahatmya commends for the hot season. The same full moon is Buddha Jayanti.

CHANDI_PURNIMA.about: Chandi Purnima, the full moon of Baishakh, is the day the Kirat peoples call Chandi, when Ubhauli, their spring festival, begins. Rai, Yakkha and Sunuwar communities worship nature and their ancestors and dance the chandi, the sakela, in great circles for health and good crops. In Banepa the same full moon begins the Chandeshwari Jatra, with the goddess's chariot pulled through the town.

GORAKHNATH_JAYANTI.about: Gorakhnath Jayanti, the full moon of Baishakh, honours Gorakhnath, the medieval yogi held to have founded the Nath order, the disciple of Matsyendranath. In Nepal he is linked with the shrine at Mrigasthali beside Pashupatinath and with Gorkha, which is named for him. Nath yogis and devotees worship at his shrines and sing his hymns; some Nath lineages do not keep a birthday for him.

APARA_EKADASHI.about: Apara Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Jestha's dark half, takes its name from apara, boundless, for the merit it is held to give. Its story is told of King Mahidhvaja, murdered by his younger brother and left a restless spirit, until the sage Dhaumya kept this fast on his behalf and freed him. Devotees fast, worship Vishnu as Trivikrama and break the fast the next morning.

SHANI_JAYANTI.about: Shani Jayanti, the new moon of Jestha's dark half, is kept as the birthday of Shani, Saturn, the son of the Sun and Chhaya. Shani is held to bring hardship to those under his influence, and on his day devotees fast and visit his shrines, offering mustard oil, black sesame, black cloth and iron, and pray that his hard influence be eased.

KUMAR_SHASHTHI.about: Kumar Shashthi, the sixth day of Jestha's bright half, is kept as the birthday of Kumar, Kartikeya, the war god and son of Shiva and Parvati, who is worshipped on the sixth. In the Kathmandu Valley the same day is the Newar festival of Sithi Nakha. Devotees visit Kumar's shrines with offerings, and households clean their wells and water spouts and share a meal of bara and other dishes.

SITHI_NAKHA.about: Sithi Nakha, the sixth day of Jestha's bright half, is a Newar festival of the Kathmandu Valley that falls on Kumar Shashthi and marks the coming of the monsoon and the planting season. Neighbourhoods clean their wells, ponds and stone spouts before the rains, Kumar is worshipped, and families gather for a feast of bara and other dishes. Many Newar families hold no weddings or new undertakings again until after the rains.

GANGA_PUJA.about: Ganga Puja, on the tenth day of Jestha's bright half, the Dashahara, honours the Ganga, whose descent from heaven to earth the day recalls. Devotees bathe in the Ganga or another river, which the texts hold to wash away ten kinds of wrongdoing, and worship the river with flowers, lamps and food, often in sets of ten. The same day is kept as Rameshwar Puja.

GURU_PADMASAMBHAVA_JAYANTI.about: Guru Padmasambhava Jayanti honours Padmasambhava, Guru Rinpoche, the eighth-century tantric master held to have brought Buddhism to Tibet. The national panchanga marks it on the tenth day of Jestha's bright half; many Tibetan Buddhist communities keep his birthday on the tenth of the sixth Tibetan month. Followers visit monasteries and his caves at Pharping, recite his prayers and hang prayer flags.

RAMESHWAR_PUJA.about: Rameshwar Puja, on the tenth day of Jestha's bright half, the Dashahara, honours Shiva as Rameshwar, the lord worshipped by Rama. The linga of Rameshwaram on the southern coast of India is told to have been installed by Rama on this day, before or after his war with Ravana. Devotees bathe, as on Ganga Puja the same day, and worship Shiva with water, bel leaves and flowers.

JYA_PUNHI.about: Jya Punhi is the Newar name for the full moon of Jestha, the full moon of the Newar month Jya. It is the main day of the jatra of Panauti, the old town at the meeting of the Roshi and Punyamati rivers in Kavre. The chariots of Indreshwar Mahadev, Bhadrakali and the town's other deities are pulled through its streets and raced, and families welcome relatives to feasts.

KABIR_JAYANTI.about: Kabir Jayanti, the full moon of Jestha, is kept as the birthday of Kabir, the fifteenth-century weaver-poet of Varanasi whose verses mock empty ritual and caste and speak of a formless God. His followers in the Kabirpanth, and many others, gather to sing his dohas and hymns, hear talks on his teaching and hold processions, especially in Varanasi and at Maghar, where he died. Bihar keeps it as a holiday.

MASTA_PURNIMA.about: Masta Purnima is the name the national panchanga gives the full moon of Jestha for the worship of Masto, a family of clan and village gods of far-western and Karnali Nepal, kept in districts such as Bajhang, Bajura, Achham and Jumla. Masto is worshipped at village shrines through a dhami, an oracle who speaks for the god, and families bring offerings there on the god's days.

BHAL_BHAL_ASHTAMI.about: Bhal Bhal Ashtami is the eighth day of Ashadh's dark half. In Bhaktapur it closes the year's cycle of the Navadurga, the masked dancers who embody the city's goddesses: they perform for the last time and withdraw until the cycle resumes. In Deopatan the same day brings the Trishul Jatra of Pashupati's area.

DEOPATAN_TRISHUL_JATRA.about: The Deopatan Trishul Jatra, on the eighth day of Ashadh's dark half, Bhal Bhal Ashtami, is a festival of Deopatan, the old settlement around the Pashupatinath temple. Shiva's trident, the trishul, is carried in procession through the locality with music, past shrines such as those of Bhuvaneshwari and Jayabageshwari, and residents and devotees worship along its route.

JAGANNATH_RATH_JATRA.about: The Jagannath Rath Jatra, on the second day of Ashadh's bright half, is the chariot festival of Jagannath, a form of Krishna, at Puri in Odisha. Jagannath, his brother Balabhadra and sister Subhadra are brought out of the temple and drawn on three huge wooden chariots by crowds to the Gundicha temple, returning about nine days later. Many towns in India hold their own chariot processions on the day.

DEOPATAN_GANGAMAI_RATH_JATRA.about: The Deopatan Gangamai Rath Jatra, on the seventh day of Ashadh's bright half, is a chariot festival of the Pashupatinath area in Kathmandu. An image of Ganga, the river goddess, is set on a chariot and pulled through Deopatan's streets with music, as residents and devotees worship her along the way. The procession is held as a prayer for good rains in the planting season.

SURYA_PUJA.about: Surya Puja, on the seventh day of Ashadh's bright half, is a worship of the Sun, Surya, on the tithi the texts give him. The texts name this seventh Vivasvat Saptami, after one of the Sun's names. Devotees bathe early, offer water mixed with red sandal, flowers and rice to the rising Sun, and many keep a fast or take a single meal without salt.

CHATURMAS_BEGINS.about: Chaturmas, the four months, begins on the eleventh day of Ashadh's bright half, Harishayani Ekadashi, and lasts until Haribodhini Ekadashi in Kartik. The period recalls Vishnu's sleep on the serpent Shesha. Householders take vows to give up chosen foods or habits for the season, ascetics stay in one place through the rains, and weddings and other rites of passage are not held.

HARISHAYANI_EKADASHI.about: Harishayani Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Ashadh's bright half, is told as the day Vishnu lies down to sleep on the serpent Shesha in the ocean of milk, to wake four months later on Haribodhini Ekadashi. It begins the Chaturmas. Devotees fast, worship Vishnu and lay his image to rest, and many take the season's vows. The Padma Purana tells its story of King Mandhata and a drought.

DAKSHINAMURTI_PUJA.about: Dakshinamurti Puja, on the full moon of Ashadh, honours Shiva as Dakshinamurti, the teacher, who is shown seated under a banyan tree facing south and teaching the sages through silence. The day is Guru Purnima, the full moon of teachers, and Shiva is worshipped in this form as the first guru. Students and devotees worship him and honour their own teachers.

DILLA_PUNHI.about: Dilla Punhi is the Newar name for the full moon of Ashadh, the full moon of the Newar month Dilla, the same day as Guru Purnima. Newar Buddhists recall on it the Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath, the Dharma Chakra Pravartana, and honour their teachers. It falls on the eve of Gunla, the Newar Buddhist holy month, which begins with the next new month.

GURU_PURNIMA.about: Guru Purnima, the full moon of Ashadh, is the day of teachers, also called Vyasa Purnima after the sage Vyasa, who is told to have arranged the Vedas and composed the Mahabharata. Students visit their teachers with flowers, fruit and gifts, receive tika and blessings, and schools hold programmes; disciples honour their spiritual gurus. Buddhists recall the Buddha's first sermon on the same full moon.

KAMIKA_EKADASHI.about: Kamika Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Shrawan's dark half, is the first ekadashi after the Chaturmas begins. Its mahatmya, told as Krishna's words to Yudhishthira, praises the worship of Vishnu with tulsi leaves on this day and the lighting of lamps before him. Devotees fast, offer tulsi and lamps to Vishnu and break the fast the next morning.

GUNLA_BEGINS.about: Gunla, the holy month of the Newar Buddhists, begins on the first day of Shrawan's bright half and lasts a lunar month. It recalls the rains retreat that the Buddha's monks kept. Through the month devotees walk to Swayambhu at dawn, many with bands playing the month's own music, recite and hear the scriptures, keep fasts, and make images of the stupa from clay.

DHAPAKHEL_NAGDAHA.about: The Dhapakhel Nagdaha fair, on Nag Panchami, the fifth day of Shrawan's bright half, is held at the Nagdaha pond of Dhapakhel in Lalitpur, which is held to be the home of a naga, a serpent god. Devotees come on the day to worship at the pond, offering durva grass, milk and rice, and a fair gathers on its banks.

NAG_PANCHAMI.about: Nag Panchami, the fifth day of Shrawan's bright half, honours the nagas, the serpent gods of water and rain, who are held to guard the home. Households paste a printed picture of the nagas above their doors with cow dung, worship it with milk, rice, flowers and sacred thread, and set out milk for the serpents. In Kathmandu worship is held at the pond of Nag Pokhari.

TULSIDAS_JAYANTI.about: Tulsidas Jayanti, the seventh day of Shrawan's bright half, is kept as the birthday of Goswami Tulsidas, the sixteenth-century poet-saint who retold the Ramayana in Awadhi as the Ramcharitmanas. His devotees read and sing the Ramcharitmanas, worship Rama, and hold gatherings and talks on his work, especially in Varanasi, where he lived and wrote.

YALA_PANCHADAN.about: Yala Panchadan, on the eighth day of Shrawan's bright half, is the Panchadan, the festival of five gifts, of Patan, which the Newars call Yala. Households give grain, rice, salt, money and fruit to Shakya and Bajracharya priests and monks who go from door to door, recalling the alms given to the Buddha. Images of Dipankara Buddha are set out in the city's courtyards.

SHRAWAN_PUTRADA_EKADASHI.about: Shrawan Putrada Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Shrawan's bright half, is the second of the year's two Putrada ekadashis, the givers of sons; the other falls in Poush. Its story is told of King Mahijit of Mahishmati, who had no son until his subjects kept this fast on the sage Lomasha's advice and gave him its merit. Couples who wish for children fast and worship Vishnu.

KWATI_PUNHI.about: Kwati Punhi is the Newar name for the full moon of Shrawan, Janai Purnima, named for kwati, a soup of nine or more sprouted beans that is eaten on the day. In the Kathmandu Valley farming families set out food for the frogs in the rice fields, thanking them for their part in bringing the rains, and households take the protective thread on the same day.

SANSKRIT_DAY.about: Sanskrit Day, on the full moon of Shrawan, honours the Sanskrit language, the language of the Vedas and of much of South Asia's classical learning. The day was chosen because the full moon of Shrawan traditionally began the year's Vedic study with the Upakarma. Schools, Sanskrit colleges and universities in Nepal and India hold recitations, lectures and programmes in the language.

ROPAI_JATRA.about: Ropai Jatra, the second day of Bhadra's dark half, the day after Gai Jatra, is a Newar festival of rice planting in the Kathmandu Valley. Groups dressed as farmers act out the planting in procession, tossing mud and seedlings at one another and at onlookers, with music and songs of the planting season, as thanks for the harvest to come.

CHANDRA_SHASHTHI.about: Chandra Shashthi, the sixth day of Bhadra's dark half, is a fast kept mainly by mothers for the long life and health of their children. They fast through the day and, when the moon rises late in the night, offer it water, flowers and fruit and break the fast. In parts of India the same tithi is Hal Shashthi, the birthday of Balarama, Krishna's brother.

GUGA_NAVAMI.about: Guga Navami, the ninth day of Bhadra's dark half, honours Guga, also called Goga or Gugga Pir, a warrior hero of Rajasthan revered by Hindus and Muslims alike as a protector against snakebite. It is kept mainly in Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab and Himachal Pradesh, and among communities from there. Devotees visit his shrines, offer milk and sweets, and fairs are held at his tomb at Gogamedi.

KUSHE_AUNSI.about: Kushe Aunsi, the new moon of Bhadra's dark half, is Nepal's Father's Day, called looking upon the father's face. Sons and daughters visit their fathers with sweets and gifts and touch their feet. Those whose fathers have died bathe at Gokarna, northeast of Kathmandu, and offer shraddha there. Priests gather kush grass on the day for the rites of the year ahead.

MOTIRAM_JAYANTI.about: Motiram Jayanti, kept on Kushe Aunsi, the new moon of Bhadra's dark half, marks the birthday of Motiram Bhatta, born in VS 1923, the poet and editor who brought Bhanubhakta Acharya's Ramayana into print and wrote the first biography of him. Literary societies and schools hold readings of his ghazals and poems and programmes on his work, and garland his portrait.

GUNLA_ENDS.about: Gunla, the holy month of the Newar Buddhists, ends on the first day of Bhadra's bright half, a lunar month after it began. The closing days bring the month's last walks to Swayambhu with music, and the month's devotions, the dawn visits, fasts, recitations and the making of clay stupas, come to a close with worship and offerings.

DAR_KHANE_DIN.about: Dar Khane Din, the second day of Bhadra's bright half, is the eve of Haritalika Teej, the day of the dar feast. Married women return to their parents' homes, and women gather in red saris to eat a rich meal together before the next day's fast without water. They sing Teej songs and dance late into the night, songs that often speak of their lives and hardships.

SURYA_SHASHTHI.about: Surya Shashthi, the sixth day of Bhadra's bright half, is a fast to the Sun, Surya. Devotees bathe early, fast through the day, and offer water, flowers and fruit to the Sun. In Varanasi the same tithi is Lolark Shashthi, when couples who wish for children bathe at the Lolark kund, a well sacred to the Sun.

ADUKHA_NAVAMI.about: Adukha Navami, the ninth day of Bhadra's bright half, comes in the week after Teej and takes its name from a-dukha, without sorrow. Married women keep a fast to Gauri, Parvati, for a life free of grief and for their husbands' well-being. Men whose wives have died make gifts on the day to a married woman, in their wife's memory.

HARIPARIVARTINI_EKADASHI.about: Hariparivartini Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Bhadra's bright half, is told as the day Vishnu, asleep since Harishayani Ekadashi, turns from one side to the other in the middle of the Chaturmas. Its mahatmya links the day with Vishnu's dwarf avatar, Vamana, and the demon king Bali. Devotees fast, worship Vishnu and break the fast on Vamana Dwadashi, the next day.

INDRADHWAJA_UTTHAN.about: Indradhwaja Utthan, the twelfth day of Bhadra's bright half, is the raising of Indra's banner pole, the yosin, that opens Indra Jatra in Kathmandu. A tall pine trunk, cut with rites in the forest and dragged into the city, is raised at Hanuman Dhoka with Indra's banner, and it stands there through the eight days of the festival.

ANANTA_CHATURDASHI.about: Ananta Chaturdashi, the fourteenth day of Bhadra's bright half, honours Vishnu as Ananta, the endless, resting on the serpent Shesha. Devotees fast and worship him, then tie a thread of fourteen knots, dyed with turmeric, on the arm for a year's protection. In Maharashtra the day closes Ganesh Chaturthi with the immersion of his images, and Digambara Jains end the ten days of Das Lakshan Parva.

BHAKTAPUR_SIDDHA_POKHARI_MELA.about: The Siddha Pokhari Mela, on the full moon of Bhadra, is a fair at Siddha Pokhari, the large old pond at the western entrance of Bhaktapur, also called Indradaha. People gather at the pond on the day, take a ritual bath and worship at its shrines, and light lamps in memory of family members who have died in the past year.

CHONAM_PARVA.about: Chonam is the main festival of the Chepang people of the hills of Makwanpur, Chitwan, Dhading and Gorkha, a harvest festival of the new crops. The national panchanga places it on the full moon of Bhadra; since VS 2068 the Chepang community has fixed its main celebration on 22 Bhadra. The first of the new harvest is offered to the ancestors and to nature by the pande, the Chepang priest, before families eat it.

INDRADAHA_SNAN.about: Indradaha Snan, on the full moon of Bhadra, is the bathing fair at Indradaha, a pond in the hills of Chandragiri, southwest of Kathmandu, held to be linked with the god Indra. Devotees keep a night vigil at the pond with lamps lit for their ancestors, bathe in it at dawn, and worship Indra and Ganesh at its shrines.

INDIRA_EKADASHI.about: Indira Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Ashwin's dark half, falls within the Sorha Shraddha, the fortnight of the ancestors. Its story is told of King Indrasena of Mahishmati, who learned from the sage Narada that his father suffered after death, and freed him by keeping this fast and giving him its merit. Devotees fast and worship Vishnu, and offer shraddha for their ancestors.

MAGHA_SHRADDHA.about: Magha Shraddha falls in the ancestors' fortnight on the thirteenth of Ashwin's dark half, when the Moon stands in or near the nakshatra Magha, the asterism whose deities are the pitris, the ancestors themselves. A shraddha given in the fortnight under Magha is held to be especially welcome to them, so families add it to the day's rite, offering pinda and tarpan in the afternoon.

AVIDHAVA_NAVAMI.about: Avidhava Navami, the ninth day of the fortnight of the dead in the dark half of Ashwin, is set aside for the shraddha of women who died before their husbands. The family offers pinda and water to the mother and the other women of the line who died married, and feeds Brahmins and a married woman in their name.

SANYASI_MAHALAYA.about: Sanyasi Mahalaya, or Yati Mahalaya, the twelfth day of the fortnight of the dead in the dark half of Ashwin, is set aside for the shraddha of renunciants, the sanyasis, and of those who took renunciation before death. Their disciples and families honour them on it and feed ascetics and Brahmins in their name.

BHARANI_SHRADDHA.about: Bharani Shraddha falls on the day of the fortnight of the dead, in the dark half of Ashwin, when the Moon stands in the asterism Bharani, whose deity is Yama. A shraddha offered on it, the Maha Bharani, is held to be as meritorious as one offered at Gaya, and many families keep it for all their dead, some especially for those who died in the past year.
