PACHALI_BHAIRAV_JATRA.about: The Pachali Bhairav Jatra, on the fifth day of Ashwin's bright half during the Dashain Navaratri, is the festival of Pachali Bhairav, a fierce guardian form of Shiva whose shrine stands near the meeting of the Bagmati and Vishnumati at Teku in Kathmandu. Devotees gather at the shrine with offerings and sacrifices, the god is honoured with a procession, and families feast.

BILVA_NIMANTRAN.about: Bilva Nimantran, on the evening of the sixth day of Ashwin's bright half during Dashain, is the invitation to the bel tree. Priests and households worship a bel tree, the wood-apple sacred to Shiva and the goddess, and invite Durga to dwell in it; the next morning a branch is cut and brought in as part of the Phulpati. The rite is marked wherever the sixth falls at dusk, which can move it by a day.

BUDDHAVATAR.about: Buddhavatar, marked on the ninth day of Ashwin's bright half, recalls the Buddha as the ninth of Vishnu's ten avatars, as the Puranas count them. The Bhagavata names the Buddha among Vishnu's descents, born in the age of Kali. Devotees who keep the day worship Vishnu in this form; it falls on Maha Navami, in the midst of Dashain.

MAHA_NAVAMI.about: Maha Navami, the ninth day of Ashwin's bright half, is the last day of the Navaratri and of the worship of Durga as Siddhidatri. In Nepal animals are sacrificed to the goddess, the Taleju temple of Kathmandu opens to the public, and tools, weapons and vehicles are worshipped. In South India the day is Ayudha Puja, in Bengal the last day of Durga Puja, and in the north girls are worshipped as the goddess.

SYAKWA_TYAKWA.about: Syakwa Tyakwa is the Newar name for Maha Navami, the ninth day of Ashwin's bright half, within Mohani, the Newar Dashain. The name speaks of the day's many sacrifices: households offer ducks, chickens and goats to the goddess, or gourds and other offerings in their place, and worship their tools, weapons and vehicles. The meat of the offerings is shared in a family feast.

DEVI_VISARJAN.about: Devi Visarjan, the tenth day of Ashwin's bright half, Vijaya Dashami, is the farewell to the goddess Durga, worshipped through the Navaratri. In Bengal, Bihar and other parts of India her clay images are carried in procession and immersed in rivers and ponds. In Nepal the goddess called into the kalash is bid farewell with rites at an auspicious hour, before tika is received from elders.

KHADGA_JATRA.about: Khadga Jatra, the sword procession, is held on the tenth day of Ashwin's bright half, Vijaya Dashami, in Newar towns of the Kathmandu Valley, among them Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur and Kirtipur. Men dressed as gods and goddesses carry swords through the streets, re-enacting the goddess's victory over the demons. In Bhaktapur a priest carries the sacred sword from the Taleju temple.

PAPANKUSHA_EKADASHI.about: Papankusha Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Ashwin's bright half, falls the day after Vijaya Dashami; its name means a goad against sin. Its story is told of Krodhana, a cruel fowler of the Vindhya hills, who near his death sought out the sage Angiras, kept this fast on his advice and was freed of his sins. Devotees fast, worship Vishnu as Padmanabha and break the fast the next morning.

KHANCHI_SARAI_PARVA.about: Khanchi Sarai Parva, the thirteenth day of Ashwin's bright half, brings the sarai to Khanchikot in Arghakhanchi in the days after the Dashain tika. The sarai is a warriors' dance of the western hills, danced with swords, shields and spears to the naumati band, and it is told as recalling the battles of the old hill kingdoms.

ARGHA_SARAI_PARVA.about: Argha Sarai Parva falls on the full moon of Ashwin, the last day of Dashain, when the sarai is danced at Argha in Arghakhanchi, where local tradition holds the dance began at the old palace. Dancers carrying swords, shields and spears move to the naumati band before large crowds, and the dance bids farewell to Dashain.

KARTIK_SNAN_BEGINS.about: Kartik Snan, the month-long vow of bathing in Kartik, begins on the full moon of Ashwin and runs to the full moon of Kartik. Those who keep it, many of them women, bathe before dawn each day in a river or at a temple's spout, worship Vishnu, light lamps and keep to a restricted diet for the whole month.

KATIN_PUNHI.about: Katin Punhi is the Newar name of the full moon of Kaula, the month of Ashwin in Nepal Sambat, the same night as Kojagrat Purnima. It closes Mohani, as the Newars call Dashain, and as elsewhere in Nepal the night is kept for Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth, with worship and a vigil.

RADHASHTAMI.about: The national panchanga names the eighth day of Kartik's dark half Radhashtami. Vaishnavas keep it as the day of Radha Kund, the pond at Govardhan in Braj held sacred to Radha, and bathe there at midnight; in northern India the same day is Ahoi Ashtami, when mothers fast for their children. Radha's birthday itself falls in Bhadra.

RAMA_EKADASHI.about: Rama Ekadashi is the eleventh day of Kartik's dark half, a few days before Tihar, and takes its name from Rama, Lakshmi. Those who keep it fast and worship Vishnu, breaking the fast on the twelfth. Its mahatmya in the Padma Purana is told of Shobhana, the son-in-law of King Muchukunda, who won a kingdom by its fast.

DHANTERAS.about: Dhanteras, or Dhanatrayodashi, is the thirteenth day of Kartik's dark half, two days before Lakshmi Puja. It is kept as the birthday of Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, and at dusk a lamp is set out for Yama. Families buy metal vessels, gold or silver for good fortune, a custom of northern India that is now widely kept in Nepal.

KAG_TIHAR.about: Kag Tihar, the first day of Tihar, falls on the thirteenth day of Kartik's dark half and honours the crow, held to be the messenger of Yama. In the morning rice and sweets are set out for the crows on rooftops and leaf plates, so that no grief comes to the house in the year, and lamps are lit in the evening.

SWONTI_CHARHE.about: Swonti Charhe is the Newars' charhe of the month of Kaula, the fourteenth of Kartik's dark half, which falls within Swonti, the Newar Tihar. The Newars mark the fourteenth of the dark half of every lunar month as a charhe, a day of worship at home; this one coincides with Narak Chaturdashi and Kukur Tihar, amid Swonti's lamps.

NARAK_CHATURDASHI.about: Narak Chaturdashi, the fourteenth day of Kartik's dark half, recalls Krishna's killing of the demon Narakasura. In India many bathe with oil before dawn and light lamps that evening, and in the south it is the main day of Deepavali. In Nepal it is the day of Kukur Tihar, when dogs are honoured with a tika and garland.

HALI_TIHAR.about: Hali Tihar, the ploughmen's Tihar, falls on the first day of Kartik's bright half with Goru Puja and Govardhan Puja. Farmers rest their oxen and ploughs for the day, honour the oxen with tika and garlands and feed them well, and the hali, the ploughmen, are themselves feasted and given gifts by the households they work for.

GOPASHTAMI.about: Gopashtami, the eighth day of Kartik's bright half, honours the cow and those who tend her. It recalls the day Krishna is told to have been first sent out with the cows as a cowherd. Cows and calves are bathed, decorated and worshipped, fed grass and sweets, and in some places the cowherds are honoured too and the cows walked round in procession.

SILANGA_MAHARUDRA_KOTIHOM_MELA.about: The Maharudra Kotihom Mela is held at Silanga in Baitadi, in Nepal's far west, on the eighth day of Kartik's bright half, among the many temple fairs of Baitadi in that fortnight. Devotees gather through the night before and the day at the shrine of Shiva as Maharudra, where the koti homa, the great fire offering, gives the fair its name.

HETAUDA_KUSHMANDA_SAROBAR_MELA.about: The Kushmanda Sarobar Mela is held on Kushmanda Navami, the ninth day of Kartik's bright half, at the Kushmanda Sarobar Triveni Dham in Hetauda, Makwanpur, a pilgrimage site of the goddess Kushmanda. Pilgrims bathe at the pond and its spouts, give ash gourds in gift, and join the fire offerings and bhajans of the fair.

KUSHMANDA_NAVAMI.about: Kushmanda Navami, the ninth day of Kartik's bright half, takes its name from the kushmanda, the ash gourd, and is also called Akshaya Navami. After a bath, an ash gourd with coins or gold hidden inside is given to a Brahmin, and the amla tree is worshipped, in which Vishnu is said to dwell from this day to the full moon. Gifts on the day are held to bring merit that never wanes.

SAKWO_CHANGU_WONE.about: Sakwo Changu Wone, Newar for 'Sankhu's going to Changu', falls on the ninth day of Kartik's bright half. The people of Sankhu, in the north-east of the Kathmandu valley, go up to the hilltop temple of Changunarayan to worship Vishnu there, and a fair is held at the temple, which the national panchanga names the Sankhu-Changu fair.

SATYAYUGADI.about: Satyayugadi, the ninth day of Kartik's bright half, is held to be the day the Satya yuga, the first and best of the four ages, began; it is one of the four yugadi days. Like the others it is kept with a bath, a shraddha for the ancestors and gifts, which the texts say bring merit that does not wane. It falls on the day of Kushmanda Navami.

BALAMBU_MAHALAXMI_JATRA.about: Balambu's Mahalaxmi Jatra, in the west of the Kathmandu valley, reaches its main day on the tenth day of Kartik's bright half, soon after the Newar new year. The Newars of Balambu cook their festival foods from the eighth, and on the tenth, after a Kumari puja, the chariots of Mahalaxmi and Ganesh are carried through the town.

FULKHARKA_GANGAJAMUNA_MELA.about: The Gangajamuna Mela is held at Phulkharka in northern Dhading at the turn of the tenth and eleventh days of Kartik's bright half, as Haribodhini Ekadashi begins. Pilgrims from many districts bathe beneath the Gangajamuna waterfall and worship the goddess Gangajamuna Mai; the rural municipality of Gangajamuna takes its name from the fair.

CHANGUNARAYAN_AKHANDA_DEEP_DARSHAN.about: On the evening of the twelfth day of Kartik's bright half a great lamp, the akhanda deep, is lit at the temple of Changunarayan above Bhaktapur and kept burning through the night into the next day. Crowds come to see it, many for relatives who died in the year, in the belief that the sight of the lamp eases the passage of the dead.

SHIVA_BAIKUNTHA_CHATURDASHI.about: Baikuntha Chaturdashi, the fourteenth day of Kartik's bright half, is the one day Vishnu and Shiva are worshipped together. It recalls Vishnu's worship of Shiva at Kashi with a thousand lotuses; on this day tulasi, Vishnu's leaf, is offered to Shiva and bel, Shiva's leaf, to Vishnu. Devotees fast, light lamps and visit the temples of both.

CHATURMAS_ENDS.about: The national panchanga closes the Chaturmas, the four months of Vishnu's sleep, on the full moon of Kartik. The vows that began on Harishayani Ekadashi in Ashadh, such as giving up a food, keeping a daily reading or eating once a day, are brought to an end with worship of Vishnu, a bath and gifts to Brahmins, and weddings and other rites may again be held.

KARTIK_SNAN_ENDS.about: Kartik Snan, the month of dawn bathing begun on the full moon of Ashwin, ends on the full moon of Kartik. Those who kept the vow take a last bath, worship Vishnu and give gifts to Brahmins and the poor to bring it to a close, and the lamps raised on poles through the month are lit for the last time.

THANKOT_MAHALAXMI_JATRA.about: Thankot's Mahalaxmi Jatra, at the foot of Chandragiri on the valley's western edge, is held on the first day of Mangsir's dark half, the day after Kartik's full moon. The Newars of Thankot carry the chariots of the goddess Mahalaxmi and of Ganesh through the town's streets to music, throwing vermilion as the procession goes.

GUHYESHWARI_JATRA.about: Guhyeshwari Jatra is held at the temple of Guhyeshwari by Pashupatinath on the ninth and tenth days of Mangsir's dark half. The image of Taleju Bhavani is brought from Hanuman Dhoka for secret tantric worship at Guhyeshwari, and then taken back by chariot through Pashupati to Basantapur, with music and a company of the Nepali Army.

UTPATTIKA_EKADASHI.about: Utpattika Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Mangsir's dark half, is the ekadashi of origins. Its story tells how a goddess sprang from Vishnu's body as he slept and killed the demon Mura, and was named Ekadashi and granted that her day's fast would free from sin. For that reason many begin a vow of keeping every ekadashi from this one.

BALA_CHATURDASHI_BALA.about: Bala Chaturdashi, the fourteenth day of Mangsir's dark half, is kept at Pashupatinath for relatives who have died. Families keep vigil there through the night before with lamps, bathe in the Bagmati at dawn, and walk through the Shleshmantak forest scattering satbij, seven kinds of grain, for the dead. Many keep it at Arjundhara in Jhapa as well.

SHADANANDA_JAYANTI.about: Shadananda Jayanti, on Vivah Panchami, the fifth day of Mangsir's bright half, remembers Bala Guru Shadananda, the lifelong brahmachari of Dingla in Bhojpur. He is remembered as a scholar and reformer who opened a school in Dingla open to all communities in the Rana era and spoke against sati; Shadananda municipality bears his name.

VIVAH_PANCHAMI.about: Vivah Panchami, the fifth day of Mangsir's bright half, recalls the wedding of Rama and Sita in Janakpur, the city of Sita's father, King Janaka. Janakpur keeps it with a week of festivities: Rama's image is brought in a wedding procession to the Janaki temple, the wedding rites are re-enacted, and pilgrims come from Nepal and India.

BAKHUMADA.about: Bakhumada, on the eighth day of Mangsir's bright half, opens the Satgaule Jatra, the festival of the seven villages around Kirtipur, south-west of Kathmandu. Its goddesses, held to be the children of Vishnudevi of Balkhu, are carried in chariots on successive days: Nagaon's on the eighth, Panga's on the ninth and Kirtipur's on the tenth.

PANGA_VAISHNAVI_DEVI_JATRA.about: Panga's jatra of the goddess Vaishnavi, Vishnudevi, falls on the ninth day of Mangsir's bright half, within the Satgaule Jatra of the seven villages around Kirtipur. The Newars of Panga bring Vishnudevi and Balkumari out of the temple in the village's central square and carry them through Panga in their chariots, and families feast their guests.

KIRTIPUR_INDRAYANI_JATRA.about: Kirtipur's Indrayani Jatra falls on the tenth day of Mangsir's bright half and closes the Satgaule Jatra of the seven villages around Kirtipur. The goddess Indrayani is carried from her shrine below the old town in a chariot through Kirtipur's streets, and families invite relatives from other towns to the feast.

GITA_JAYANTI.about: Gita Jayanti, the eleventh day of Mangsir's bright half, marks the day Krishna is held to have spoken the Bhagavad Gita to Arjuna on the field of Kurukshetra. It falls on Mokshada Ekadashi, so many fast, and the Gita is recited at temples and in homes, often from beginning to end, with talks on its teaching.

MOKSHADA_EKADASHI.about: Mokshada Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Mangsir's bright half, is the ekadashi said to give release. Its mahatmya tells of King Vaikhanasa, who kept its fast to free his father from suffering after death, so the day's merit is often offered to the ancestors. It falls with Gita Jayanti, and those who keep it fast, worship Vishnu and break the fast on the twelfth.

DHANYA_PURNIMA.about: Dhanya Purnima, the grain full moon, is the full moon of Mangsir, when the rice harvest has been brought in. The new rice is offered in thanks and cooked for the household; for the Newars it is Yomari Punhi, and the Kirat peoples begin Udhauli on the same day. The state's holiday notices name the day with Udhauli and Yomari Punhi.

YOMARI_PUNHI.about: Yomari Punhi, the Newar name of Mangsir's full moon, celebrates the rice harvest. Yomari, steamed dumplings of new rice flour filled with chaku and sesame, are made in every house, offered to Annapurna and the household gods, and eaten with family; children go from house to house singing for yomari, and the day is a holiday in the Kathmandu valley.

SAFALA_EKADASHI.about: Safala Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Paush's dark half, is the ekadashi that is said to make all undertakings bear fruit, safala. Its mahatmya tells of Lumpaka, a king's exiled son, who kept its fast and vigil unknowingly in the forest and was restored to his kingdom. Those who keep it fast, worship Vishnu, keep vigil and break the fast on the twelfth.

GAYA_MAUNI_AUNSI.about: Gaya Aunsi, the new moon of Paush, is a day for the shraddha of the ancestors, named after Gaya in Bihar, the great place of offerings to the dead. In Nepal crowds gather at Gokarneshwar in Kathmandu and other riverside tirthas to bathe and offer pinda to three generations of ancestors, and many go to Gaya itself to make the offering there.

TOL_LHOSAR.about: Tol Lhosar, held to be the oldest of the Lhosars, falls on the first day of Paush's bright half, a month before Sonam Lhosar. It is the new year of the high valleys of Humla, Jumla, Dolpa, Mugu and Manang: houses are cleaned, people bathe for purity, tsampa is offered at the household shrine, the elders give their blessing and the family feasts.

SETO_MACHHINDRANATH_SNAN.about: Seto Machhindranath Snan, Jana Baha Dyah Nhawan, falls on the eighth day of Paush's bright half. The white image of Karunamaya, Avalokiteshvara, is brought out into the courtyard of Jana Baha in Kathmandu and bathed before the crowds by the priests, and is then repainted and restored; his chariot festival follows in Chaitra.

CHANGUNARAYAN_KALASH_JATRA.about: Changunarayan's Kalash Jatra falls on the full moon of Paush, the day the Swasthani fast begins. Priests carry silver images of Changunarayan, Lakshmi and Saraswati and a kalash of holy water from the hilltop temple above Bhaktapur to Hanuman Dhoka, where the kalash is worshipped in Taleju's precinct before the Kumari, and then take it back to Changu.

MAGH_SNAN_BEGINS.about: Magh Snan, the month of bathing in Magh, begins on the full moon of Paush and runs to the full moon of Magh. Those who keep it bathe each morning before sunrise in a river or at a confluence, worship Vishnu as Madhava and give alms; in the Kathmandu valley many bathe at the Shali river at Sankhu and at the ghats of the Bagmati.

SWASTHANI_VRAT_BEGINS.about: The Swasthani Vrata, the month-long worship of the goddess Swasthani, begins on the full moon of Paush. In homes across Nepal a chapter of the Swasthani Vrata Katha, the goddess's story with the tales of Shiva and Parvati, is read aloud each evening for a month, and many women keep a fast, eating one pure meal a day; at Sankhu devotees bathe each morning in the Shali river.

SHATTILA_EKADASHI.about: Shattila Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Magh's dark half, is the ekadashi of the six uses of sesame, tila. Those who keep it use sesame in six ways: in the bath and in an unguent, in the fire offering, in water offered to the ancestors, in food, and in gifts. They fast, worship Vishnu and break the fast on the twelfth.

ARYAGHAT_MADHAV_NARAYAN_MELA.about: The Madhav Narayan Mela is held at Aryaghat, the riverside ghat of Pashupatinath on the Bagmati, on the new moon of Magh, in the middle of the month of the Madhav Narayan vow and the Swasthani reading. Those keeping the month's vow come to bathe in the Bagmati and worship Madhav Narayan, Vishnu, and a fair gathers on the banks.

SKANDA_SHASHTHI.about: The national panchanga marks Skanda Shashthi on the sixth day of Magh's bright half. The sixth of the bright half is held sacred to Skanda, Kartikeya, the son of Shiva and Parvati and the commander of the gods' army, and those who keep the day fast and worship him; in the Tamil south his great Skanda Shashthi falls in the autumn.

ACHALA_SAPTAMI.about: Achala Saptami, the seventh day of Magh's bright half, is also called Ratha Saptami and Surya Jayanti, and is kept for the Sun, whose chariot is said to turn north on this day. Before sunrise devotees bathe in a river with leaves of the arka plant on the head and limbs, offer arghya to the rising Sun and give gifts.

BHISHMASHTAMI.about: Bhishmashtami, the eighth day of Magh's bright half, is held to be the day Bhishma, the grandsire of the Mahabharata, gave up his life on his bed of arrows after waiting for the Sun's northward course. As Bhishma left no sons, the texts ask all to offer him tarpana, water with sesame, on this day, and some keep a fast.

BHISHMA_DWADASHI.about: Bhishma Dwadashi, the twelfth day of Magh's bright half, follows Jaya Ekadashi and closes the days named for Bhishma that begin with Bhishmashtami. It is kept with the worship of Vishnu as Krishna, whose praise Bhishma is told to have sung from his bed of arrows, with a fast and with gifts of sesame.

CHANGU_MADHAV_NARAYAN_MELA.about: The Madhav Narayan Mela at Changunarayan falls on the twelfth day of Magh's bright half, near the end of the month of the Madhav Narayan vow and the Swasthani reading. Devotees keeping the vow, many of them from Sankhu and Bhaktapur, come to the hilltop temple above Bhaktapur with their kalash to worship Vishnu, and a fair gathers at Changu.

MAGH_SNAN_ENDS.about: Magh Snan, the month of morning bathing begun on the full moon of Paush, ends on the full moon of Magh. Those who kept it take a last bath at a river or confluence, worship Vishnu and give gifts to Brahmins and the poor to close the vow, and the day draws bathers to the tirthas of Nepal and to Prayag in India.

SWASTHANI_VRAT_ENDS.about: The Swasthani Vrata ends on the full moon of Magh, after a month of evening readings of the Swasthani Vrata Katha. The last chapter is read, the goddess is worshipped with offerings in sets of 108, such as rotis, flowers and fruits, and these are shared among the family and given away; those who kept the fast break it.

CHIR_SWAYEGU.about: Chir Swayegu, the raising of the chir, falls on the eighth day of Phagun's bright half and opens Holi in the Kathmandu valley. At Basantapur, by the old palace of Hanuman Dhoka, a tall pole hung with strips of coloured cloth is raised; it stands for the week of Holi, and on the full moon it is taken down and burned, and people take home pieces of its cloth for luck.

AMALAKI_EKADASHI.about: Amalaki Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Phagun's bright half, a few days before Holi, is the ekadashi of the amla tree, amalaki, held dear to Vishnu. Those who keep it fast, worship Vishnu at the foot of an amla tree, bathing and garlanding it and keeping vigil near it, and break the fast on the twelfth.

GOVINDA_DWADASHI.about: Govinda Dwadashi, the twelfth day of Phagun's bright half, follows Amalaki Ekadashi and is kept for Vishnu as Govinda, the cowherd Krishna. Those who fasted on the ekadashi break their fast on this day after worshipping Govinda, and the day is held fit for a bath and gifts in the days before Holi.

NALA_MACHHINDRANATH_RATH_JATRA.about: Nala's Machhindranath Jatra falls on the third day of Chaitra's dark half, two days after his bath. Nala Karunamaya, a form of Avalokiteshvara whose image is told to have come from Bungamati, is carried round the town of Nala near Banepa in a palanquin, the khat, rather than a chariot, and the town gathers with music and offerings.

SHITALASHTAMI.about: Shitalashtami, the eighth day of Chaitra's dark half, a week after Holi, is kept for Shitala, the goddess who guards against smallpox and fevers. In northern India it is also called Basoda: no fire is lit for cooking, and the family eats food cooked the day before and offers it to the goddess, cold, as her name suggests.

PAPMOCHANI_EKADASHI.about: Papmochani Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Chaitra's dark half, is the ekadashi that is said to free from sin, the last of the year's ekadashis before the new lunar year. Its mahatmya tells of the sage Medhavi, who was freed by its fast from the fault of his love for the nymph Manjughosha. Those who keep it fast, worship Vishnu and break the fast on the twelfth.

KOKA_KAUSHIKI_SANGAM_MELA.about: The Koka Kaushiki Sangam Mela is held on the first day of Paush's dark half, the day after Mangsir's full moon, where the Koka river meets the Koshi, the Kaushiki of the texts, by Barahakshetra in Sunsari. Pilgrims bathe at the confluence and visit the shrines of the area, a pilgrimage ground of eastern Nepal, and a fair gathers on the riverbank.

VARUTHINI_EKADASHI.about: Varuthini Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Baishakh's dark half, is the ekadashi said to protect, varuthin, like armour, and its mahatmya counts it equal in merit to great gifts. Those who keep it fast, worship Vishnu, avoid certain foods and break the fast on the twelfth; the national panchanga gives the Smartas' day where the Vaishnavas' differs.

YOGINI_EKADASHI.about: Yogini Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Ashadh's dark half, comes before Harishayani and the start of the Chaturmas. Its mahatmya tells of Hemamali, the gardener of Kubera, who was cursed with leprosy for neglecting his duty and was cured by its fast. The national panchanga gives the Smartas' day; the Vaishnavas often keep it a day later.

KOJAGRAT_PURNIMA.about: Kojagrat Purnima, the full moon of Ashwin, closes Dashain, and tika from the elders may still be taken until that day. Its name is read as 'who is awake?', the question Lakshmi is said to ask that night, so she is worshipped in the evening and households stay awake, often over games. In Bengal and Assam it is kept at home as Kojagori Lakshmi Puja.

KAMADA_EKADASHI.about: Kamada Ekadashi, the eleventh day of Chaitra's bright half, is the first ekadashi of the lunar year and is said to fulfil desires, kama. Its mahatmya tells of Lalita, whose husband Lalit was cursed to become a demon and was restored by the merit of her fast. Those who keep it fast, worship Vishnu and break the fast on the twelfth; the national panchanga gives the Smartas' day.

SI_PUNHI.about: Si Punhi is the Newar name of the full moon of Magh, the full moon of Silla in Nepal Sambat. It closes the month in which the Swasthani story is read each evening, from Mila Punhi, Paush's full moon, to Si Punhi, and the Newars mark it with the last reading, worship and a bath, as the Swasthani and Magh Snan vows end.

HAYAGRIVA_JAYANTI.about: Hayagriva Jayanti, on the full moon of Shrawan, recalls the appearance of Hayagriva, the horse-headed form of Vishnu, told as recovering the Vedas stolen by demons and restoring them to Brahma. It falls on Janai Purnima, the day Brahmins renew their sacred thread and the Veda study begins anew, and Hayagriva is worshipped as the lord of learning.

SHIVA_PAVITRAROPAN.about: Shiva Pavitraropan, the offering of the pavitra to Shiva, falls on the full moon of Shrawan. The pavitra is a garland of many knotted cotton or silk threads, offered to the god once a year to make good any lapses in his worship through the year; on this day it is placed on Shiva's linga in temples and household shrines.

ARJUNDHARA_MELA.about: The fair of Arjundhara and Satakshi Dham in Jhapa opens on the thirteenth day of Mangsir's dark half, on the eve of Bala Chaturdashi. Arjundhara's Jaleshwar shrine, called the Pashupatinath of the east, draws great crowds from eastern Nepal and India, who keep the night and scatter satbij for their dead as at Pashupati.

WALKE_PARVA.about: Walke Parva, or Balke, is a festival of Nepal's far west on the first of Bhadra, Bhadra Sankranti, in mid-August. Its name is taken to mean a gift. Households clean their homes as the rains end, then give relatives and neighbours milk, curd, the tender heart of taro and green vegetables as a blessing; married daughters come home to feast, and the young swing and dance the deuda.

KALKI_JAYANTI.about: Kalki Jayanti, which the national panchanga sets on the sixth day of Shrawan's bright half, honours Kalki, the tenth avatar of Vishnu, who is foretold to appear at the end of the Kali yuga to end its wrongs and begin a new age. As his coming lies in the future, the day is kept with worship of Vishnu, a fast and readings of the prophecy.

VARAHA_JAYANTI.about: Varaha Jayanti, which the national panchanga sets on the third day of Shrawan's bright half, recalls Vishnu's avatar as Varaha, the boar, told as diving into the cosmic ocean to raise the earth on his tusks after the demon Hiranyaksha had sunk it. Devotees fast and worship Vishnu in his boar form; many almanacs give the day a month later, in Bhadra.

PANAUTI_JATRA.about: The Panauti Jatra, Jya Punhi, reaches its height on the full moon of Jestha in Panauti, the old Newar town at the meeting of the Punyamati and Roshi rivers in Kavre. The chariots of Indreshwar Mahadev, Bhadrakali and Unmatta Bhairav are brought out, raced through the town and run against one another, and the town feasts its guests.

PANAUTI_SNAN_MELA.about: The Panauti bath falls on the full moon of Jestha, the day of the Panauti Jatra. Pilgrims bathe at the confluence of the Punyamati and Roshi rivers at Panauti in Kavre, a tirtha whose waters are held especially purifying on this day, and visit the temple of Indreshwar Mahadev by the river, while a fair gathers in the town.

BAHIDYO_BOYEGU.about: Bahidyo Boyegu, the showing of the gods of the bahi, falls on the twelfth day of Shrawan's bright half, in Gunla, the holy month of Newar Buddhism. The monasteries of Kathmandu and Patan bring out their images of Dipankara Buddha and their old paubha paintings and display them in the courtyards for the day, and people go from bahi to bahi to see them.

LALITPUR_NARSINGH_JATRA.about: Patan's Narsingh Jatra, Upaku La Sayah, falls on the fifth day of Bhadra's dark half, five days after Janai Purnima, and recalls Narasimha's victory over the demon Hiranyakashipu. A masked dancer as Narasimha, with others as Lakshmi, Saraswati and Prahlada, goes round the core of Patan with musicians from Swotha, a custom held to date from the eighteenth century.

GOVATSA_DWADASHI.about: Govatsa Dwadashi, the twelfth day of Kartik's dark half, honours the cow and her calf and opens the Diwali days in western India, where it is called Vasu Baras. In the evening a cow with her calf is worshipped with flowers and food, and women who keep the vow fast for their children and eat nothing from the cow that day.

KASHI_BADA_GANESH_UTSAV.about: The Bada Ganesh festival of Kashi falls on the fourth day of Magh's dark half, the Sankashti Chaturthi also called Sakat Chauth or Tilkuta Chauth. Crowds fill the temple of Bada Ganesh in Varanasi; across northern India mothers fast through the day for their children's welfare, worship Ganesh with sesame sweets, and eat only after the Moon has risen.

NARASIMHA_JAYANTI.about: Narasimha Jayanti, the fourteenth day of Baishakh's bright half, recalls Vishnu's appearance as Narasimha, half man and half lion, who burst from a pillar at dusk to kill the demon king Hiranyakashipu and protect his devotee Prahlada. Devotees fast and worship Narasimha at dusk, the hour of his appearance, and read the story of Prahlada.

PADMINI_EKADASHI.about: Padmini Ekadashi is the eleventh day of the bright half of an adhik maas, the leap month added to the lunar year about once in three years, so it comes only in those years. Kept within the leap month, which is dedicated to Vishnu as Purushottama, it is held to be especially meritorious; devotees fast, worship Vishnu and break the fast on the twelfth.

PARAMA_EKADASHI.about: Parama Ekadashi is the eleventh day of the dark half of an adhik maas, the leap month added to the lunar year about once in three years, and so is kept only in those years, after Padmini Ekadashi. As with the other ekadashi of the leap month, which is given to Vishnu as Purushottama, devotees fast, worship Vishnu and break the fast on the twelfth.

TOKHA_SAPAN_TIRTHA_SNAN.about: The Tokha Sapan Tirtha Snan is the new-year bath at Sapan Tirtha, a sacred pond and shrine at Tokha on the northern edge of the Kathmandu Valley, on the first of Baisakh. Pilgrims bathe there believing the goddess of the place grants what is asked in dreams and cures illness. The mela opens Tokha's own Bisket festival, with chariots pulled through the town in the following days.

YOSIN_PATAN.about: Yosin Patan, the felling of the yosin, takes place in Bhaktapur on the evening of the first of Baisakh, at the height of Bisket Jatra. The tall pole raised the evening before at Yosinkhel, hung with long banners, is pulled down by crowds hauling on ropes from either side. Its fall marks the beginning of the new year in the city.

YOSIN_UTTHAN.about: Yosin Utthan, the raising of the yosin, takes place in Bhaktapur on the last day of Chaitra, during Bisket Jatra. A tall wooden pole, cut and brought in for the festival and hung with two long banners, is hauled upright at Yosinkhel by crowds pulling on ropes. It stands overnight and is felled the next evening, the first of Baisakh, to mark the new year.

BHAKTAPUR_MAHAKALI_MAHALAXMI_JATRA.about: The Bhaktapur Mahakali Mahalaxmi Jatra falls on the second of Baisakh, the day after the new year, during Bisket Jatra. The goddesses Mahakali and Mahalaxmi, two of the eight mother goddesses who guard Bhaktapur, are carried in their palanquins through the city's quarters with music. It is one of the series of goddess processions that fill the days after the yosin falls.

TOKHA_CHANDESHWARI_JATRA.about: The Tokha Chandeshwari Jatra is the main chariot procession of the goddess Chandeshwari at Tokha, north of Kathmandu, on the second of Baisakh. It belongs to Tokha's Bisket festival, which begins with the new-year bath at Sapan Tirtha. The goddess's chariot is pulled through the town's lanes along with the palanquins of other deities, and local people keep the day with feasts.

THIMI_BALKUMARI_JATRA.about: The Thimi Balkumari Jatra, held on the second of Baisakh, is the new-year festival of Madhyapur Thimi, east of Kathmandu. Some thirty-two palanquins of deities from the town's quarters are carried to the temple of the goddess Balkumari and around it, while crowds throw vermilion powder until streets and people turn red. It is widely known as the Sindoor Jatra.

BHAKTAPUR_BRAHMAYANI_JATRA.about: The Bhaktapur Brahmayani Jatra falls on the third of Baisakh, during Bisket Jatra. Brahmayani, the mother goddess whose shrine stands on the bank of the Hanumante river east of the city, is carried in her palanquin through Bhaktapur's quarters. Her procession continues the round of the city's guardian goddesses that follows the new year.

BHAKTAPUR_CHHUMA_GANESH_JATRA.about: The Bhaktapur Chhuma Ganesh Jatra falls on the fourth of Baisakh, near the close of Bisket Jatra. Chhuma Ganesh, one of the city's Ganesha shrines, is carried in procession through Bhaktapur in the evening, with music. It is among the last of the processions before the chariots of Bhairav and Bhadrakali end the festival.

BISKET_JATRA_ENDS.about: Bisket Jatra ends in Bhaktapur on the fifth of Baisakh, the ninth day of the festival. The chariots of Bhairav and of the goddess Bhadrakali are pulled for the last time, with the city's upper and lower halves straining against each other on the ropes, and are brought back to rest. The gods are then returned to their temples.

KANDAKARAK_PUJA.about: The Kandakarak Puja is kept on the evening of the first of Shrawan, Saune Sankranti. Households worship Kandakarna, a demon held to bring itch and skin disease, with medicinal plants, and then throw burning torches out of the house to send luto, the sickness of the planting season, away. The rite is part of the Luto Falne custom of the hills.

KHEER_KHANE_DIN.about: Kheer Khane Din, the day of eating kheer, is the fifteenth of Shrawan, at the end of July. In the heavy rains of the monsoon, families cook kheer, rice simmered in milk with sugar, held to be warming and wholesome, and invite married daughters and friends to share it. The National Dairy Development Board has kept the day as Kheer Day since VS 2078.

KIRTIPUR_BAGH_BHAIRAV_JATRA.about: The Kirtipur Bagh Bhairav Jatra is held on the first of Bhadra, in mid-August, at the temple of Bagh Bhairav, the tiger-faced Bhairav who guards the hill town of Kirtipur. An image made for the festival is carried through the streets with traditional music and the lakhe dance, and devotees walk many rounds of the temple, some the full hundred and eight, for health and success.

VISHWAKARMA_PUJA.about: Vishwakarma Puja, on Kanya Sankranti around 17 September, when the Sun enters Virgo, honours Vishwakarma, the divine architect and craftsman. Factories, workshops, garages and offices clean their tools and machines and worship them before his image, and the workers share a meal. In Bengal and Bihar the day is also known for its kites.

MAKAR_SNAN.about: Makar Snan is the holy bath of Makara Sankranti, the first of Magh in mid-January, when the Sun enters Capricorn. The hours after the crossing are held especially holy, and crowds bathe at confluences and riverside shrines such as Devghat, Ridi, Barahakshetra and the Triveni of Nawalparasi, giving alms before eating the season's sesame, chaku and yam.

DEVGHAT_MAKAR_SNAN.about: The Devghat Makar Snan is the Makara Sankranti bath at Devghat, the Harihar Kshetra, where the Kali Gandaki and Trishuli rivers meet on the border of Tanahun and Chitwan. On the first of Magh pilgrims from across Nepal and India gather at the confluence for the Makar Mela, bathing at dawn, giving alms and visiting the area's temples and ashrams.

BISKET_JATRA_BEGINS.about: Bisket Jatra begins in Bhaktapur on the fourth-last day of Chaitra, in April, four days before the new year. The god Bhairav is set in his great three-tiered chariot and the goddess Bhadrakali in hers, and the chariots are pulled through the city in a tug of war between its upper and lower halves, opening nine days and eight nights of festival.

BHUMIRAJ.about: Bhumiraj, the earth's season, is the day the Sun enters the asterism Ardra, in late June, when the monsoon rains set in. The name holds the earth to be in her monthly season, and by old custom ploughing and sowing are set aside for three days, much as at the Ambubachi of Assam. The national panchanga sets the Bhumi Puja, the worship of the earth, three days later.

BHUMI_PUJA.about: Bhumi Puja, the worship of the earth, falls three days after Bhumiraj, the Sun's entry into the asterism Ardra, in late June or early July. After the days of rest given to the earth, farming families worship the land before the rice planting begins in earnest, asking for good rains and a good harvest.

CHHANDA_DIWAS.about: Chhanda Diwas, Metre Day, falls on the eighth of Baisakh, in April. It recalls the day in VS 2053 when the poet Madhav Viyogi began a campaign to save metrical verse, as free verse came to dominate Nepali poetry. Literary circles across the country mark it with readings of poems written in the classical metres, the chhanda.

KIRAT_SAMAJ_SUDHAR_DIWAS.about: Kirat Samaj Sudhar Diwas, Kirat Social Reform Day, falls on the twenty-fourth of Baisakh, in May. It recalls the gathering at Panchthar in VS 1988 at which Falgunanda Lingden, the Kirat religious reformer, set out his points for reforming Kirat society, among them giving up costly sacrifices and drink. Kirat communities mark it with assemblies and programmes.

LAW_DAY.about: Law Day falls on the twenty-sixth of Baisakh, in May. It recalls Baisakh 26, VS 2009, when the act creating the Pradhan Nyayalaya, Nepal's first supreme court and the forerunner of today's Supreme Court, received royal assent, separating the judiciary from the executive. The Supreme Court and the legal community mark it with a ceremony, speeches and awards.

REPUBLIC_DAY.about: Republic Day falls on the fifteenth of Jestha, in late May. It recalls Jestha 15, VS 2065 (28 May 2008), when the first meeting of the elected Constituent Assembly declared Nepal a federal democratic republic and ended the monarchy of the Shah dynasty. It is a public holiday, with an official ceremony and programmes across the country.

CASTE_BASED_DISCRIMINATION_AND_UNTOUCHAB.about: The National Day for the Elimination of Caste-based Discrimination and Untouchability falls on the twenty-first of Jestha, in early June. It recalls Jestha 21, VS 2063 (4 June 2006), when the reinstated House of Representatives declared Nepal free of untouchability. Government bodies and Dalit organisations hold programmes on ending caste discrimination; offices stay open.

NATIONAL_PADDY_DAY.about: National Paddy Day falls on the fifteenth of Asar, in late June, at the height of the rice-planting season. The government named it in VS 2061 and has kept it since VS 2062 to honour rice, the country's staple, and its farmers. Ministers and officials join planting festivals in the fields, and people eat curd and beaten rice, as on the old Dahi Chiura Khane Din.

BHANU_JAYANTI.about: Bhanu Jayanti, on 13 July, Asar 29 in Nepal, marks the birth in 1814 of Bhanubhakta Acharya, whose Nepali Ramayana made him the language's first great poet, the adikavi. Nepali speakers in Nepal, Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills keep it with processions, garlands at his statue and readings of his verse; West Bengal gives the day as a holiday in Darjeeling and Kalimpong.

NATIONAL_DAY_AGAINST_HUMAN_TRAFFICKING.about: The National Day against Human Trafficking falls on the twentieth of Bhadra, in early September. The government, the police and organisations working with survivors hold rallies, talks and awareness programmes on the trafficking of women, men and children, within Nepal and across its borders, and on the protection the Human Trafficking and Transportation (Control) Act gives to victims.

CIVIL_SERVICE_DAY.about: Civil Service Day falls on the twenty-second of Bhadra, in September. It recalls the issue on that date of Nepal's first Civil Service Act, of VS 2013, and has been kept since VS 2061. The government honours civil servants for their work, holds programmes on public service, and keeps its offices open.

NATIONAL_CHILDREN_S_DAY.about: National Children's Day falls on the twenty-ninth of Bhadra, in mid-September. It recalls the day in VS 2047 (14 September 1990) when Nepal ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. Schools, child clubs and the government hold programmes on children's rights, with performances by the children themselves.

VASTU_DIWAS.about: Vastu Diwas, Architecture Day, falls on the first of Asoj, Kanya Sankranti, in mid-September, the same day as the Vishwakarma Puja. Architects, engineers, builders and craftsmen mark it in honour of Vishwakarma, the divine architect, with worship of their tools and machines and with programmes on building and design.

FALGUNANDA_JAYANTI.about: Falgunanda Jayanti falls on the twenty-fifth of Kartik, in November, the birth anniversary of Falgunanda Lingden, born in VS 1941, the reformer of the Kirat religion and one of Nepal's national figures. Kirat communities, especially in the eastern hills, hold processions, prayers and programmes, and the government gives the followers of the Kirat religion a holiday.

LEKHNATH_PAUDYAL_JAYANTI.about: Lekhnath Paudyal Jayanti falls on the fifteenth of Poush, in late December, the birth anniversary of Lekhnath Paudyal, born in Kaski in VS 1941, a master of classical Nepali verse honoured with the title Kavi Shiromani, crown of poets. Literary bodies hold readings of his poems and present awards in his name.

ARANIKO_MEMORIAL_DAY.about: Araniko Memorial Day falls on the twenty-third of Poush, in January. It honours Araniko, the thirteenth-century Newar artist and architect of Patan who went to the court of Kublai Khan and built the White Stupa of Beijing. Kept since VS 2058, the day is marked by Nepal's artists' associations, and in China as well, with exhibitions and programmes.

ELECTION_DAY.about: Election Day falls on the seventh of Falgun, in February, the same day as National Democracy Day. It recalls the first general election held under adult suffrage, which began on Falgun 7, VS 2015 (18 February 1959). The Election Commission marks it with messages and programmes on voters' rights and taking part in elections.

NEW_YEAR_S_DAY_AD.about: New Year's Day, 1 January, opens the year of the Gregorian calendar, the civil calendar of India and of most of the world, and several Indian states list it as a holiday. The year is greeted at midnight with gatherings and fireworks, the day is spent with family and friends, and many churches hold a service.

INTERNATIONAL_WOMEN_S_DAY.about: International Women's Day, on 8 March, celebrates women's achievements and calls for their equal rights. Born of the labour and suffrage movements of the early twentieth century, it has been marked by the United Nations since 1975. In Nepal it is a public holiday, kept with rallies, programmes on women's rights and awards to women in public life.

WORLD_WATER_DAY.about: World Water Day, on 22 March, draws attention to fresh water and to the people who live without safe water to drink. The United Nations General Assembly proclaimed it in 1992, following the Rio conference on environment and development, and each year's observance takes a theme. Government bodies, schools and water groups hold rallies and programmes.

WORLD_TUBERCULOSIS_DAY.about: World Tuberculosis Day, on 24 March, recalls the day in 1882 when Robert Koch announced that he had found the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. Kept by the World Health Organization and its partners, it raises awareness of a disease that remains a leading cause of death. Nepal's health authorities hold rallies, screening and programmes on its treatment.

INTERNATIONAL_LABOUR_DAY.about: International Labour Day, 1 May, honours workers and their movement. The Paris congress of the Second International called for it in 1889, recalling the American strikes of May 1886 for an eight-hour day; in India it was first marked at Madras in 1923. Trade unions hold rallies and meetings, and several states give the day as a holiday.

WORLD_PRESS_FREEDOM_DAY.about: World Press Freedom Day, on 3 May, upholds the freedom of the press and honours journalists who have lost their lives in their work. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 1993 on UNESCO's recommendation, marking the Windhoek Declaration of 1991 by African journalists. In Nepal, journalists' bodies hold programmes and rallies on the freedom of expression.

WORLD_RED_CROSS_DAY.about: World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day, on 8 May, is the birthday of Henry Dunant, born in 1828, whose work after the battle of Solferino led to the founding of the Red Cross. It honours the movement's volunteers and the principles of humanity and neutrality. The Nepal Red Cross Society marks it with rallies, blood donation and first-aid programmes.

WORLD_NO_TOBACCO_DAY.about: World No Tobacco Day, on 31 May, is kept by the World Health Organization to warn of the harm of tobacco and to urge people to give it up. The World Health Assembly first called for a day without smoking in 1987 and set 31 May in 1989. In Nepal health workers and anti-tobacco groups hold rallies and programmes on smoke-free places.

WORLD_ENVIRONMENT_DAY.about: World Environment Day, on 5 June, recalls the opening of the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment at Stockholm in 1972, and is led by the UN Environment Programme. It calls for action on pollution, climate and nature, under a new theme each year. In Nepal it is kept with tree planting, clean-up campaigns and programmes.

INTERNATIONAL_SPORTS_JOURNALISTS_DAY.about: International Sports Journalists Day, on 2 July, marks the founding of the International Sports Press Association, AIPS, in Paris on 2 July 1924, during the Olympic Games. It honours the work of sports reporters and photographers. In Nepal the sports journalists' forum marks it with programmes and awards for sports reporting.

WORLD_POPULATION_DAY.about: World Population Day, on 11 July, draws attention to population issues such as family planning, health and gender equality. It grew from the interest raised by the Day of Five Billion, 11 July 1987, and was set by the UNDP Governing Council in 1989 and endorsed by the General Assembly in 1990. In Nepal it is marked with programmes on reproductive health and population.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_THE_WORLD_S_INDIGEN.about: The International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples, on 9 August, marks the first meeting of the UN Working Group on Indigenous Populations in 1982. It upholds the rights, languages and cultures of indigenous peoples. In Nepal the Adivasi Janajati federation and its member communities mark it with rallies in traditional dress, cultural performances and programmes on their rights.

INTERNATIONAL_LITERACY_DAY.about: International Literacy Day, on 8 September, was proclaimed by UNESCO in 1966 and first kept in 1967 to remind the world that literacy is a matter of dignity and human rights. In Nepal, where it is kept as Education and Literacy Day, schools and education offices hold rallies and programmes on reading, adult literacy and lifelong learning.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_PEACE.about: The International Day of Peace, on 21 September, is a day the United Nations devotes to strengthening peace and asks all sides to observe a ceasefire. First proclaimed in 1981, it was fixed to 21 September in 2001. In Nepal, the birthplace of the Buddha, it is marked with peace rallies, prayers and programmes.

WORLD_TOURISM_DAY.about: World Tourism Day, on 27 September, marks the adoption of the World Tourism Organization's statutes on that date in 1970, and has been kept since 1980. It highlights tourism's social, cultural and economic value. In Nepal, where tourism is a mainstay of the economy, the tourism board and trade hold rallies, exhibitions and programmes.

UNITED_NATIONS_DAY.about: United Nations Day, on 24 October, marks the coming into force of the Charter of the United Nations on 24 October 1945, when the organisation was born. Nepal, a member since 1955 and a large contributor of peacekeepers, marks the day with programmes by the government and the UN offices in Kathmandu on the organisation's work.

WORLD_DIABETES_DAY.about: World Diabetes Day, on 14 November, is the birthday of Frederick Banting, who with Charles Best discovered insulin in 1921. Begun in 1991 by the International Diabetes Federation and the World Health Organization, it became a United Nations day in 2006. Hospitals and health groups in Nepal hold free blood-sugar tests, walks and awareness programmes.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_PERSONS_WITH_DISABI.about: The International Day of Persons with Disabilities, on 3 December, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 1992 to promote the rights and well-being of people with disabilities in every part of society. In Nepal, organisations of disabled people hold rallies and programmes, and every employee with a disability is given the day as a holiday.

HUMAN_RIGHTS_DAY.about: Human Rights Day, on 10 December, marks the adoption of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948. In Nepal the National Human Rights Commission, the government and rights groups hold programmes, rallies and award ceremonies on human rights and justice.

INDIA_REPUBLIC_DAY.about: Republic Day, 26 January, marks the coming into force of the Constitution of India in 1950, when India became a republic. The date recalls the Congress's call for complete independence, purna swaraj, first marked on 26 January 1930. The President takes the salute at a parade on Kartavya Path in New Delhi, and the flag is raised across the country.

INDIA_INDEPENDENCE_DAY.about: Independence Day, 15 August, marks the end of British rule over India in 1947, under the Indian Independence Act. The Prime Minister raises the flag at the Red Fort in Delhi and addresses the nation, and the flag goes up over offices, schools and homes; in Delhi and other northern cities the sky fills with kites.

GANDHI_JAYANTI.about: Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October, is the birthday of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, born at Porbandar in 1869, who led India's struggle for independence by non-violent resistance. Prayer meetings with his favourite hymns are held at Raj Ghat in Delhi, where he was cremated, and across the country, and the United Nations keeps the day as the International Day of Non-Violence.

GOOD_FRIDAY.about: Good Friday, the Friday before Easter, recalls the crucifixion and death of Jesus Christ. Christians keep it with fasting and solemn services, often from noon to three in the afternoon, the hours he is told to have hung on the cross, and walk the Stations of the Cross in prayer.

HOLI.about: Holi, the festival of colours, is played on the morning after Holika's bonfire, the first day of Chaitra's dark half, as the full moon of Falgun turns. It recalls the burning of the demoness Holika and the escape of the boy Prahlada, and in Braj the play of Krishna and Radha. People drench one another with coloured powder and water, visit friends, and share sweets such as gujiya.

FAGU_PURNIMA.about: Fagu Purnima, the full moon of Phagun, is Holi in Nepal's hills and the Kathmandu valley, a public holiday in the hill and mountain districts; the Terai plays Holi a day later. People throw coloured powder and water at one another in the streets, and that evening the chir raised at Basantapur a week before is taken down and burned.

ASHUNYA_SHAYANA.about: The Ashunya Shayana Vrata, the vow of the bed never empty, falls on the second tithi of the dark half after Ashadh's full moon, and is repeated on the dark second of the three months that follow. It is kept for a lasting marriage: Lakshmi and Vishnu are worshipped on a decked bed, and after arghya to the rising Moon the keeper eats a single night meal.

MAHAVIR_NIRVANA.about: Mahavir Nirvana, the new moon of Kartik and the night of Diwali, recalls the passing of Mahavira, the twenty-fourth Tirthankara, at Pava in Bihar, by tradition in 527 BCE. Jains light lamps for the light of knowledge that went out with him, as the Kalpasutra tells, and fast; Digambara temples offer a laddu at dawn, and pilgrims gather at Pavapuri.

VIRA_NIRVANA_NEW_YEAR.about: The Vira Nirvana new year, the first day of Kartik's bright half, opens a new year of the era counted from Mahavira's nirvana the night before. Jains also recall that Gautama, Mahavira's chief disciple, attained omniscience as that night ended. They begin the year at the temple and greet one another for the year ahead.

PARYUSHANA.about: Paryushana, the holiest season of the Shvetambara Jains, begins eight days before Samvatsari, on the twelfth of the dark fortnight that precedes Bhadra's bright half. For eight days Jains fast as far as each is able, go daily to the temple and the upashraya, and hear the monks read the Kalpasutra; it closes with Samvatsari's confession and forgiveness.

SAMVATSARI.about: Samvatsari, the fourth of Bhadra's bright half for most Shvetambara Jains, is the last day of Paryushana and the holiest day of the Jain year. Many keep a full fast, and all join the long annual pratikramana, confessing the year's faults; then they ask forgiveness of everyone they may have hurt, with the words michchhami dukkadam. Gujarat lists it as a holiday.

PARYUSHANA_TRAYODASHI.about: For the Shvetambara Jains who keep Samvatsari on the fifth of Bhadra's bright half, Paryushana begins a day later than in the common reckoning, on the thirteenth of the dark fortnight before it. Its eight days are kept the same way, with fasts, daily worship and the reading of the Kalpasutra, and end in the annual confession and forgiveness.

SAMVATSARI_PANCHAMI.about: Samvatsari on the bright fifth is kept by the Shvetambara Jains who hold to the fifth of Bhadra's bright half, the day from which, by tradition, the teacher Kalakacharya moved the observance to the fourth. It is the same day of fasting, annual pratikramana and forgiveness asked of all, one day after the more common Samvatsari.

DASA_LAKSHANA.about: Das Lakshana, the great festival of the Digambara Jains, runs ten days from the fifth of Bhadra's bright half to the fourteenth. Each day is given to one of the ten virtues, from supreme forgiveness to supreme chastity, and a chapter of the Tattvartha Sutra is read and explained; many fast. It is followed by Kshamavani, the day of mutual forgiveness.

CHAITRA_AYAMBIL_OLI.about: The Chaitra Ayambil Oli of the Shvetambara Jains begins on the seventh of Chaitra's bright half and runs nine days to the full moon. Each day honours one of the nine padas of the Siddhachakra, from the Arihantas to austerity, and those keeping it eat one plain meal of boiled grain, without ghee, oil, milk, sugar or spice; the story of King Shripal and Mayanasundari is read.

CHAITRA_AYAMBIL_OLI_END.about: The Chaitra Ayambil Oli ends on the full moon of Chaitra, the ninth day of its fast, given to austerity, the last of the Siddhachakra's nine padas. Those who kept all nine ayambil meals worship the Siddhachakra and break the fast the next morning. The same full moon draws Jain pilgrims to the hill of Shatrunjaya at Palitana.

ASHVINA_AYAMBIL_OLI.about: The Ashvina Ayambil Oli, the autumn twin of the Chaitra Oli, begins on the seventh of Ashwin's bright half and runs nine days to the full moon. Shvetambara Jains honour the nine padas of the Siddhachakra in turn and eat one plain meal a day of boiled grain without ghee, oil, milk, sugar or spice, and the story of King Shripal is read in the upashrayas.

ASHVINA_AYAMBIL_OLI_END.about: The Ashvina Ayambil Oli ends on the full moon of Ashwin, the ninth day of its fast, given to austerity, the last of the Siddhachakra's nine padas. Those who kept all nine ayambil meals worship the Siddhachakra, often with a festive puja in the temple, and break their fast the next morning.

JAIN_PARVA_DVITIYA.about: The second of each fortnight is one of the twelve parva tithis of the Jain month, the days a lay Jain sets apart for stricter practice: the second, fifth, eighth, eleventh and fourteenth of both halves, and the full and new moons. On them many eat no green vegetables, keep a fast or a single meal, and go to the temple and to the day's pratikramana.

JAIN_PARVA_PANCHAMI.about: The fifth of each fortnight is one of the twelve parva tithis of the Jain month, the days a lay Jain sets apart for stricter practice: the second, fifth, eighth, eleventh and fourteenth of both halves, and the full and new moons. Many keep it without green vegetables and with a fast; the fifth of Kartik's bright half is Jnana Panchami, when the scriptures are honoured.

JAIN_PARVA_ASHTAMI.about: The eighth of each fortnight is one of the twelve parva tithis of the Jain month, the days a lay Jain sets apart for stricter practice: the second, fifth, eighth, eleventh and fourteenth of both halves, and the full and new moons. With the fourteenth it is the most strictly kept, often with a fast, a day of retreat in the upashraya, and no green vegetables.

JAIN_PARVA_EKADASHI.about: The eleventh of each fortnight is one of the twelve parva tithis of the Jain month, the days a lay Jain sets apart for stricter practice: the second, fifth, eighth, eleventh and fourteenth of both halves, and the full and new moons. Many fast and eat no green vegetables; the eleventh of Margashirsha's bright half is Maun Ekadashi, kept in silence and fasting.

JAIN_PARVA_CHATURDASHI.about: The fourteenth of each fortnight is one of the twelve parva tithis of the Jain month, the days a lay Jain sets apart for stricter practice: the second, fifth, eighth, eleventh and fourteenth of both halves, and the full and new moons. It closes the fortnight with its pratikramana, the pakkhi, in which the fortnight's faults are confessed, and many fast.

JAIN_PARVA_PURNIMA.about: The full moon is one of the twelve parva tithis of the Jain month, the days a lay Jain sets apart for stricter practice: the second, fifth, eighth, eleventh and fourteenth of both halves, and the full and new moons. Many fast and avoid green vegetables, and the full moons of Kartik and Chaitra draw pilgrims to Shatrunjaya.

JAIN_PARVA_AMAVASYA.about: The new moon is one of the twelve parva tithis of the Jain month, the days a lay Jain sets apart for stricter practice: the second, fifth, eighth, eleventh and fourteenth of both halves, and the full and new moons. Many fast and avoid green vegetables; the new moon of Kartik, at Diwali, recalls the nirvana of Mahavira.

MAUNA_PANCHAMI.about: Mauna Panchami, the fifth of Shravan's dark half, is Mithila's day of serpent worship, kept as the monsoon brings snakes out of the ground. The nagas and the snake goddess Bishahara are worshipped with milk and flowers for the family's safety, and for newly married Maithil women it is the first day of the fortnight of Madhushravani.

MADHUSHRAVANI_ARAMBHA.about: Madhushravani, kept by newly married Maithil women in their first monsoon as wives, begins on the fifth of Shravan's dark half and lasts about a fortnight. Each evening the young wives go out in groups, singing, to gather flowers, and next morning they worship Gauri, Bishahara and the nagas with them, while an elder woman tells the day's story of Shiva, Parvati and the serpents.

MADHUSHRAVANI_SAMAPTI.about: Madhushravani ends on the third of Shravan's bright half, the last day of the young wives' fortnight of worship. The husband usually comes for it, and the bride goes through the temi, in which her knees are touched with a lit wick, now often a cold one, as a sign of her steadfastness. The day closes with worship of Gauri, a feast and gifts from the husband's family.

CHAURCHAN.about: Chaurchan, the fourth of Bhadra's bright half, is Mithila's festival of the moon, kept on the evening of the day on which the moon is otherwise not to be looked at. Women fast through the day and at moonrise, in the courtyard, offer arghya to the moon with curd set in new clay pots, fruit and sweets, praying to be kept from false blame. The offerings are then shared as prasad.

OTHGAN.about: Othgan is the meal eaten before dawn on the eve of Jitiya, the mothers' fast of the eighth of Ashwin's dark half, kept in Mithila and across the plains of Bihar and Nepal. Mothers eat curd, beaten rice and sweets before the first light, and then begin the waterless fast of Jivitputrika for their children's long life, which lasts until the next day.

SAMA_CHAKEVA_ARAMBHA.about: Sama-Chakeva, Mithila's festival of sisters and brothers, begins on the seventh of Kartik's bright half, after Chhath, as the birds come down from the hills for winter. Sisters shape clay figures of Sama, her brother Chakeva, the slanderer Chugla and others, and sing to them each evening; it is told as the story of Krishna's daughter Sama, turned into a bird on a false charge and freed by her brother.

SAMA_CHAKEVA_VISARJANA.about: Sama-Chakeva ends on the full moon of Kartik, when sisters bid farewell to the clay figures they have sung to for a week. They carry them out in procession, singing, set fire to the figure of the slanderer Chugla, and immerse or break the figures of Sama and Chakeva in the fields or a river, praying for their brothers' long life.

VIDYAPATI_SMRITI_DIVAS.about: Vidyapati Smriti Divas, the thirteenth of Kartik's bright half, remembers Vidyapati, the fourteenth- and fifteenth-century poet of Mithila whose Maithili songs of Radha and Krishna and of Shiva are still sung; a verse ascribed to him names this tithi as the day of his death. Maithils in Nepal and India mark it with his songs, recitations and gatherings in his honour.

JUR_SITAL.about: Jur Sital is the Maithil new year, kept on the first days of Baishakh, when the Sun enters Aries. On the first day, Satuain, sattu and gram are eaten; on the next, elders pour cool water on the heads of the young as a blessing, food cooked the day before is eaten cold while the hearth rests, trees are watered, and young people play with water and mud.

CHHATRAPATI_SHIVAJI_JAYANTI.about: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Jayanti, 19 February, is the birthday of Shivaji, born at the fort of Shivneri in 1630, who founded the Maratha kingdom and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. Maharashtra keeps it with processions, garlands at his statues, and plays and songs of his life, and many climb to Shivneri and his other forts; some also keep the day by its tithi.

AMBEDKAR_JAYANTI.about: Ambedkar Jayanti, 14 April, is the birthday of Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar, born at Mhow in 1891, the jurist and leader of the Dalits who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and in 1956 turned to Buddhism. Crowds gather at his statues and at Chaityabhoomi in Mumbai and Dikshabhoomi in Nagpur, and processions, readings and meetings are held across India.

MAHARASHTRA_DAY.about: Maharashtra Day, 1 May, marks the founding of the state of Maharashtra in 1960, when the Bombay Reorganisation Act divided the old Bombay State into Maharashtra and Gujarat along the lines of language, after the Samyukta Maharashtra movement. The Governor takes the salute at a parade at Shivaji Park in Mumbai, and the flag is raised at government offices.

BANK_ACCOUNTS_CLOSING.about: The yearly closing of bank accounts, on 1 April, is a bank holiday at the start of India's financial year, which runs from April to March. Banks stay closed to the public for the day while they close their books for the year that ended on 31 March; government offices and other businesses work as usual. Several states list it among their holidays.

VIVEKANANDA_JAYANTI.about: Swami Vivekananda Jayanti marks the birth in Calcutta, on 12 January 1863, of Narendranath Datta, the monk Vivekananda, disciple of Ramakrishna and founder of the Ramakrishna Mission, whose address at Chicago in 1893 made him known abroad. India keeps 12 January as National Youth Day, and the Ramakrishna Math and Mission celebrate his birth on its tithi, the seventh of Paush's dark half.

NETAJI_JAYANTI.about: Netaji Jayanti, 23 January, is the birthday of Subhas Chandra Bose, born at Cuttack in 1897, who twice led the Indian National Congress and later the Indian National Army against British rule. In Bengal conches and sirens sound at a quarter past noon, the hour of his birth, and processions and tributes follow; the Government of India keeps the day as Parakram Diwas.

THAKUR_PANCHANAN_BARMA_JAYANTI.about: Thakur Panchanan Barma Jayanti, on the first of Falgun in the Bengali calendar, around 14 February, marks the birth in 1866 of Panchanan Barma, the lawyer and reformer from Cooch Behar who led the Kshatriya movement of the Rajbanshi people of North Bengal for social standing and education. West Bengal keeps it as a holiday, and Rajbanshi bodies gather at his statues.

DOLA_YATRA.about: Dol Jatra, the full moon of Falgun, is the swing festival of Krishna, kept in Bengal, Odisha and Assam on the day of Holi's colours. Images of Radha and Krishna are smeared with coloured powder, abir, and rocked on a decorated swing or carried in procession, and people play with colours. In Bengal it is also Gaura Purnima, and in Assam the Barpeta satra holds its great Doul.

HARICHAND_THAKUR_JAYANTI.about: Harichand Thakur Jayanti, the thirteenth of the dark half of Madhu, the month of Chaitra, marks the birth in 1812 of Harichand Thakur, founder of the Matua faith among the Namasudras of Bengal. Matuas gather in great numbers for the Baruni Mela at Thakurnagar in West Bengal and Orakandi in Bangladesh, take a holy dip, and sing kirtan to drums and gongs, waving red flags.

EASTER_SATURDAY.about: Easter Saturday, also called Holy Saturday, is the day between Good Friday and Easter, when Christians recall Jesus Christ lying in the tomb. Churches stay bare and quiet through the day; after dark the Easter Vigil begins with a new fire, from which the paschal candle is lit, and moves into the first celebration of Easter.

POHELA_BOISHAKH.about: Pohela Boishakh, the first of Boishakh, around 14 or 15 April, is the Bengali new year. Shopkeepers open new account books, the haal khata, with a puja and sweets for their customers; people wear new clothes, greet one another with Shubho Noboborsho, and join morning processions and music, and in Dhaka the Mangal Shobhajatra procession, which UNESCO lists as heritage.

RABINDRA_JAYANTI.about: Rabindra Jayanti, the twenty-fifth of Boishakh in the Bengali calendar, early in May, is the birthday of Rabindranath Tagore, born at Jorasanko in Calcutta in 1861, poet, composer and founder of Visva-Bharati, and in 1913 the first Asian to win the Nobel Prize for Literature. Bengalis mark it with his songs, Rabindra sangeet, readings and dance-dramas, above all at Santiniketan.

HUL_DIWAS.about: Hul Diwas, 30 June, recalls the Santhal hul, the rising that began on that day in 1855 at Bhognadih, when thousands of Santhals gathered under the brothers Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu against moneylenders, landlords and the East India Company's rule. Santhal communities gather at memorials to Sidhu and Kanhu with songs and dances, and West Bengal gives Santhal employees the day off.

DURGA_CHATURTHI.about: Maha Chaturthi, the fourth of Ashwin's bright half, is when Bengal's Durga Puja begins to fill the streets. Most of the images of the goddess have reached their pandals, many neighbourhood pujas open to visitors, and crowds start going round them in the evenings, though the goddess is not yet invoked; West Bengal lists the day among its Puja holidays.

DURGA_PANCHAMI.about: Maha Panchami, the fifth of Ashwin's bright half, is the eve of Durga Puja's main days in Bengal. The pandals are finished and lit, families shop for new clothes for the days ahead, and the crowds grow; the next evening, Shashthi, the goddess is awakened and invited into her image with the bodhon.

DURGA_SHASHTHI.about: Durga Puja, Bengal's greatest festival, runs from the sixth to the tenth of Ashwin's bright half. On Shashthi the goddess is awakened, the bodhon; Saptami, Ashtami and Navami bring her worship with her children in thousands of pandals, the offering of flowers at Ashtami and the sandhi puja, and on Dashami her image is taken to the river and immersed.

KALI_PUJA.about: Kali Puja, the new moon of Kartik, the night of Diwali, is kept in Bengal, Assam and Odisha for the goddess Kali, on the night the north gives to Lakshmi. She is worshipped through the night in homes, at temples such as Kalighat and Dakshineswar, and in pandals across the towns, while houses are lit with lamps and the sky with fireworks.

BIRSA_MUNDA_JAYANTI.about: Birsa Munda Jayanti, 15 November, is the birthday of Birsa Munda, born at Ulihatu in 1875, who led the Munda people of Chota Nagpur in the ulgulan, the great tumult, against landlords and British rule, and died in Ranchi jail in 1900. Adivasi communities honour him with tributes, songs and dances, and the Government of India keeps the day as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas.

VISHU.about: Vishu, the first of the Malayalam month of Medam, around 14 April, when the Sun enters Aries, is Kerala's new year by the solar reckoning. Overnight a kani is arranged of rice, gold, a mirror, fruit, golden konna flowers and an image of Krishna before a lamp, to be the first sight of the year on waking; elders give the young coins, the kaineettam, and the day brings firecrackers and a feast.

MANNAM_JAYANTHI.about: Mannam Jayanthi, 2 January, is the birthday of Mannathu Padmanabhan, born at Perunna near Changanassery in 1878, the reformer who founded the Nair Service Society in 1914 and led a march of caste Hindus in support of the Vaikom Satyagraha against untouchability in 1924. Kerala keeps it as a public holiday, and the Society holds gatherings at its headquarters at Perunna.

MAUNDY_THURSDAY.about: Maundy Thursday, the Thursday before Easter, recalls the Last Supper of Jesus Christ with his disciples and his washing of their feet. Churches hold an evening service with the washing of feet; in Kerala, where it is called Pesaha, Syrian Christian families break an unleavened Pesaha bread at home and share it with sweet coconut milk, and the state lists the day as a holiday.

EASTER.about: Easter, the Sunday after the first full moon of spring, celebrates the resurrection of Jesus Christ on the third day after his crucifixion, and ends the forty days of Lent. Christians gather for services at night or at dawn, greet one another with the news that Christ is risen, and break the Lenten fast with a festive meal; in Kerala it is a day of family feasts.

KARKIDAKA_VAVU.about: Karkidaka Vavu, the new moon of the Malayalam month of Karkidakam, in July or August, is Kerala's great day of offerings to the dead. Families fast on the day before, and at dawn crowds gather on river banks and beaches, at Aluva on the Periyar, Varkala's Papanasam, Thirunelli and Thiruvallam, to offer vavu bali, rice balls and water for their ancestors, and then bathe.

FIRST_ONAM.about: First Onam, or Uthradom, the day before Thiruvonam in the Malayalam month of Chingam, is the eve of Onam, Kerala's harvest festival. Households finish the shopping for the feast in the rush called the Uthrada paachil, the flower carpet laid at the door each day since Atham, ten days before, grows to its largest, and the vegetables are cut for the next day's sadya.

THIRUVONAM.about: Thiruvonam, the day of the Thiruvonam asterism in Chingam, in August or September, is the main day of Onam, Kerala's harvest festival. It is told as the day the beloved king Mahabali, whom Vishnu as Vamana sent below the earth, returns to see his people. Families lay a large pookalam, wear new clothes, the onakkodi, and sit down to the sadya on plantain leaves.

THIRD_ONAM.about: Third Onam, the day of the Avittam asterism after Thiruvonam, carries the festival on into its holidays. Families visit relatives who could not come for the feast, the sadya's dishes are served again, and villages hold Onam games, songs and dances; Kerala keeps the day as a public holiday.

FOURTH_ONAM.about: Fourth Onam, the day of the Chathayam asterism in Chingam, closes Onam's four days of holidays. In Thrissur it brings the Pulikali, in which troupes of men painted as tigers and hunters dance through the town to drums, and it is also Sree Narayana Guru Jayanthi, kept on the same asterism.

SREE_NARAYANA_GURU_JAYANTHI.about: Sree Narayana Guru Jayanthi, on the Chathayam asterism of Chingam, the fourth day of Onam, is the birthday of Narayana Guru, born at Chempazhanthy near Thiruvananthapuram in 1856, the saint and reformer who taught 'one caste, one religion, one god for man' and opened temples to those barred by caste. Processions and meetings are held across Kerala, above all at his birthplace and at Sivagiri.

SREE_NARAYANA_GURU_SAMADHI.about: Sree Narayana Guru Samadhi Day, the fifth of the Malayalam month of Kanni, around 21 September, marks the passing of Narayana Guru at Sivagiri near Varkala in 1928. His followers keep it with fasting, silent prayer and readings of his works, and thousands gather at his samadhi at Sivagiri; Kerala keeps the day as a public holiday.

AYYANKALI_JAYANTHI.about: Ayyankali Jayanthi, 28 August, is the birthday of Ayyankali, born at Venganoor near Thiruvananthapuram in 1863, the leader of the Pulaya people who in 1893 drove a bullock cart down a public road closed to his caste and later led a strike of farm labourers to win schooling for their children. Tributes are paid at his statue at Vellayambalam, and Kerala keeps the day as a holiday.

AVANI_AVITTOM.about: Avani Avittom is the Tamil and Malayalam name for the Yajurveda Upakarma, kept on the full moon of Shravan, in the solar month of Avani. Brahmins of the Yajurveda bathe, offer water to the seers of the Veda, put on a new sacred thread, the poonool, and resume the Veda's recitation; on the next day they recite the Gayatri a thousand and eight times. Kerala lists it as a restricted holiday.

AYYA_VAIKUNDA_SWAMI_JAYANTHI.about: Ayya Vaikunda Swami Jayanthi falls on the twentieth of the Tamil month of Masi, early in March, the day in 1833 that the Ayyavazhi faith holds Vaikundar to have come forth from the sea at Tiruchendur. Ayyavazhi followers, many of them Nadars of southern Kerala and Kanyakumari, walk in procession to the mother shrine at Swamithope and share a common meal; Kerala lists it as a restricted holiday.

THAI_PONGAL.about: Pongal, the first of the Tamil month of Thai, around 14 January, when the Sun turns north into Capricorn, is the Tamil harvest festival. In front of the house, decorated with kolam, the new rice is boiled with milk and jaggery in a new pot until it brims over, to cries of 'Pongalo Pongal', and offered to the Sun with sugarcane, before the family eats together.

THIRUVALLUVAR_DAY.about: Thiruvalluvar Day, the second of Thai, the day after Pongal, honours Tiruvalluvar, the poet of the Tirukkural, the classical Tamil work on virtue, wealth and love; Tamil Nadu gives its Thiruvalluvar Award on it. The same day is Mattu Pongal, when cattle are bathed, their horns painted and garlanded, and fed pongal, and in the south the bull-taming of jallikattu is held.

UZHAVAR_THIRUNAL.about: Uzhavar Thirunal, the farmers' festival, falls on the third of Thai and closes the Pongal holidays; it is also Kaanum Pongal, the day for going out and seeing family and friends. Families visit relatives and go on outings to beaches, parks and temples, sharing the last of the Pongal food; Tamil Nadu keeps the day as a public holiday.

PUTHANDU.about: Puthandu, the Tamil new year, falls on the first of Chithirai, around 14 April, when the Sun enters Aries. Houses are cleaned and decorated with kolam, families visit temples and hear the new year's almanac read, and the meal includes mango pachadi, sweet, sour and bitter at once, for the mixed fortunes of the year ahead.

THAI_POOSAM.about: Thai Poosam, the full moon of Thai when the Moon is in the asterism Pusam, is a festival of the god Murugan. It is told as the day Parvati gave him the spear, the vel, with which he overcame the demon Surapadman. Devotees fast, then walk to his hill shrines, above all Palani, carrying kavadi, and some pierce their skin with small spears; Tamils abroad keep it too, as at Batu Caves in Malaysia.

AYUDHA_PUJA.about: Ayudha Puja, on Navami, the ninth day of Navaratri in Ashwin's bright half, is the worship of tools and instruments. Tools, machines and vehicles are cleaned, marked with sandal paste and kumkum and worshipped, and workshops close; books and instruments are laid before Saraswati, and on Vijayadashami, the next day, they are taken up again and children begin their schooling.

MAGH_BIHU.about: Magh Bihu, or Bhogali Bihu, is Assam's harvest festival at the turn of the month of Magh, in mid-January. On the eve, uruka, young people build huts and a tall meji of straw and bamboo in the fields and the community feasts through the night; at dawn the meji is burnt with prayers for a good year, and the days go to pitha, laru, curd and beaten rice.

MAGH_BIHU_SECOND.about: The second day of Magh Bihu carries on Assam's harvest festival of mid-January. Families visit relatives with pitha and laru and the feasting goes on, while villages hold the traditional games of Bihu, such as tekeli bhonga, breaking pots blindfold, and contests of strength; Assam keeps the day as a holiday.

BOHAG_BIHU.about: Bohag Bihu, or Rongali Bihu, Assam's spring festival and new year, opens around 14 April, on the last day of Chaitra, with Goru Bihu, the Bihu of the cattle. Cattle are taken to the river or pond, bathed with a paste of turmeric and black gram, lightly struck with sprigs of dighloti and makhioti, and given new tethers, to songs wishing them strength.
