BOHAG_BIHU_SECOND.about: The second day of Bohag Bihu, the first of Bohag, is Manuh Bihu, the Bihu of the people and Assam's new year's day. People bathe and put on new clothes, bow to their elders and give them gamosas, the woven towels of Assam, and share pitha and sweets; in the evenings Bihu dancers and groups singing husori go from house to house.

BOHAG_BIHU_THIRD.about: The third day of Bohag Bihu is Gosai Bihu, the Bihu of the gods, when the household's deities are worshipped and prayers offered for the year ahead. The festival goes on with visits to relatives, Bihu dances and songs in the villages, and gatherings at the Bihu stages, which last well into the month.

KATI_BIHU.about: Kati Bihu, or Kongali Bihu, the Bihu of want, falls on the first of the month of Kati, in mid-October, when the rice is still growing in the fields and the granaries are low. It is a quiet day: in the evening lamps are lit at the foot of the tulsi plant, at the granary and in the paddy fields, and sky lamps are raised on bamboo poles to guard the crop.

GWTHAR_BATHOU_SAN.about: Gwthar Bathou San, kept on a Tuesday in the month of Magh, late in January, is the holy day of Bathou, the traditional faith of the Bodo people of Assam, honouring Bathoubwrai, the supreme god, whose emblem is the sijou plant at the household and village altar. Followers gather for prayers led by the douri, the priest, with offerings of flowers and fruit, songs, dances and a shared meal; Assam keeps it as a holiday.

ME_DAM_ME_PHI.about: Me-Dam-Me-Phi, 31 January, is the Tai Ahom festival of offerings to the ancestors and the gods, as its name says. Families make offerings to their dead at home, and public rites are led by the Ahom priests, the Deodhai and Bailung, chanting in Tai from the old manuscripts; Assam keeps the day as a holiday.

BIR_CHILARAI_DIVAS.about: Bir Chilarai Divas, the full moon of Magh, honours Chilarai, or Shukladhwaja, the sixteenth-century general of the Koch kingdom and brother of King Nara Narayan, whose campaigns spread Koch rule across the north-east and who was a patron of Sankardeva. Assam has kept his birth anniversary as a holiday since 2005, with tributes at his statues and meetings in his memory.

SATI_SADHANI_DIVAS.about: Sati Sadhani Divas, 21 April, honours Sadhani, the last queen of the Chutia kingdom of Sadiya, who is told to have leapt to her death from the hill of Chandragiri in 1524 rather than submit to the Ahom conquerors. Assam has kept the day since 2017, with tributes and meetings in her memory, especially in Upper Assam.

DAMODARDEVA_TITHI.about: Damodardeva Tithi, a lunar day in the Assamese month of Bohag, in April, marks the passing in 1598 of Damodardeva, a disciple of Sankardeva who founded the Patbausi satra near Barpeta and the Brahmasamhati branch of Assamese Vaishnavism. His satras and namghars keep the day with congregational singing of the Lord's name and readings of his life.

MADHABDEVA_JANMOTSAV.about: Madhabdeva Janmotsav, a lunar day in the Assamese month of Jeth, in May or June, celebrates the birth in 1489 at Letekupukhuri of Madhabdeva, the chief disciple and successor of Sankardeva, who composed the Naam Ghosa and many borgeets. Satras and namghars across Assam keep it with naam-prasanga, processions and bhaona performances.

MADHABDEVA_TIROBHAV.about: Madhabdeva Tirobhav Tithi, a lunar day in the Assamese month of Bhada, in August or September, marks the passing of Madhabdeva in 1596 at Bheladonga in Cooch Behar. The satras of Assam, above all Barpeta, keep it with naam-prasanga through the day, readings of his life and his Naam Ghosa, and offerings at the namghar.

SANKARDEVA_JANMOTSAV.about: Srimanta Sankardeva Janmotsav, the bright tenth of the Assamese month of Ahin, in September or October, celebrates the birth in 1449 at Bordowa of Sankardeva, the saint, poet and playwright who founded Assam's Ekasarana Vaishnava faith and its namghars and satras. It is kept at Bordowa and in namghars across Assam with naam-prasanga, processions and his plays, the ankiya bhaona.

SANKARDEVA_TIROBHAV.about: Srimanta Sankardeva Tirobhav Tithi, the bright second of the Assamese month of Bhada, in August or September, marks the passing of Sankardeva in 1568 at Bheladonga in Cooch Behar. Namghars and satras across Assam keep it with naam-prasanga through the day, readings from his works and offerings at the namghar.

KARAM_PUJA.about: Karam Puja, the eleventh of Bhadra's bright half, is a harvest festival of the Adivasi peoples of Chota Nagpur, among them the Oraon and Munda, kept in Assam by the tea-garden communities. Young women fast, a branch of the karam tree is brought in and set up in the dancing ground, the story of Karma and Dharma is told, and people sing and dance the jhumur around it through the night.

LACHIT_DIVAS.about: Lachit Divas, 24 November, is the birthday of Lachit Borphukan, born in 1622, the Ahom general who defeated a Mughal army in the naval battle of Saraighat on the Brahmaputra in 1671. Assam honours him with tributes and meetings, and the best passing-out cadet of India's National Defence Academy receives a gold medal in his name.

ASOM_DIVAS.about: Asom Divas, or Sukapha Divas, 2 December, honours Sukapha, the Tai prince who crossed the Patkai hills from the east and in 1228 founded the Ahom kingdom, which ruled the Brahmaputra valley for six centuries and gave Assam its name. Assam has kept the day since 1996 with meetings and tributes in his memory, especially at Charaideo, his capital.

BASAVA_JAYANTI.about: Basava Jayanti, the third of Baishakh's bright half, the day of Akshaya Tritiya, is the birthday of Basavanna, the twelfth-century poet, reformer and minister at Kalyana who led the Lingayat movement of devotion to Shiva and rejected caste and temple ritual. Lingayats carry his image in procession, and his vachanas, short poems in Kannada, are recited and sung across Karnataka.

DEVARA_DASIMAYYA_JAYANTI.about: Devara Dasimayya Jayanti, in March by the lunar calendar, honours Devara Dasimayya, the tenth- or eleventh-century weaver and devotee of Shiva who is held to be the earliest of the Kannada vachana poets, signing his verses to Ramanatha. Weaving communities, who claim him as their own, carry his image in procession and recite his vachanas; Karnataka lists the day as a restricted holiday.

MADHVA_NAVAMI.about: Madhva Navami, the ninth of Magh's bright half, recalls the day the philosopher Madhvacharya, teacher of the Dvaita school of Vedanta, is held to have left the world while teaching the Aitareya Upanishad, by tradition in 1317, retiring to Badari in the Himalayas. Madhvas keep it with worship at the Udupi Krishna temple and the mathas, readings of his works and devotional songs.

VALMIKI_JAYANTI.about: Maharshi Valmiki Jayanti, the full moon of Ashwin, honours Valmiki, the sage held to have composed the Ramayana, the adikavi or first poet. It is told that the grief of a crane whose mate was shot by a hunter moved him to speak the first shloka. The Valmiki and other communities who revere him hold processions with his image and readings of the Ramayana, in Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh and the Punjab.

KANAKADASA_JAYANTI.about: Kanakadasa Jayanti, in the month of Kartik, in November, honours Kanakadasa, the sixteenth-century poet-saint of the Haridasa movement, born a Kuruba at Kaginele, whose Kannada songs to Krishna questioned caste. At Udupi a window in the temple wall, the Kanakana kindi, is told as the place where Krishna turned to give him sight when he was kept outside. Karnataka keeps the day as a holiday with processions and his songs.

SWARNA_GOWRI_VRATA.about: Swarna Gowri Vrata, the third of Bhadra's bright half, the day before Ganesha Chaturthi, is the Karnataka form of the Gauri vow of that tithi. Married women set up an image of Gowri, Parvati, the mother of Ganesha, worship her for a happy married life, and give one another trays of gifts, the bagina, with turmeric, kumkum, bangles and a blouse piece; it is told that Gowri comes home a day before her son.

KANNADA_RAJYOTSAVA.about: Kannada Rajyotsava, 1 November, marks the forming of the Kannada-speaking state in 1956, when the States Reorganisation Act joined the Kannada regions of Bombay, Madras, Hyderabad and Coorg to Mysore State, renamed Karnataka in 1973. The red and yellow Kannada flag is raised across the state, Kannada songs and programmes fill the day, and the state gives its Rajyotsava awards.

KANYA_MARIYAMMA_JAYANTI.about: Kanya Mariyamma Jayanti, 8 September, is the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary. Among the Konkani Catholics of coastal Karnataka it is Monti Fest: after a novena in which children bring flowers to her statue each day, the new crop of rice is blessed at mass, and families share it in a vegetarian meal, the novem jevan, served on plantain leaves. Karnataka lists it as a restricted holiday.

CHRISTMAS_EVE.about: Christmas Eve, 24 December, is the eve of the feast of the birth of Jesus Christ. Christians decorate their homes with stars and cribs, carol singers go from house to house, and the night brings the midnight mass, with which Christmas begins; several Indian states give the day as a holiday.

SOURAMANA_UGADI.about: Souramana Ugadi, the new year of the solar calendar, falls on Mesha Sankranti, around 14 April, when the Sun enters Aries. It is kept in coastal Karnataka, where the Tulu-speaking people call it Bisu: the year's first sight, the Bisu kani, is arranged with the harvest, fruit and vegetables before the household gods, the elders bless the young, and the family feasts.

UTTARAYANA_PUNYAKALA.about: Uttarayana Punyakala, Makara Sankranti, around 14 January, is the day the Sun enters Capricorn and its northward course, held to be an auspicious time for bathing and giving. In Karnataka people exchange ellu-bella, a mix of sesame and jaggery, with a wish for sweet words; Gujarat fills the sky with kites, Bihar eats curd and beaten rice, and pilgrims bathe at Prayag and other tirthas.

RAMANUJACHARYA_JAYANTI.about: Ramanujacharya Jayanti honours Ramanuja, the teacher of Vishishtadvaita and of the Shri Vaishnava tradition, on the day of his birth star, Ardra, in the spring month of Chaitra or Baishakh. The Shri Vaishnava temples of southern India, and those of his followers in Nepal, mark it with worship, processions of his image and recitation of the hymns of the Alvars.

BHOGI.about: Bhogi, the day before Makara Sankranti, opens the three-day Sankranti festival in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Before dawn families light bonfires, the Bhogi mantalu, and throw old and unwanted things into them, to make way for the new; the doorsteps are decorated with coloured muggulu patterns, and in the evening young children are showered with regi fruit, the bhogi pallu, as a blessing.

KANUMU.about: Kanumu, the day after Makara Sankranti, is the third day of the Sankranti festival in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana and the day of the cattle. Cattle are bathed, their horns painted and decorated, and they are worshipped and fed in thanks for the harvest; families feast, many on meat, and visit one another, and some villages hold bull races and cockfights.

JAGJIVAN_RAM_JAYANTI.about: Babu Jagjivan Ram Jayanti, 5 April, is the birthday of Jagjivan Ram, born at Chandwa in Bihar in 1908, the Dalit leader and freedom fighter who sat in India's cabinets for some three decades, as minister of labour, of agriculture during the Green Revolution and of defence in the war of 1971, and was Deputy Prime Minister in 1977 to 1979. Tributes are paid at his statues.

BATHUKAMMA.about: Engili Pula Bathukamma, on the new moon that ends the fortnight of the dead in Bhadra, opens Bathukamma, Telangana's nine-day festival of women and of flowers, kept until Durgashtami. Each evening women stack seasonal flowers, such as tangedu and gunuka, in tiers into a cone, the bathukamma, honouring the goddess Gauri, sing and dance in a circle around it, and set it afloat on a pond or lake.

SADDULA_BATHUKAMMA.about: Saddula Bathukamma, on Durgashtami, the eighth of Ashwin's bright half, is the last and grandest day of Telangana's festival of flowers. Women build the tallest bathukammas of the nine days, sing and dance around them in great gatherings, and immerse them in lakes and tanks at dusk; the day is named for the saddulu, the flavoured rice dishes of lemon, tamarind, sesame and coconut that are offered and shared.

VIJAYA_DASHAMI_NEXT_DAY.about: The day after Vijaya Dashami, the eleventh of Ashwin's bright half, is given as a holiday in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Bihar to round off the Dasara festival. Families travel home or visit relatives after the festival, and in Bihar and elsewhere the immersion processions of the goddess's images often continue into this day.

BOXING_DAY.about: Boxing Day, 26 December, the day after Christmas, takes its name from the old English custom of giving Christmas boxes, gifts of money or goods, to servants, tradesmen and others who served through the year; it is also the feast of Saint Stephen. Telangana and Andhra Pradesh give it as a holiday, and Christians spend it with family and in visits.

CHETI_CHAND.about: Cheti Chand, the second of Chaitra's bright half, when the new moon is first seen, is the Sindhi new year and the birthday of Jhulelal, the patron saint of the Sindhis, held to be a form of the god of water. Sindhis carry the bahirano, an offering of lamp, flour, sugar and fruit, in procession to a river or the sea, sing and dance the chhej, and greet the year.

VIKRAM_SAMVAT_NEW_YEAR.about: Bestu Varas, the first of Kartik's bright half, the day after Diwali, is the Gujarati new year, the start of a new year of the Vikram Samvat as Gujarat reckons it. People rise early, visit temples, where the Annakut, a mountain of food, is offered, and go from house to house greeting relatives and friends with Saal Mubarak; merchants begin the year in the account books they worshipped at Diwali.

SARDAR_PATEL_JAYANTI.about: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Jayanti, 31 October, is the birthday of Vallabhbhai Patel, born at Nadiad in Gujarat in 1875, a leader of the freedom struggle and India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, who brought the princely states into the Union. Since 2014 India keeps the day as Rashtriya Ekta Diwas, the National Unity Day, with runs and pledges for unity, and tributes at the Statue of Unity.

MAHALAYA_AMAVASYA.about: Mahalaya Amavasya, the new moon that ends the fortnight of the dead in the dark half of Ashwin, is the day of shraddha for all the ancestors, the Sarvapitri Amavasya, kept especially for those whose death tithi is not known or was missed. Families offer water and pinda at rivers and the sea, and the next day the Navaratri of the goddess begins.

BIRUDA_PANCHAMI.about: Biruda Panchami, the fifth day of Bhadra's bright half, opens the Gaura festival of Nepal's far west. Women fast and put five kinds of grain to soak in a copper vessel; this biruda is offered to Gaura and Maheshwar over the following days, washed at the water source, and shared as prasad at the festival's height.

MAHALAXMI_VRAT_BEGINS.about: The Mahalaxmi Vrat, sixteen days of worship of Lakshmi, begins on the eighth day of Bhadra's bright half, when the eighth runs past midnight. Those who keep it, mostly women, tie on a thread of sixteen strands and sixteen knots, worship Mahalaxmi each day and keep a fast or a restricted diet for the length of the vow.

MAHALAXMI_VRAT_ENDS.about: The Mahalaxmi Vrat ends on the eighth day of Ashwin's dark half, sixteen days after it began, on the day the eighth holds the moonrise. Its closing puja is held in the evening, often before an image of Lakshmi seated on an elephant; the knotted thread is offered up, the moon is given arghya and the vow is broken with a meal.

VAT_SAVITRI_VRAT.about: Vat Savitri Vrat falls on the new moon of Jestha and recalls Savitri, who followed Yama and won back the life of her husband Satyavan. Married women fast for their husbands' long life, worship the banyan tree, the vat, and wind threads round it as they circle it, and hear Savitri's story; in Mithila it is kept as Barsait.

INDRADHWAJA_PATAN.about: Indradhwaja Patan, the lowering of Indra's banner, closes Indra Jatra on the fourth day of Ashwin's dark half. The tall pole, the lingo, raised at Hanuman Dhoka at the festival's start is ceremonially lowered that night after the last of the Kumari's chariot processions, marking the departure of the gods and the end of the festival for the year.

NANICHAYA.about: Nanichaya, on the fourth day of Ashwin's dark half, is the last of the three chariot processions of Indra Jatra in Kathmandu. The chariots of the living goddess Kumari, of Ganesh and of Bhairav are pulled from Basantapur through the old city, and when they return to Hanuman Dhoka the lingo is lowered and Indra Jatra ends.

NEPALI_ARMY_DAY.about: Nepali Army Day is kept on Maha Shivaratri, the fourteenth night of Phagun's dark half. The army marks the day with a ceremony at Tundikhel in Kathmandu before the head of state, with a parade, displays of arms and drill and a salute of guns, and units across the country hold their own celebrations.

JYAPU_DIWAS.about: Jyapu Diwas, the day of the Jyapu, the Newar farmers of the Kathmandu valley, is kept on Yomari Punhi, the full moon of Mangsir, when the rice harvest is in. Organised by the Jyapu Samaj, it is marked with processions in traditional Jyapu dress, the farmers' music and dances, and cultural programmes, alongside the day's yomari.

RAVIDAS_JAYANTI.about: Sant Ravidas Jayanti, the full moon of Magh, is the birthday of Ravidas, the fifteenth-century poet-saint of Varanasi, a leatherworker by caste, whose songs of devotion to a formless God stand in the Guru Granth Sahib. Ravidassias and others take out processions singing his hymns, read the scripture through and serve langar; many gather at his birthplace, Seer Govardhanpur in Varanasi.

AGRASEN_JAYANTI.about: Maharaja Agrasen Jayanti, the first of Ashwin's bright half, the first day of Navaratri, honours Agrasen, the legendary king of Agroha, held to be the forefather of the Agrawal community. He is told to have asked each family coming to settle in his city to be given a brick and a coin by every household. The Agrawals keep the day with processions, tributes and community meals.

HOLI_SECOND_DAY.about: The second day of Holi, which Uttar Pradesh and Bihar give as a holiday with the first, prolongs the festival of colours of early Chaitra. Where the colours were not played the day before, or in towns that keep their own day, the play goes on; elsewhere it is the day of Holi milan, when people visit one another in clean clothes, embrace and share sweets and snacks.

KARPOORI_THAKUR_JAYANTI.about: Jannayak Karpoori Thakur Jayanti, 24 January, is the birthday of Karpoori Thakur, born at Pitaunjhia, now Karpoori Gram, in Bihar's Samastipur district in 1924, the socialist leader and twice Chief Minister of Bihar who brought in reservations for the backward classes in 1978. He was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2024. Bihar and Uttar Pradesh honour him with tributes and meetings.

KASHYAP_NISHADRAJ_JAYANTI.about: Maharshi Kashyap and Maharaja Nishadraj Guhya Jayanti, 5 April, honours two figures revered by the Nishad, Kashyap and other boating and fishing communities of Uttar Pradesh: the Vedic sage Kashyapa, and Guha, king of the Nishadas at Shringaverapura, who in the Ramayana welcomes Rama in exile and ferries him across the Ganga. The communities hold processions and meetings, and the state lists the day as a holiday.

CHANDRASHEKHAR_JAYANTI.about: Chandra Shekhar Jayanti, 17 April, is the birthday of Chandra Shekhar, born at Ibrahimpatti in Uttar Pradesh's Ballia district in 1927, the socialist leader known for his walk across India, the Bharat Yatra of 1983, who was Prime Minister of India in 1990 and 1991. Uttar Pradesh lists the day among its holidays, and tributes are paid to him, especially in Ballia.

MAHARANA_PRATAP_JAYANTI.about: Lok Nayak Maharana Pratap Jayanti, 9 May, is the birthday of Pratap Singh, born at Kumbhalgarh in 1540, the ruler of Mewar who refused to submit to the Mughal emperor Akbar and fought him at Haldighati in 1576. He is honoured, especially by Rajputs, with processions, tributes at his statues and retellings of his life and of his horse Chetak.

UDA_DEVI_SHAHEED_DIWAS.about: Veerangana Uda Devi Martyrdom Day, 16 November, honours Uda Devi, a Pasi woman who fought for Awadh in the rising of 1857 and is told to have shot many British soldiers from the branches of a pipal tree at Sikandar Bagh in Lucknow before she was killed there, on 16 November 1857. The Pasi community and the state honour her with tributes at her statue at Sikandar Bagh.

CHARAN_SINGH_JAYANTI.about: Chaudhary Charan Singh Jayanti, 23 December, is the birthday of Charan Singh, born at Noorpur in western Uttar Pradesh in 1902, the leader of the farmers who carried land reform as a minister in Uttar Pradesh and was Prime Minister of India in 1979 and 1980. India keeps the day as Kisan Diwas, Farmers' Day, with meetings and tributes at his memorial, Kisan Ghat, in Delhi.

EASTER_MONDAY.about: Easter Monday, the day after Easter, continues the celebration of the resurrection of Jesus Christ; the Gospel read in many churches tells of the risen Christ meeting two disciples on the road to Emmaus. Christians keep it as a day of rest, visits and outings, and Uttar Pradesh lists it among its holidays.

UTKAL_DIVAS.about: Utkal Divas, 1 April, marks the founding of Orissa, now Odisha, as a separate province on the lines of language in 1936, formed from parts of the Bihar and Orissa province, the Madras Presidency and the Central Provinces after a long movement led by Madhusudan Das and others. Odisha keeps it as a holiday with cultural programmes and tributes to the leaders of the movement.

PAHILI_RAJA.about: Pahili Raja, the day before Mithuna Sankranti, in mid-June, is the first of the three days of Raja, Odisha's festival of the earth and of womanhood at the start of the rains, when the earth is held to be menstruating and at rest. Ploughing and digging stop, and girls and young women, in new clothes, keep from household work, play on swings hung from the trees, sing Raja songs and eat pitha.

NUAKHAI.about: Nuakhai, the fifth of Bhadra's bright half, is the harvest festival of western Odisha, the eating of the new rice. At an hour fixed by astrologers the first rice of the season is offered to the goddess Samaleswari at Sambalpur and to the household deities, and then eaten by the family together; people greet their elders with Nuakhai juhar, and the day ends with songs and dances.

SAVITRI_AMAVASYA.about: Sabitri Amabasya, the new moon of Jyeshtha, is kept in Odisha by married women for their husbands' long life. It recalls Savitri, who followed Yama, the god of death, and won back the life of her husband Satyavan. Women fast, dress as brides, and worship Savitri with fruit and offerings, often at a banyan tree, hearing her story read before they break the fast.

JHULANA_PURNIMA.about: Jhulana Purnima, the full moon of Shravan, closes the Jhulana Yatra, the swing festival in which images of Radha and Krishna are rocked on decorated swings in temples and homes for the last days of the bright fortnight, to songs and kirtan. The same full moon is Raksha Bandhan, when sisters tie rakhi on their brothers' wrists.

BAHUDA_JATRA.about: Bahuda Yatra, the tenth of Ashadha's bright half, is the return journey of the Puri chariot festival. Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra, who rode to the Gundicha temple on Ratha Yatra, the second of the same fortnight, are pulled back in their great wooden chariots to the main temple by crowds of devotees, halting on the way at the shrine of Mausi Maa, where Jagannath is offered poda pitha.

KUMAR_PURNIMA.about: Kumar Purnima, the full moon of Ashwin, is kept in Odisha by unmarried girls, in the name of Kumara, Kartikeya, the handsome son of Shiva. They rise early, bathe and put on new clothes, and fast; in the moonlit evening they worship the moon with a dish of offerings, eat together, and sing and play games, among them a game of cowrie shells.

RAHAS_PURNIMA.about: Rahas Purnima, the full moon of Kartik, is the day Odisha recalls Krishna's rasa dance with the gopis, closing the holy month of Kartik. Before dawn people bathe in rivers and tanks and float small boats of banana bark with lamps, the boita bandana, in memory of the sea voyages of Odisha's old traders, and the Bali Jatra fair opens at Cuttack.

ANLA_NAVAMI.about: Anla Navami, the ninth of Kartik's bright half, is the Akshaya Navami, kept in Odisha in the middle of the holy month of Kartik with worship of the amla tree. Women keeping the Kartik vow of simple meals, the habisha, fast and worship the amla, and many go to the temple of Sakshigopal near Puri, where the feet of Radha are shown to devotees only on this day.

PRATHAMASHTAMI.about: Prathamastami, the eighth of the dark half of Margashirsha, is the Odia festival of the first-born. The eldest child of the family, son or daughter, is given new clothes and sits before the elder women, who wave lamps and pray to the goddess Shashthi for the child's long life; a special pitha, the enduri, steamed in turmeric leaves, is made, and the maternal uncle's family sends gifts.

GURU_GOBIND_SINGH_JAYANTI.about: Guru Gobind Singh Jayanti, the seventh of Paush's bright half, is the birthday of Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru of the Sikhs, born at Patna in 1666, who founded the Khalsa in 1699 and named the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, as the Guru after him. Sikhs read the scripture through, take out processions led by five Khalsa in saffron, and serve langar; Takht Patna Sahib, his birthplace, draws pilgrims.

RAM_MOHAN_ROY_JAYANTI.about: Raja Ram Mohan Roy Jayanti, 22 May, is the birthday of Ram Mohan Roy, born at Radhanagar in Bengal in 1772, the scholar and reformer who campaigned against sati, which was abolished in 1829, argued for modern education and women's rights, and founded the Brahmo Sabha. Odisha lists the day among its holidays, and meetings are held in his memory.

BRAHMO_SAMAJ_FOUNDATION_DAY.about: Brahmo Samaj Foundation Day, 20 August, marks the first meeting in Calcutta in 1828 of the Brahmo Sabha, founded by Ram Mohan Roy, which grew into the Brahmo Samaj, a reforming movement that worshipped one formless God without images. Brahmo congregations hold services of prayer, hymns and readings on the day, and Odisha lists it among its holidays.

GEN_Z_MARTYRS_DAY.about: Gen Z Martyrs' Day falls on the twenty-third of Bhadra, in early September. It remembers the young people killed on Bhadra 23 and 24, VS 2082 (8 and 9 September 2025), in the Gen Z protests against corruption and a social-media ban that brought down the government. The state named the day in VS 2082, and it is kept with candlelight vigils and tributes to those declared martyrs.

BP_SMRITI_DIWAS.about: BP Smriti Diwas falls on the sixth of Shrawan, in July, the anniversary of the death of Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala on Shrawan 6, VS 2039 (21 July 1982). BP, as he is known, was Nepal's first elected prime minister, a leader of the Nepali Congress and a novelist. His party and admirers lay garlands at his statues and hold memorial programmes.

KAMAIYA_MUKTI_DIWAS.about: Kamaiya Mukti Diwas, Kamaiya Liberation Day, falls on the second of Shrawan, in July. It recalls Shrawan 2, VS 2057 (17 July 2000), when the government declared the kamaiyas free: bonded labourers, mostly Tharu, held by debt to landlords in the western Terai. Freed kamaiya families and their organisations hold rallies and programmes on rehabilitation and land.

MADAN_ASHRIT_SMRITI_DIWAS.about: Madan-Ashrit Smriti Diwas falls on the third of Jestha, in May. It remembers Madan Bhandari, general secretary of the CPN-UML, and Jivraj Ashrit, its leader, who died when their jeep fell into the Trishuli river at Dasdhunga, Chitwan, on Jestha 3, VS 2050 (16 May 1993). Their party marks it with tributes and programmes across the country.

NATIONAL_RECONCILIATION_DAY.about: National Unity and Reconciliation Day falls on the sixteenth of Poush, at the end of December. It recalls Poush 16, VS 2033 (30 December 1976), when Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala returned to Nepal from eight years of exile in India, calling for national unity and reconciliation, and was arrested on arrival. The Nepali Congress and his followers mark it with programmes.

NATIONAL_SCIENCE_DAY.about: National Science and Technology Day falls on the first of Asoj, in mid-September, the founding day of Amrit Science Campus in Kathmandu, Nepal's first science college. First kept in VS 2070, it is marked by scientists, science teachers and students with exhibitions, talks and programmes on science and technology in Nepal.

NATIONAL_TEA_DAY.about: National Tea Day falls on the fifteenth of Baisakh, in late April or early May. It is kept by the National Tea and Coffee Development Board to promote Nepali tea, grown above all in the eastern hills of Ilam, Dhankuta and Panchthar and in Jhapa, and the farmers and workers who produce it. It is marked with programmes, tastings and fairs.

NEPAL_NURSING_DAY.about: Nepal Nursing Day falls on the fifteenth of Magh, in late January, the day the Nursing Association of Nepal was founded in VS 2018, one of the country's oldest professional bodies. Nurses mark it with programmes on their profession, the honouring of senior nurses, and health camps.

INTERNATIONAL_MOTHER_LANGUAGE_DAY.about: International Mother Language Day, on 21 February, was proclaimed by UNESCO in 1999 to promote linguistic and cultural diversity and teaching in the mother tongue. The date recalls the students killed in Dhaka on 21 February 1952 while demanding recognition for Bangla. In Nepal, home to more than a hundred languages, language bodies hold programmes and readings.

WORLD_HEALTH_DAY.about: World Health Day, on 7 April, marks the founding of the World Health Organization, whose constitution came into force on 7 April 1948. Each year the WHO chooses a theme of global health for the day. In Nepal the health ministry, hospitals and health workers hold free health camps, rallies and programmes on that theme.

EARTH_DAY.about: Earth Day, International Mother Earth Day, falls on 22 April. It began in the United States in 1970 as a day of action for the environment, and the UN General Assembly proclaimed it International Mother Earth Day in 2009, recognising the earth and its ecosystems as our common home. It is kept with tree planting, clean-ups and programmes on protecting the planet.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_FAMILIES.about: The International Day of Families, on 15 May, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 1993 to draw attention to families as the basic unit of society and to the social, economic and demographic changes that affect them. It is marked with programmes and discussions on family welfare, care for children and elders, and balance between work and home.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_UNITED_NATIONS_PEAC.about: The International Day of United Nations Peacekeepers, on 29 May, honours the men and women who serve in UN peace operations and remembers those who died in service. The date recalls the first UN peacekeeping mission, in 1948. Nepal, among the largest contributors of troops and police since 1958, marks it with ceremonies honouring its peacekeepers and their fallen.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_YOGA.about: The International Day of Yoga, on 21 June, the longest day of the year in the northern hemisphere, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2014 to spread awareness of the health benefits of yoga. Across Nepal, yoga centres, schools and government offices hold mass yoga sessions in parks and public squares in the morning.

INTERNATIONAL_YOUTH_DAY.about: International Youth Day, on 12 August, was endorsed by the UN General Assembly in 1999, following the World Conference of Ministers Responsible for Youth at Lisbon in 1998. It draws attention to young people's issues and their part in society. In Nepal youth organisations and the National Youth Council hold programmes, rallies and sports events.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_OLDER_PERSONS.about: The International Day of Older Persons, on 1 October, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 1990 to recognise the contribution of older people and to raise the issues of ageing. In Nepal it is kept as Senior Citizens' Day, when local governments and organisations honour elders, hold health camps and run programmes on their care and rights.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_NON_VIOLENCE.about: The International Day of Non-Violence, on 2 October, is the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, born in 1869, the leader of India's independence movement and of non-violent resistance. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 2007 to spread the message of non-violence through education and public awareness. It is marked with programmes on peace and tolerance.

WORLD_TEACHERS_DAY.about: World Teachers' Day, on 5 October, marks the adoption on 5 October 1966 of the ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers, which set out teachers' rights and duties. Kept by UNESCO since 1994, it celebrates teachers' work. In Nepal teachers' unions and schools hold programmes and honour teachers.

WORLD_MENTAL_HEALTH_DAY.about: World Mental Health Day, on 10 October, was begun in 1992 by the World Federation for Mental Health and is supported by the World Health Organization. It raises awareness of mental illness, seeks to end the stigma around it, and calls for better care. In Nepal hospitals, psychiatrists and support groups hold talks, walks and programmes.

WORLD_FOOD_DAY.about: World Food Day, on 16 October, marks the founding of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations in 1945. Proclaimed by the FAO in 1979, it calls for action against hunger and for food security and sustainable farming. In Nepal the agriculture ministry and farm groups hold programmes and food fairs.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_FOR_THE_ERADICATION_OF.about: The International Day for the Eradication of Poverty, on 17 October, recalls the gathering of some hundred thousand people at the Trocadéro in Paris on 17 October 1987 to honour the victims of extreme poverty. The UN General Assembly recognised it in 1992. It is marked with programmes that give voice to people living in poverty.

WORLD_CHILDREN_S_DAY.about: World Children's Day, on 20 November, marks the dates on which the UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of the Child in 1959 and the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989. First set as Universal Children's Day in 1954, it promotes children's welfare and their rights. Schools and child-rights groups hold programmes in which children take part.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_FOR_THE_ELIMINATION_OF.about: The International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, on 25 November, recalls the Mirabal sisters, political activists murdered in the Dominican Republic on that date in 1960. Designated by the UN General Assembly in 1999, it opens sixteen days of activism against gender-based violence, which in Nepal are kept with rallies and programmes until Human Rights Day.

WORLD_AIDS_DAY.about: World AIDS Day, on 1 December, was first kept in 1988, the first international day for global health. It raises awareness of HIV and AIDS, remembers those who have died, and supports people living with HIV. Health workers and support groups in Nepal mark it with red-ribbon rallies, free testing and candlelight vigils.

INTERNATIONAL_VOLUNTEER_DAY.about: International Volunteer Day, on 5 December, was designated by the UN General Assembly in 1985 to thank volunteers and to promote volunteering for economic and social development. Coordinated by the UN Volunteers programme, it is marked with recognition of volunteers' work, community clean-ups and service projects.

INTERNATIONAL_ANTI_CORRUPTION_DAY.about: International Anti-Corruption Day, on 9 December, was designated by the UN General Assembly in 2003, when it adopted the United Nations Convention against Corruption, which opened for signature at Mérida that December. In Nepal the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority and civil groups hold programmes on good governance and fighting corruption.

INTERNATIONAL_MOUNTAIN_DAY.about: International Mountain Day, on 11 December, was designated by the UN General Assembly after the International Year of Mountains, 2002, and has been kept since 2003. It highlights the importance of mountains for fresh water, food and biodiversity, and the lives of mountain people. Nepal, home to eight of the world's ten highest peaks, marks it with programmes on mountain livelihoods and climate.

INTERNATIONAL_MIGRANTS_DAY.about: International Migrants Day, on 18 December, recalls the adoption on that date in 1990 of the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families. It was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2000. In Nepal, from which millions work abroad, it is kept with programmes on the rights and safety of migrant workers.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_EDUCATION.about: The International Day of Education, on 24 January, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2018 to celebrate the role of education in peace and development. It calls for inclusive, good-quality education for every child and adult, with UNESCO leading the observance. Schools and education bodies mark it with programmes and discussions.

WORLD_WETLANDS_DAY.about: World Wetlands Day, on 2 February, marks the signing of the Convention on Wetlands at Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971, and became a United Nations day in 2021. It raises awareness of wetlands such as lakes, marshes and floodplains, which shelter wildlife and store water. In Nepal, which lists ten wetlands under the convention, it is kept with clean-ups and programmes.

WORLD_RADIO_DAY.about: World Radio Day, on 13 February, marks the day United Nations Radio began broadcasting in 1946. Proclaimed by UNESCO in 2011 and endorsed by the General Assembly in 2012, it celebrates radio as a medium that reaches the widest audience. In Nepal, where community radio serves remote areas, broadcasters hold programmes and special broadcasts.

WORLD_DAY_OF_SOCIAL_JUSTICE.about: The World Day of Social Justice, on 20 February, was declared by the UN General Assembly in 2007 and first kept in 2009. It supports efforts to end poverty, promote full employment and decent work, and secure equality between men and women and social well-being for all. It is marked with programmes on fair work and social protection.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_HAPPINESS.about: The International Day of Happiness, on 20 March, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2012, on an initiative of Bhutan, to recognise happiness and well-being as goals that public policy should pursue alongside economic growth. Since 2013 it has been marked with talks and campaigns, and the World Happiness Report is released around the day.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_FOR_THE_ELIMINATION_OF.about: The International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, on 21 March, recalls 21 March 1960, when police at Sharpeville in South Africa opened fire on a peaceful protest against apartheid's pass laws and killed sixty-nine people. The UN General Assembly proclaimed it in 1966. It is marked with programmes against racism and discrimination of every kind.

WORLD_METEOROLOGICAL_DAY.about: World Meteorological Day, on 23 March, marks the coming into force of the convention that created the World Meteorological Organization on 23 March 1950. Each year it takes a theme on weather, climate or water. In Nepal the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology marks it with programmes and open days on forecasting and climate.

WORLD_AUTISM_AWARENESS_DAY.about: World Autism Awareness Day, on 2 April, was designated by the UN General Assembly in 2007 to raise awareness of autism and to support the full participation of autistic people in society. Buildings are lit in blue in many places, and in Nepal parents' groups and care organisations hold walks and programmes on early diagnosis and inclusion.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_SPORT_FOR_DEVELOPME.about: The International Day of Sport for Development and Peace, on 6 April, recalls the opening of the first modern Olympic Games at Athens on 6 April 1896. Proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2013, it celebrates the power of sport to promote health, peace and social change. In Nepal it is kept as World Sports Day, with games, runs and sports programmes.

INTERNATIONAL_WELLNESS_DAY.about: International Wellness Day, on 15 April, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly on 10 March 2026 on a resolution put forward by Nepal. It promotes awareness of the benefits of practising wellness, through healthy ways of living and the traditional knowledge of peoples and communities, beside the days of yoga and meditation, and is marked with wellness programmes.

WORLD_BOOK_AND_COPYRIGHT_DAY.about: World Book and Copyright Day, on 23 April, was proclaimed by UNESCO in 1995 to promote reading, publishing and the protection of authors' rights. The date was chosen because Miguel de Cervantes and William Shakespeare both died around 23 April 1616. Libraries, schools and publishers mark it with book fairs, readings and talks.

WORLD_MALARIA_DAY.about: World Malaria Day, on 25 April, was established by the World Health Assembly in 2007, growing out of Africa Malaria Day. It draws attention to the prevention and control of malaria, a disease carried by mosquitoes. In Nepal, where malaria persists in parts of the Terai and inner valleys, health offices hold awareness programmes and distribute bed nets.

WORLD_INTELLECTUAL_PROPERTY_DAY.about: World Intellectual Property Day, on 26 April, marks the coming into force of the convention establishing the World Intellectual Property Organization on 26 April 1970. Set by WIPO's member states in 2000, it shows how patents, trademarks, designs and copyright encourage invention and creativity. It is marked with talks and programmes on protecting creative work.

WORLD_REMEMBRANCE_AND_RECONCILIATION_DAY.about: The Time of Remembrance and Reconciliation for Those Who Lost Their Lives During the Second World War spans 8 and 9 May, the anniversary of the war's end in Europe in 1945. Declared by the UN General Assembly in 2004, it invites countries to honour all the war's victims, soldiers and civilians, and to reflect on reconciliation, with ceremonies and wreath-layings.

WORLD_TELECOMMUNICATION_AND_INFORMATION_.about: World Telecommunication and Information Society Day, on 17 May, marks the founding of the International Telecommunication Union, signed at Paris on 17 May 1865. The UN General Assembly gave the day its present name in 2006, after the World Summit on the Information Society. It is marked with programmes on connecting everyone to telecommunications and the internet.

WORLD_BEE_DAY.about: World Bee Day, on 20 May, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2017 on a proposal from Slovenia. The date is the birthday of Anton Janša, born in 1734, a Slovenian pioneer of modern beekeeping. It draws attention to bees and other pollinators and their part in food production. In Nepal beekeepers and agricultural offices hold honey fairs and programmes.

WORLD_CULTURE_DAY.about: The World Day for Cultural Diversity for Dialogue and Development, on 21 May, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2002, after UNESCO's Universal Declaration on Cultural Diversity of 2001. It celebrates the richness of the world's cultures and the part dialogue between them plays in peace and development. It is marked with cultural performances and programmes.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_FOR_BIOLOGICAL_DIVERSI.about: The International Day for Biological Diversity, on 22 May, marks the adoption of the text of the Convention on Biological Diversity on 22 May 1992. The UN General Assembly moved the day to this date in 2000. It raises awareness of the variety of life on earth and the threats it faces. In Nepal forest and conservation offices hold programmes and plantings.

GLOBAL_DAY_OF_PARENTS.about: The Global Day of Parents, on 1 June, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2012 to honour parents throughout the world for their commitment to their children and their lifelong sacrifice. It recognises the family's primary responsibility for raising and protecting children, and is marked with programmes on parenting and family life.

WORLD_BICYCLE_DAY.about: World Bicycle Day, on 3 June, was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2018 to recognise the bicycle as a simple, affordable, clean and lasting means of transport that serves health and the environment. Cycling groups in Kathmandu and other cities mark it with group rides and calls for safe cycle lanes.

WORLD_OCEANS_DAY.about: World Oceans Day, on 8 June, was first proposed at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 and recognised by the UN General Assembly in 2008. It celebrates the oceans, which cover most of the planet and shape its climate, and calls for their protection from pollution and overfishing. It is marked with clean-ups and programmes.

WORLD_DAY_AGAINST_CHILD_LABOUR.about: The World Day Against Child Labour, on 12 June, was launched by the International Labour Organization in 2002 to focus attention on the millions of children who work instead of going to school, many in hazardous conditions. In Nepal the labour ministry, unions and child-rights groups hold rallies and programmes to end child labour.

WORLD_BLOOD_DONOR_DAY.about: World Blood Donor Day, on 14 June, is the birthday of Karl Landsteiner, born in 1868, who discovered the ABO blood groups. Established by the World Health Assembly in 2005, it thanks voluntary, unpaid blood donors and encourages more people to give blood. In Nepal the Red Cross and hospitals hold blood donation drives and honour regular donors.

WORLD_DAY_TO_COMBAT_DESERTIFICATION_AND_.about: The World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought, on 17 June, marks the adoption of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification on 17 June 1994, and was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly that year. It raises awareness of land degradation and drought and of ways to restore land. It is marked with tree planting and programmes.

WORLD_REFUGEE_DAY.about: World Refugee Day, on 20 June, was designated by the UN General Assembly in 2000, the fiftieth year of the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, and has been kept since 2001. It honours the strength of people forced to flee their homes and calls for their protection. Nepal, which has long hosted Tibetan and Bhutanese refugees, marks it with programmes.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_AGAINST_DRUG_ABUSE_AND.about: The International Day against Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking, on 26 June, was decided by the UN General Assembly in 1987, after an international conference on the subject held in Vienna. It calls for action against drug abuse and the drug trade. In Nepal the police, the home ministry and rehabilitation centres hold rallies and awareness programmes.

MICRO_SMALL_AND_MEDIUM_SIZED_ENTERPRISES.about: Micro-, Small and Medium-sized Enterprises Day, on 27 June, was designated by the UN General Assembly in 2017 to recognise the part small businesses play in jobs, livelihoods and sustainable development. In Nepal, where most firms are small and family-run, business associations and the industry ministry mark it with fairs and programmes.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_SIGN_LANGUAGES.about: The International Day of Sign Languages, on 23 September, marks the founding of the World Federation of the Deaf on that date in 1951, and was proclaimed by the UN General Assembly in 2017. It raises awareness of sign languages and of the rights of deaf people. In Nepal the National Federation of the Deaf holds rallies and programmes on Nepali Sign Language.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_FOR_THE_TOTAL_ELIMINAT.about: The International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons, on 26 September, was declared by the UN General Assembly in 2013, after its first high-level meeting on nuclear disarmament. It calls on the world to reduce and finally abolish nuclear weapons, and is marked with meetings and public programmes on disarmament.

WORLD_POST_DAY.about: World Post Day, on 9 October, marks the founding of the Universal Postal Union at Bern on 9 October 1874. Declared by the union's congress at Tokyo in 1969, it recalls the part the post plays in everyday life and trade. Nepal, a member of the union since 1956, marks it with programmes and stamp exhibitions by the postal service.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_FOR_DISASTER_RISK_REDU.about: The International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction, on 13 October, was first kept in 1989 and fixed to this date by the UN General Assembly in 2009. It promotes a culture of preparing for and reducing the risk of disasters. In Nepal, exposed to earthquakes, floods and landslides, the disaster authorities hold drills and awareness programmes.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_RURAL_WOMEN.about: The International Day of Rural Women, on 15 October, was established by the UN General Assembly in 2007 and first kept in 2008. It recognises the part rural women play in farming, food security and the life of rural communities, and the hardships they face. In Nepal, where women do much of the farm work, it is marked with programmes and honours for women farmers.

WORLD_DEVELOPMENT_INFORMATION_DAY.about: World Development Information Day, on 24 October, the same date as United Nations Day, was instituted by the UN General Assembly in 1972 to draw public attention to the problems of development and the need for international cooperation in solving them. It is marked with programmes on spreading information about development.

WORLD_CITIES_DAY.about: World Cities Day, on 31 October, was designated by the UN General Assembly in 2013 and is led by UN-Habitat. It promotes cooperation in meeting the opportunities and challenges of cities as more of the world's people live in them. In Nepal's fast-growing cities, municipalities and planners hold programmes on urban planning, housing and services.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_FOR_TOLERANCE.about: The International Day for Tolerance, on 16 November, marks the adoption by UNESCO's member states of the Declaration of Principles on Tolerance on 16 November 1995, the United Nations Year for Tolerance. It promotes respect and understanding among cultures and peoples, and is marked with programmes on living together in diversity.

WORLD_TOILET_DAY.about: World Toilet Day, on 19 November, was begun by the World Toilet Organization in 2001 and made a United Nations day in 2013. It draws attention to the billions of people who live without safe sanitation. Nepal, declared free of open defecation in 2019, marks it with programmes on clean, safe toilets for all.

WORLD_TELEVISION_DAY.about: World Television Day, on 21 November, marks the first World Television Forum, held at the United Nations on 21 and 22 November 1996. Proclaimed by the General Assembly that year, it recognises television's influence on decision-making and on drawing the world's attention to conflict and development. Broadcasters mark it with programmes.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_FOR_THE_ABOLITION_OF_S.about: The International Day for the Abolition of Slavery, on 2 December, marks the adoption by the UN General Assembly on 2 December 1949 of the Convention for the Suppression of the Traffic in Persons. It focuses on ending modern forms of slavery, such as trafficking, forced labour, bonded labour and forced marriage. Nepal abolished its kamaiya and haliya systems of bonded labour in 2000 and 2008.

WORLD_SOIL_DAY.about: World Soil Day, on 5 December, was designated by the UN General Assembly in 2013 on the FAO's recommendation, and is the birthday of King Bhumibol of Thailand, a patron of the cause. It draws attention to healthy soil and its sustainable management. In Nepal the soil science and agriculture offices mark it with soil testing and programmes for farmers.

INTERNATIONAL_CIVIL_AVIATION_DAY.about: International Civil Aviation Day, on 7 December, marks the signing of the Convention on International Civil Aviation at Chicago on 7 December 1944, which created the International Civil Aviation Organization. It was recognised by the UN General Assembly in 1996. In Nepal the civil aviation authority marks it with programmes on air safety and connectivity.

INTERNATIONAL_CUSTOMS_DAY.about: International Customs Day, on 26 January, marks the first session of the Customs Co-operation Council, now the World Customs Organization, held in Brussels on 26 January 1953. It honours the work of customs officers in collecting revenue, easing trade and guarding borders. Nepal's Department of Customs marks it with programmes and awards for its staff.

WORLD_CANCER_DAY.about: World Cancer Day, on 4 February, is led by the Union for International Cancer Control and grew out of the Charter of Paris against Cancer signed on 4 February 2000. It aims to raise awareness of cancer and press for its prevention, early detection and treatment. In Nepal hospitals and cancer societies hold screening camps, rallies and talks.

INTERNATIONAL_CHILDHOOD_CANCER_DAY.about: International Childhood Cancer Day, on 15 February, is kept by Childhood Cancer International, a network of parents' and survivors' groups, since 2002. It draws attention to children and adolescents with cancer, their families and survivors, and to their need for timely diagnosis and treatment. Children's hospitals and support groups in Nepal mark it with programmes.

WORLD_CONSUMER_RIGHTS_DAY.about: World Consumer Rights Day, on 15 March, recalls 15 March 1962, when US President John Kennedy told Congress of consumers' rights to safety, information, choice and to be heard. Kept by Consumers International since 1983, it presses for fair and safe markets. Consumer groups and the government in Nepal mark it with rallies and programmes on market checks.

WORLD_ORAL_HEALTH_DAY.about: World Oral Health Day, on 20 March, is kept by the FDI World Dental Federation to raise awareness of the health of the mouth and teeth and its link with general health. Dentists and dental colleges in Nepal mark it with free dental check-ups, school programmes on brushing and talks on preventing tooth decay and gum disease.

WORLD_THEATRE_DAY.about: World Theatre Day, on 27 March, was begun in 1961 by the International Theatre Institute and first kept in 1962. Each year a figure of the stage writes an international message that is read out in theatres worldwide. Theatre groups in Nepal mark it with plays, readings of the message and the honouring of artists.

INTERNATIONAL_DANCE_DAY.about: International Dance Day, on 29 April, was begun in 1982 by the Dance Committee of the International Theatre Institute. The date is the birthday of Jean-Georges Noverre, the eighteenth-century French ballet master who reformed dance as an art. Dance schools and troupes in Nepal mark it with performances of classical, folk and modern dance.

INTERNATIONAL_NURSES_DAY.about: International Nurses Day, on 12 May, is the birthday of Florence Nightingale, born in 1820, whose work in the Crimean War founded modern nursing. The International Council of Nurses has kept it since 1974 with a theme each year. Nurses in Nepal mark it with programmes, the lighting of lamps and the honouring of nurses.

INTERNATIONAL_DAY_OF_ACTION_FOR_WOMEN_S_.about: The International Day of Action for Women's Health falls on 28 May. It was called at the International Women and Health Meeting in Costa Rica in 1987 and is coordinated by women's health networks. It presses for women's health and their sexual and reproductive rights, and in Nepal is marked with health camps, rallies and programmes on safe motherhood.

WORLD_MUSIC_DAY.about: World Music Day, on 21 June, began as the Fête de la musique, first held by the French Ministry of Culture in 1982 on the day of the June solstice. Musicians of every kind play free in streets and public places, and the idea has spread to many countries. In Nepal it is marked with open-air concerts in Kathmandu and other towns.

WORLD_PHYSIOTHERAPY_DAY.about: World Physiotherapy Day, on 8 September, marks the founding of World Physiotherapy, then the World Confederation for Physical Therapy, in 1951. Kept since 1996, it honours the work of physiotherapists in helping people move and recover from injury and illness. Physiotherapists in Nepal mark it with free check-up camps and programmes.

WORLD_ALZHEIMER_S_DAY.about: World Alzheimer's Day, on 21 September, has been kept since 1994 by Alzheimer's Disease International, within the World Alzheimer's Month of September. It raises awareness of Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, and of the stigma that people living with them and their carers face. It is marked with programmes on memory and the care of older people.

WORLD_RABIES_DAY.about: World Rabies Day, on 28 September, is the anniversary of the death of Louis Pasteur, who made the first rabies vaccine. Kept since 2007 by the Global Alliance for Rabies Control, it presses for the end of deaths from rabies, which spreads mostly through dog bites. In Nepal it is marked with dog vaccination campaigns and awareness programmes.

WORLD_HEART_DAY.about: World Heart Day, on 29 September, is kept by the World Heart Federation to raise awareness of heart disease and stroke, the world's leading causes of death, and of the ways to reduce the risk. Hospitals and heart groups in Nepal mark it with free check-ups, walks and talks on diet, exercise and quitting tobacco.

WORLD_ANIMAL_DAY.about: World Animal Day, on 4 October, the feast of Saint Francis of Assisi, patron saint of animals, was begun by Heinrich Zimmermann in Berlin in 1925 and adopted by an international animal-protection congress in Florence in 1931. It promotes animal welfare. Animal-welfare groups in Nepal mark it with free vaccination and treatment for street animals and programmes on their care.

GLOBAL_HANDWASHING_DAY.about: Global Handwashing Day, on 15 October, was begun in 2008 by the Global Handwashing Partnership. It promotes washing hands with soap at key times, a simple habit that prevents diarrhoea, pneumonia and other infections. In Nepal schools and health workers mark it with handwashing demonstrations for children.

NATIONAL_MAGAR_DAY.about: National Magar Day falls on the fifteenth of Falgun, in late February. It marks the founding of the Nepal Magar Sangh, the Magar people's organisation, which grew from the first national convention of the Nepal Langhali Parivar Sangh, held in Tanahun in VS 2039. Magar communities across Nepal mark it with rallies in traditional dress, cultural performances and programmes on their language and culture.

PASANG_LHAMU_SMRITI_DIWAS.about: Pasang Lhamu Smriti Diwas falls on the tenth of Baisakh, in late April. It remembers Pasang Lhamu Sherpa, the first Nepali woman to climb Everest, who reached the summit on 22 April 1993 and died on the way down. The Pasang Lhamu Sherpa Mountaineering Foundation and climbers mark it with tributes and programmes.

SOCIAL_SERVICE_DAY.about: Social Service Day falls on the sixth of Asoj, in September. It is kept by the Social Welfare Council, the government body that coordinates Nepal's non-governmental organisations, together with social organisations, to honour voluntary social service. It is marked with programmes and the honouring of social workers.

NATIONAL_BHAKKA_DAY.about: National Bhakka Day falls on the twenty-ninth of Poush, in January. It is kept by the Koch Rajbanshi and other indigenous communities of the eastern Terai to celebrate bhakka, a cake of rice flour steamed over a pot and eaten in the cold months. They mark it by making and sharing bhakka, with cultural programmes in traditional dress.

NATIONAL_FLAG_DAY.about: National Flag Day falls on the first of Poush, in mid-December. It honours Nepal's flag, the only national flag in the world that is not a rectangle: two stacked crimson pennants with a blue border, bearing a white moon and sun. The day is kept with flag-raising and programmes on the flag's meaning and the rules for drawing it.

NATIONAL_YOGA_DAY.about: National Yoga Day falls on the first of Magh, Maghe Sankranti, in mid-January. The Council of Ministers named the day in VS 2072 to promote yoga as part of Nepal's heritage and health. Yoga centres, ashrams and schools hold group yoga and meditation sessions and talks on the practice.

NATIONAL_JOURNALISM_DAY.about: National Journalism Day falls on the twenty-fourth of Baisakh, in May. It recalls Baisakh 24, VS 1958 (1901), when the first issue of the Gorkhapatra, Nepal's first newspaper and now its oldest daily, came out as a weekly. The government recognised the day in VS 2073, and journalists mark it with programmes and awards.

NATIONAL_FILM_DAY.about: National Film Day falls on the fifteenth of Asoj, in early October. The Council of Ministers named it in VS 2082 to honour Nepali cinema, choosing the date on which Aama, the first feature film made in Nepal, was first shown. The film industry and the Film Development Board mark it with screenings, talks and awards.

LANGUAGE_DAY.about: Language Day falls on the twenty-fourth of Baisakh, in May, and is kept by Bagmati Province. It recalls Baisakh 24, VS 2081, when the province's offices began to use Tamang and Nepal Bhasa beside Nepali under its official-language act. The province gives a public holiday, and language bodies hold programmes and readings.

SINDOOR_JATRA.about: Sindoor Jatra, the vermilion festival, is held in Madhyapur Thimi on the second of Baisakh, the day after the new year. Palanquins of the town's deities are carried to the temple of the goddess Balkumari and around it to the sound of drums, while the crowds throw handfuls of orange-red vermilion over the gods and one another until the streets are coloured.

NATIONAL_DRESS_DAY.about: National Dress Day falls on 1 January and has been kept since VS 2070 by youth organisations as the National Dress and Topi Day. It encourages people to wear Nepal's national dress, the daura-suruwal for men and the gunyu-cholo or sari for women, on the first day of the Gregorian year, with rallies and gatherings in national dress.

NATIONAL_TOPI_DAY.about: National Topi Day falls on 1 January, kept since VS 2070 by youth organisations together with National Dress Day. It honours the Nepali topi, above all the dhaka topi woven in Palpa patterns and the plain black bhadgaule topi, and encourages people to wear one on the first day of the Gregorian year.

VALENTINE_S_DAY.about: Valentine's Day, on 14 February, takes its name from Saint Valentine, a Christian martyr of Rome whose feast falls that day. Since the late Middle Ages it has been linked with romantic love, and it is now kept in many countries, Nepal's towns among them, by couples who exchange cards, roses and gifts.

PI_DAY.about: Pi Day, on 14 March, is named for the date written in the American style as 3/14, the first digits of pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. Begun in 1988 at the Exploratorium in San Francisco, it is kept by teachers and students with mathematics puzzles and talks; UNESCO has kept the same date as the International Day of Mathematics since 2020.

APRIL_FOOLS_DAY.about: April Fools' Day, on 1 April, is a custom of playing harmless tricks and spreading hoaxes, after which the one fooled is called an April fool. Its origin is uncertain, but it has been known in Europe for some five centuries. It is now kept in many countries, Nepal included, by friends, the press and online.

WORLD_HERITAGE_DAY.about: World Heritage Day, the International Day for Monuments and Sites, falls on 18 April. Proposed by the International Council on Monuments and Sites in 1982 and approved by UNESCO in 1983, it promotes the protection of cultural heritage. Nepal, with the Kathmandu Valley's monuments and Lumbini on the World Heritage List, marks it with heritage walks, exhibitions and programmes.

WORLD_HYPERTENSION_DAY.about: World Hypertension Day, on 17 May, is kept by the World Hypertension League to raise awareness of high blood pressure, a leading cause of heart disease and stroke that often goes unnoticed. Hospitals and health groups mark it with free blood-pressure checks and programmes on diet, exercise and treatment.

SAGARMATHA_DAY.about: Sagarmatha Day, International Everest Day, falls on 29 May. It recalls 29 May 1953, when Tenzing Norgay Sherpa and Edmund Hillary became the first to stand on the summit of Sagarmatha, Mount Everest. In Nepal climbers, the tourism trade and the Sherpa community mark it with rallies, the honouring of mountaineers and programmes on the mountains.

INTERNATIONAL_OLYMPIC_DAY.about: International Olympic Day, on 23 June, marks the founding of the International Olympic Committee at the Sorbonne in Paris on 23 June 1894. Kept since 1948, it encourages people of all ages to take part in sport. The Nepal Olympic Committee marks it with an Olympic Day run and sports events.

WORLD_PHARMACISTS_DAY.about: World Pharmacists Day, on 25 September, marks the founding of the International Pharmaceutical Federation in 1912. The federation's council instituted it in 2009 to honour pharmacists' part in health care and the safe use of medicines. Pharmacists' associations in Nepal mark it with programmes and health camps.

NON_RESIDENT_NEPALI_DAY.about: Non-Resident Nepali Day falls on 11 October, the day the Non-Resident Nepali Association was founded at its first global conference in Kathmandu in 2003. Declared NRN Day by the government, it honours Nepalis living abroad and their ties to and investment in the homeland. The association's councils around the world mark it with gatherings.

WORLD_STANDARDS_DAY.about: World Standards Day, on 14 October, recalls the meeting of delegates from twenty-five countries in London on 14 October 1946 that led to the founding of the International Organization for Standardization. Kept since 1970 by ISO, the IEC and the ITU, it honours the work of making international standards. In Nepal the standards bureau marks it with programmes.

WORLD_RADIOGRAPHY_DAY.about: World Radiography Day, on 8 November, marks the discovery of X-rays by Wilhelm Röntgen on 8 November 1895. Kept by the International Society of Radiographers and Radiological Technologists, it honours radiographers and the part medical imaging plays in diagnosis. Radiographers' societies in Nepal hold programmes and awareness events.

WORLD_FREEDOM_DAY.about: World Freedom Day, on 9 November, recalls the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989, which led to the end of communist rule in central and eastern Europe. It is proclaimed each year by the President of the United States, as it has been since 2001, and is marked with programmes on freedom and democracy.

INTERNATIONAL_STUDENTS_DAY.about: International Students' Day, on 17 November, recalls 17 November 1939, when the Nazi occupiers stormed the universities of Prague, executed student leaders and sent many students to concentration camps. First kept in 1941, it honours students' activism and their right to education. Student unions mark it with rallies and programmes.

WORLD_FIRST_AID_DAY.about: World First Aid Day falls on the second Saturday of September. Begun by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in 2000, it promotes first-aid training so that more people can save lives in an emergency. The Nepal Red Cross Society marks it with demonstrations and first-aid training.

WORLD_SMILE_DAY.about: World Smile Day falls on the first Friday of October. It was launched in 1999 by Harvey Ball, the American artist who drew the yellow smiley face in 1963, to set aside a day for smiles and acts of kindness. It is marked by schools and community groups with small kindnesses and cheerful events.

WORLD_SIGHT_DAY.about: World Sight Day falls on the second Thursday of October. Coordinated by the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness, it draws attention to blindness and visual impairment and to the eye care that could prevent much of it. In Nepal eye hospitals and the Nepal Netra Jyoti Sangh mark it with free eye camps and awareness rallies.

MATATI_CHARHE.about: Matati Charhe is the Newars' charhe of the month of Chaula, the fourteenth day of Baishakh's dark half, on the eve of Mata Tirtha Aunsi. The Newars mark the fourteenth of the dark half of every lunar month as a charhe, a day of worship at home, and name each after its month or its rite; Matati Charhe is the Chaula one.

SITHI_CHARHE.about: Sithi Charhe is the Newars' charhe of the month of Bachhala, the fourteenth day of Jestha's dark half, a week before Sithi Nakha. On this charhe Newar households worship Sithi, Kumar or Kartikeya, the son of Shiva and Parvati, together with other gods of the house, ahead of his festival.

GATHAMUGA_CHARHE.about: Gathamuga Charhe, the Newars' charhe of Dilla, is the fourteenth day of Shrawan's dark half, the day of Ghantakarna. In each neighbourhood boys build an effigy of the demon from reeds and collect money from passers-by; at dusk it is dragged through the streets and burned or thrown in the river, and iron rings or nails are fixed on doors to keep evil out.

GHANTAKARNA_CHATURDASHI.about: Ghantakarna Chaturdashi, the fourteenth day of Shrawan's dark half, recalls the killing of the demon Ghantakarna, who is told to have terrorised the people until a frog tricked him into a well. Effigies of the demon are made of reeds at crossroads, dragged away at dusk and burned, and iron nails are fixed on doors; the Newars keep it as Gathamuga Charhe.

JUGA_CHARHE.about: Juga Charhe is the Newars' charhe of the month of Gunla, the fourteenth of Bhadra's dark half, on the eve of Kushe Aunsi. The Newars mark the fourteenth of the dark half of every lunar month as a charhe, a day of worship at home, and name each after its month or its rite; Juga Charhe falls in Gunla, the holy month of Newar Buddhism.

NALASWANE_CHARHE.about: Nalaswane Charhe is the Newars' charhe of the month of Yanla, the fourteenth of Ashwin's dark half, two days before Nalaswane, as the Newars call Ghatasthapana. It falls in the fortnight of the ancestors, on the day of the chaturdashi shraddha, offered for those who died by weapons or by accident, and is marked with worship at home.

DISHI_CHARHE.about: Dishi Charhe is the Newars' charhe of the month of Thinla, the fourteenth day of Paush's dark half, on the eve of Gaya Aunsi. The Newars mark the fourteenth of the dark half of every lunar month as a charhe, a day of worship at home, and name each after its month or its rite; Dishi Charhe is the Thinla one.

SAMRAT_ASHOK_ASHTAMI.about: Samrat Ashok Ashtami, the eighth of Chaitra's bright half, honours Ashoka, the Maurya emperor of the third century BCE, who ruled from Pataliputra, present-day Patna, and after the war in Kalinga turned to Buddhism and to rule by dharma, proclaimed in his edicts on rocks and pillars. Bihar, which named the tithi as his birthday in 2015, has kept it since 2016.

CHHATH_KHARNA.about: Kharna, the second of Chhath's four days, falls on the fifth of Kartik's bright half, the day before the evening arghya. Those keeping Chhath fast through the day, then at dusk offer and eat kheer made with jaggery, with roti and fruit, shared afterwards as prasad. From that meal their fast without water runs until the morning arghya.

CHHATH_SECOND_DAY.about: The morning arghya, on the seventh of Kartik's bright half, closes Chhath. Before dawn the worshippers return to the rivers and ponds where they stood the evening before, and offer arghya to the rising Sun standing in the water, with their baskets of thekua, fruit and sugarcane. They then break their fast and share the prasad.

BIHAR_DIWAS.about: Bihar Diwas, 22 March, marks the separation of Bihar from the Bengal Presidency in 1912, when the province of Bihar and Orissa was created. The state keeps it as a holiday with cultural programmes, exhibitions and functions at Patna's Gandhi Maidan and in the districts, and Biharis abroad mark it too.

VEER_KUNWAR_SINGH_JAYANTI.about: Veer Kunwar Singh Jayanti, 23 April, honours Kunwar Singh, the elderly zamindar of Jagdishpur in Bhojpur who led the rising of 1857 in Bihar and fought the British across northern India. The date recalls his victory near Jagdishpur on 23 April 1858, three days before he died of his wounds; Bihar keeps it with tributes, especially at Jagdishpur and Arrah.

ANUGRAH_NARAYAN_SINHA_JAYANTI.about: Anugrah Narayan Sinha Jayanti, 18 June, is the birthday of Anugrah Narayan Sinha, born in 1887 in what is now Aurangabad district, a companion of Gandhi in the Champaran satyagraha of 1917 and, after independence, Bihar's first Deputy Chief Minister and Finance Minister, remembered as Bihar Vibhuti. Bihar honours him with tributes and meetings.

JAYAPRAKASH_NARAYAN_JAYANTI.about: Jayaprakash Narayan Jayanti, 11 October, is the birthday of Jayaprakash Narayan, born at Sitab Diara in 1902, the socialist leader of the Quit India movement who in 1974 led the Bihar movement for 'total revolution' against corruption and opposed the Emergency of 1975 to 1977. Known as Lok Nayak, he is honoured with tributes and meetings across Bihar.

SHRI_KRISHNA_SINHA_JAYANTI.about: Shri Krishna Sinha Jayanti, 21 October, is the birthday of Shri Krishna Sinha, born in 1887, the freedom fighter known as Bihar Kesari who was the first Chief Minister of Bihar, from 1946 until his death in 1961, and whose government abolished the zamindari system in the state. Bihar honours him with tributes and meetings.

RAJENDRA_PRASAD_JAYANTI.about: Dr Rajendra Prasad Jayanti, 3 December, is the birthday of Rajendra Prasad, born at Ziradei in Bihar's Siwan district in 1884, the lawyer and freedom fighter who presided over the Constituent Assembly and was the first President of India, from 1950 to 1962. Bihar honours him with tributes, and lawyers in India keep the day as Advocates' Day.

MAWLID.about: Mawlid, or Milad-un-Nabi, the twelfth of the Islamic month of Rabi al-Awwal, marks the birth of the Prophet Muhammad, kept on that date by Sunni Muslims, while many Shia keep the seventeenth. Gatherings recite the story of his birth and poems in his praise, mosques and streets are lit, processions are taken out, and food is given to the poor; some Muslims do not keep the day.

SIRUWA_PAVANI.about: Siruwa Pavani is the new-year festival of the Tharu and other communities of the eastern Terai, kept at the start of Baisakh. Elders bless the young by pouring cool water on their heads, people splash water and mud on one another in play, and families feast and visit. The Ministry of Home Affairs gives a holiday for it in Jhapa, Morang, Sunsari, Siraha and Saptari.

BHOTO_JATRA.about: Bhoto Jatra closes the long chariot festival of Rato Machhindranath, Patan's god of rain, at Jawalakhel, usually in May or June. Before the crowds, and in the presence of the head of state, an official holds up the god's jewelled vest, the bhoto, from each side of the chariot so that all may see it. The day is a holiday in the Kathmandu Valley.

GAI_PUJA.about: Gai Puja, the worship of the cow, is kept in Tihar as the goddess Lakshmi's own day for the cow. Cows are bathed, given a tika and garlands of marigold and fed the best of the house's food. The texts set the cows' worship and play on the first day of Kartik's bright half, with Govardhan Puja, while many households in the hills honour the cow on the morning of Lakshmi Puja.

GORU_PUJA.about: Goru Puja, the worship of the ox, falls on the first day of Kartik's bright half, the fourth day of Tihar, together with Govardhan Puja and Mha Puja. Oxen that plough the fields are given a rest from work, bathed and honoured with tika, garlands and good food, and a small hill of cow dung is worshipped as Govardhan.

PRAUSHTHAPADI_SHRADDHA.about: Praushthapadi Shraddha, on the full moon of Bhadra, opens the sixteen days of shraddha, the Sorha Shraddha, that run through Ashwin's dark half, the fortnight of the ancestors. It is offered in the afternoon for those who died on a full moon, and households begin the season of tarpana and pinda for their forebears.

KALARATRI.about: Kalaratri, the black night, is the night of Maha Ashtami in Dashain, named for the fierce form of the goddess. Through that night animals are sacrificed to Durga at the Kot courtyard of Hanuman Dhoka and at Taleju's and the other goddesses' temples, and many households keep worship late into the night.

SUKHRATRI.about: Sukhratri, the night of ease, is the night of Lakshmi Puja on the new moon of Kartik. After the evening puja the houses stay lit with lamps to welcome Lakshmi, and families stay up late; games of cards and dice, an old custom of the night, are played in homes across Nepal.

KIJA_PUJA.about: Kija Puja is the Newar name of Bhai Tika, the second day of Kartik's bright half; kija means younger brother. Sisters seat their brothers before mandalas, worship them for long life, give them a tika and a garland of makhamali flowers and serve them a feast with the auspicious sagan, and brothers give gifts in return.

AKASHDEEPADAN_ARAMBHA.about: Akashdeepadan, the gift of a lamp to the sky, begins with Kartik Snan on the full moon of Ashwin. Each evening through the month of Kartik a lamp is raised high on a bamboo pole or hung above the house, offered to Vishnu and held to light the way of the ancestors; the lamps are kept until the full moon of Kartik.

YAMADEEPADAN.about: Yamadeepadan, the gift of a lamp to Yama, is kept at dusk on Dhanteras, the thirteenth day of Kartik's dark half. A lamp is set outside the house facing south, the direction of Yama, the god of death, with a prayer that no untimely death come to the household; it opens the five days of lamps that run to Bhai Tika.

SORHA_SHRADDHA_SAMAPTI.about: The national panchanga closes the Sorha Shraddha, the sixteen days of shraddha, on the new moon of Ashwin, the day of Pitri Visarjan, when the ancestors are given leave. Shraddha is offered that day for all forebears, including those whose day of death is unknown, and crowds gather at Pashupati and other riverside tirthas for tarpana before Dashain begins.

CHHATH_NAHAY_KHAY.about: Nahay Khay, 'bathe and eat', is the first of Chhath's four days, the fourth of Kartik's bright half. Those who will keep the fast clean the house, bathe in a river or pond, and eat a single pure meal, cooked without onion or garlic, of rice, lentils and bottle gourd; the family eats after them.

BHAI_TIKA.about: Bhai Tika falls on the second tithi of the bright half of Kartik, the fifth and last day of Tihar. Sisters draw a mandala for each brother, ring him with a line of oil and water, and give him a seven-coloured tika and a garland of makhamali flowers for long life, recalling Yamuna's worship of her brother Yama. Brothers give gifts in return, and the sisters feed them.

GHATASTHAPANA.about: Ghatasthapana, the setting up of the sacred jar, falls on the first tithi of the bright half of Ashwin and opens Dashain's nine nights, the Navaratri. At an auspicious hour a kalash of water is set up in the house's puja room as the seat of Durga, and barley and maize are sown in sand around it to sprout as jamara, which is tended in the dark and given with the tika on the tenth day.

DEEPAMALIKA.about: Deepamalika, the row of lamps, is a name for the new-moon night of Kartik, the third day of Tihar, when Lakshmi, goddess of wealth, is worshipped.
